anchor: CDR's got the lead on this one, ground in support.
positive: During the emergency, the station commander directs the immediate response on board while mission control on Earth backs the crew up.

anchor: Bird's drifting east, E-W stationkeeping burn tonight.
positive: The satellite is drifting out of its assigned longitude box, so an east-west stationkeeping maneuver is scheduled tonight to push it back into place.

anchor: Screening's clean for the next seventy-two hours, no maneuver needed.
positive: Collision checks against all tracked objects show no risky close approaches for the next three days, so the satellite can stay on its current orbit.

anchor: Booster's on the droneship, good landing!
positive: The reusable first stage touched down successfully on the uncrewed landing barge at sea and can be recovered and flown again.

anchor: Fairing sep confirmed, spacecraft sep in two minutes.
positive: The protective nose shell around the satellite has split away on schedule, and the satellite itself will be released from the rocket in about two minutes.

anchor: Engine cutoff. Folks, you're clear to unstrap and float.
positive: The engine has shut down and the capsule is coasting in weightlessness, so passengers may release their seat restraints and move around the cabin.

subtopic: Mission control roles and voice loops
anchor: Flight control team's job, in brief?
positive: Running the mission from launch to landing: watching spacecraft systems, planning and executing maneuvers, troubleshooting anomalies, protecting crew and vehicle, and handling communications with the spacecraft.

anchor: do flight controllers have like set playbooks for emergencies or do they just wing it
positive: Mostly playbooks. Known contingencies like system failures, comm loss or medical emergencies have predefined procedures built from analysis, simulations and past missions, and the team drills them constantly.

subtopic: Mission control roles and voice loops
anchor: What does the flight director actually do in mission control?
positive: The flight director leads the flight control team, polls each discipline for status and holds final authority on real-time decisions about the vehicle and crew, within the flight rules.

subtopic: Mission control roles and voice loops
anchor: No change is sent to the crew until the flight director approves it on the flight loop.
positive: nothing goes up to the astronauts until the person running the room says okay

subtopic: Mission control roles and voice loops
anchor: voice loops
positive: Continuous audio channels in mission control, each dedicated to a team or function, that let controllers and crew talk in real time.

anchor: Program alarm. It's a twelve-oh-two.
positive: Apollo 11's lander computer reporting it was overloaded during powered descent; controllers judged the alarm safe and called 'we're go on that alarm' so the landing could continue.

anchor: flight rules
positive: Decisions agreed before a mission that spell out what the flight control team will do in specific failure or off-nominal situations, so critical calls aren't improvised under time pressure.

anchor: SRP's pushing us off nominal, plan a trim burn.
positive: Solar radiation pressure has nudged the spacecraft off its planned trajectory, so a small correction maneuver should be scheduled.

anchor: Rev C isn't validated, we fly Rev B.
positive: The newest revision of the procedure hasn't finished validation, so the crew should execute the previous approved version.

anchor: We're eating into margin, replan the timeline.
positive: Activities are using up more of the reserved time or resources than expected, so the schedule needs to be reworked.

anchor: Tethers swapped, translating aft along the truss.
positive: The spacewalker has moved their safety tether to a new anchor and is now hand-walking toward the rear of the station's truss structure.

anchor: PDAM is go, Progress thrusters in thirty.
positive: A pre-determined debris avoidance maneuver has been approved, and in thirty minutes the station will fire a docked Progress cargo ship's thrusters to move clear of debris.

anchor: Deorbit burn complete, entry interface in forty.
positive: The braking maneuver is finished and the spacecraft will reach the top of the atmosphere in about forty minutes.

anchor: Instructors are throwing a depress at us next run.
positive: In the upcoming simulator session, the training team will inject a cabin depressurization failure for the crew to work through.

anchor: Payload's running from the ground, hands off till sample swap.
positive: Researchers on Earth are operating the experiment remotely, so the crew shouldn't touch it until the scheduled sample exchange.

anchor: Smoke alarm in Node 3, grab a PFE.
positive: A smoke detector has triggered in one of the station's modules, so a crew member should get a portable fire extinguisher and respond.

anchor: Gloves are brutal, losing feeling in my fingertips.
positive: The stiff, pressurized suit gloves are squeezing the astronaut's hands so much that their fingertips are going numb, a common spacewalk complaint.

anchor: Surgeon wants a PMC with you after this pass.
positive: The flight surgeon has asked for a private medical conference, a confidential call with the crew member, at the next communication window.

anchor: New ding on window three, looks like an MMOD hit.
positive: A small fresh chip has appeared on one of the windows, probably from a micrometeoroid or tiny piece of orbital debris striking it.

anchor: SPE in progress, everybody to the shelter.
positive: A solar particle event is underway, so the crew should move into the most heavily shielded part of the spacecraft until radiation levels drop.

anchor: Main processor took an SEU, it's running on the backup string.
positive: A radiation-induced bit flip upset the primary computer, so the spacecraft has switched over to its redundant processor.

anchor: Kp's spiking, safe the payload.
positive: Geomagnetic activity is rising sharply, so the satellite's instruments should be put into a protective low-activity mode until the storm calms down.

anchor: all nine Merlins look good, stage one nominal
positive: Every one of the nine Merlin 1D engines on the Falcon 9 first stage is running as expected and the booster is performing normally.

anchor: SRB sep confirmed
positive: The solid rocket boosters have burned out and separated cleanly from the core stage, exactly as planned.

anchor: MECO... stage sep... MVac ignition
positive: The first-stage main engines have cut off, the two stages have separated, and the second stage's vacuum-optimized Merlin engine has lit.

anchor: LOX inlet pressure trending low on engine two
positive: The oxidizer pressure arriving at engine 2's pump is falling below expected, which could lead to cavitation if it keeps dropping.

anchor: HPFTP spin-up looks clean
positive: The high-pressure fuel turbopump accelerated normally during engine start, with nothing abnormal seen.

anchor: cat bed heaters on, RCS should be warm in twenty
positive: The heaters on the hydrazine thrusters' catalyst beds have been switched on, and the reaction control system should be up to firing temperature in about twenty minutes.

anchor: main engine burn complete, delta-v right on the money
positive: The spacecraft's bipropellant main engine has finished its planned maneuver and delivered almost exactly the velocity change that was targeted.

anchor: pad's clear, go for hypergol load
positive: All personnel are out of the hazard area, so the team is cleared to start remotely loading the toxic hypergolic propellants.

anchor: back in the thrust arc after safe mode recovery
positive: The spacecraft has recovered from a safe mode and resumed its long, continuous ion-engine thrusting segment along the planned trajectory.

anchor: grid short on thruster two, try a clearing pulse
positive: A conductive flake is likely bridging the screen and accelerator grids on thruster 2, so operators will send a high-current pulse to vaporize it and clear the short.

anchor: MR drifting rich, PU valve correcting
positive: The mixture ratio is shifting toward too much fuel, and the propellant utilization valve is adjusting the flow to bring it back on target.

anchor: Hydrogen leak at the tail service mast QD, we're over the limit.
positive: Liquid hydrogen is escaping at the quick-disconnect fitting where the fuel line joins the rocket, and the concentration exceeds the allowed limit, so loading has to stop.

anchor: kero load complete, LOX topping continues
positive: The RP-1 fuel tank is full; liquid oxygen is still being added to replace what boils off until just before launch.

anchor: range says the ground cloud is drifting toward the beach
positive: The exhaust cloud left at the pad after launch is being carried by wind toward the shoreline, so the safety team may need to warn people in that area.

anchor: helium reg holding tank press steady, no step-down
positive: The regulator supplying helium is keeping propellant tank pressure constant, with no unexpected drop seen.

anchor: we're into the propellant reserve, scrub the optional trims
positive: The spacecraft has started using the propellant set aside for emergencies, so all nonessential correction burns are canceled.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: A globally distributed ground station network hands a satellite's link from one station to the next, maintaining contact through most of its orbit.
positive: stations all over the world pass the satellite along like a relay so somebody's always got it

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: LOS in two, wrap up the command load.
positive: Loss of signal is two minutes away as the satellite drops below the horizon, so any remaining commands need to be sent before contact ends.

anchor: umbilicals retracted, swing arm clear
positive: The ground connections supplying power, data and propellant have pulled away from the vehicle and the access arm has swung safely out of the way.

subtopic: Mission control roles and voice loops
anchor: do control centers talk to the astronauts directly or is it all just computers
positive: Both. Software and automation handle much of the monitoring, but human flight controllers make the decisions, solve problems and talk directly with the crew.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: who talks to spacecraft that are way past the moon
positive: NASA's Deep Space Network: big dish antennas near Goldstone in California, Madrid in Spain and Canberra in Australia, spaced around the globe so at least one can always see a distant probe.

subtopic: Mission control roles and voice loops
anchor: FCR (Flight Control Room)
positive: The main operations room in Houston's mission control, where front-room flight controllers sit at consoles under the Flight Director.

anchor: Flight, GNC, we're go for the burn
positive: The guidance, navigation and control officer is telling the flight director that, from their discipline, everything is ready for the planned engine burn.

anchor: Range radar has skin track on the second stage.
positive: The tracking radar is following the upper stage by its reflected echo alone, without relying on a transponder aboard the vehicle.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: dish is stowed for winds, no tracks tonight
positive: The antenna has been parked in its safe position because of high winds, so all of tonight's tracking passes are canceled.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Lost the link, rover's dropped into safe mode.
positive: Communication with the rover was interrupted and it automatically stopped normal activities, holding a protective state that keeps power and temperature safe until controllers reconnect.

anchor: Wing's latched at full extension, current coming up.
positive: The solar array has unfolded completely and locked in place, and the power it produces is rising as expected.

anchor: Sep confirmed, both breakwires open.
positive: Separation is confirmed: the wires running across the interface have broken, proving the two pieces physically came apart.

anchor: Arm's in position, ready for capture on your go.
positive: The robotic arm is lined up with the arriving vehicle's grapple fixture, and the operator is waiting for permission to grab it.

anchor: Latch valve closed, thruster branch B isolated.
positive: The valve that feeds propellant to the second group of thrusters has been shut, so that branch can no longer leak or fire.

anchor: approaching peak heating, expect blackout shortly
positive: The capsule is nearing its point of maximum aerodynamic heating, and the plasma sheath around it will soon block radio contact for a few minutes.

anchor: Contact light. Engine stop.
positive: A probe under the lander's footpad has touched the surface, so the crew is shutting down the descent engine to complete the touchdown.

anchor: Sixty seconds.
positive: Mission control is telling the landing crew they have about a minute of descent propellant left before hitting the land-or-abort limit.

anchor: touchdown, struts stroked normal, vehicle's level
positive: The lander is on the ground, its leg shock absorbers compressed by the expected amount, and it is sitting upright without a dangerous tilt.

anchor: shield thermocouples tracking prediction through peak
positive: Temperature sensors embedded in the heat shield are reading close to the model predictions as the vehicle passes through maximum heating.

anchor: hazard map complete, diverting to alternate site
positive: The onboard sensors have finished scanning the terrain below, and the lander is steering toward a backup landing spot judged free of rocks and steep slopes.

anchor: bags inflated, first bounce confirmed
positive: The lander's cushioning airbags have puffed up around it, and it has hit the ground and started bouncing across the surface before coming to rest.

anchor: E plus two-forty, chute deploy on time
positive: Four minutes after entry interface the parachute deployed exactly when the planned sequence called for it.

anchor: heatshield sep confirmed, radar acquiring ground
positive: The heat shield has been jettisoned and the landing radar is beginning to lock onto the surface to measure altitude and descent rate.

anchor: seven minutes of terror, why do ppl call the mars landing that
positive: Entry, descent and landing on Mars takes roughly seven minutes and runs entirely autonomously. Because the one-way radio delay is typically longer than that, by the time the team hears entry has begun, the lander is usually already down.

anchor: tango delta nominal
positive: Touchdown happened as planned; tango delta is phonetic shorthand for TD, meaning touchdown.

anchor: drogues out, mains reefed
positive: The small stabilizing drogue parachutes have deployed and the main parachutes are partly open, deliberately restricted so they inflate gradually and limit opening shock.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: we're single-string on the transmitter now
positive: The redundant transmitter is gone, so the spacecraft is running on one unit with no backup and any further failure would cut the link.

anchor: ammonia in the cabin, crew to the Russian segment, close the hatch
positive: Toxic coolant may be leaking into the station's air, so everyone retreats to the Russian side and seals it off from the contaminated US modules until the atmosphere is checked.

anchor: TCM-2 is go, about a meter per second
positive: The second trajectory correction maneuver is approved, a tiny engine firing of roughly one meter per second to fine-tune the path toward the target planet.

anchor: closest approach in ten, flyby altitude on the money
positive: The spacecraft reaches its nearest point to the planet for the gravity assist in ten minutes, and the predicted flyby altitude matches the plan exactly.

anchor: new OD's in, uplinking updated ephemeris
positive: A fresh orbit determination solution has refined the spacecraft's position and velocity estimate, and the new predicted trajectory is being sent up to the vehicle.

anchor: Pc's over threshold, start planning a DAM
positive: The probability of collision with a tracked object now exceeds the action limit, so the team should begin planning a debris avoidance maneuver.

anchor: Tower cleared, pitch and roll underway.
positive: The rocket has risen past the launch tower and started its programmed turn and tilt onto the planned flight path toward orbit.

anchor: rollout complete, vehicle hard-down on the pad
positive: The rocket has finished its move from the assembly building to the launch pad and is now firmly secured in place.

anchor: if sumthing goes wrong in the countdown do they gotta restart from zero??
positive: Not necessarily. Minor problems are handled by holding the clock and fixing them, bigger ones may trigger a recycle back to an earlier safe point, and if the window closes the launch is scrubbed for another day.

anchor: I've heard the term built-in hold many times; what does it really mean?
positive: A planned pause written into the countdown at a fixed point, such as T-minus 4 hours, where the clock stops so teams can review status, catch up on late tasks and confirm readiness without time pressure.

anchor: they'll call it off if the rocket looks sick, the weather's bad or the range isn't clear
positive: Abort criteria monitored continuously during the countdown include vehicle health parameters, weather limits and range safety status.

anchor: countdown recycle
positive: Resetting the countdown to an earlier point in the sequence after a problem, so the steps from there can be repeated without starting over from the beginning.

anchor: Calling a hold at T-minus thirty-one seconds, ground pressure dropout.
positive: A ground-system pressure reading dropped out late in the countdown, so the launch team is stopping the clock until the problem is understood.

anchor: terminal count, autosequence has control
positive: The countdown has entered its final minutes, and the automated sequencer is now running the launch steps instead of manual ground commands.

anchor: window's instantaneous today, any slip and we scrub
positive: There is only a single moment when the rocket can launch to reach its target orbit, so if the countdown is delayed at all the launch must be called off for the day.

anchor: last-minute anomaly in pre-launch checks, then what?
positive: The team diagnoses it from telemetry and inspection, reports to the launch director, and engineering decides whether it can be fixed quickly, needs a delay or forces a scrub.

anchor: SimSup just threw us a hydraulics failure
positive: The simulation supervisor, who scripts the training scenario, has introduced a simulated hydraulic system failure for the team to work through.

anchor: pad is clear, all personnel accounted for
positive: Everyone has left the launch pad hazard area and every worker has been confirmed safe, so hazardous operations like propellant loading can begin.

anchor: Launch rules include minimum temperature limits, partly because cold stiffens seals; the 1986 Challenger accident was traced to O-rings that lost resilience in freezing weather.
positive: too cold on the pad and it's a no-go, frozen o-rings are what brought down challenger

anchor: red on upper-level winds, we're no-go for now
positive: Measured winds high in the atmosphere exceed the vehicle's limits, so the launch cannot proceed until they ease.

anchor: tracker's sun-blinded, we're propagating on gyros
positive: Sunlight in the star tracker's field of view is preventing it from seeing stars, so the spacecraft's orientation is being estimated from gyroscope data alone until the tracker recovers.

anchor: wheel three tach is noisy, power it down and fly on the other three
positive: One reaction wheel's speed sensor is giving erratic readings, so the team will switch that wheel off and control attitude with the remaining three.

anchor: CMG two is offline, holding attitude on the remaining three
positive: The station has lost a control moment gyroscope, but the remaining three still have enough capacity to keep it correctly oriented.

anchor: slew to science attitude complete, settling
positive: The spacecraft has finished turning toward its observation target and is waiting for leftover motion to damp out before the instruments start collecting data.

anchor: Torquers are dumping wheel momentum this pass.
positive: The magnetic coils are pushing against Earth's field to bleed off stored momentum from the reaction wheels so they don't saturate.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Pass is short, compress the hyperspectral cube before downlink.
positive: There isn't much ground station contact time, so the large multi-band image dataset should be compressed onboard before it is sent down.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: AOS Svalbard, X-band locked, starting the science dump.
positive: The Svalbard ground station has acquired the spacecraft's signal, the X-band receiver is locked, and stored science data is now being downlinked.

anchor: Arrays feathered for the docking, we're on batteries.
positive: The solar wings have been turned edge-on to the approaching vehicle to protect them during docking, so the spacecraft is temporarily running from stored battery power.

anchor: Eclipse entry in two, batteries take the bus.
positive: In two minutes the spacecraft enters Earth's shadow, and the batteries will start supplying the main power bus instead of the solar arrays.

anchor: SSPC tripped on the heater line, leave it open till we troubleshoot.
positive: The electronic breaker feeding a heater circuit cut power due to overcurrent, and the team wants it kept off until they find the cause.

anchor: RTG's down a couple more watts, shed that heater.
positive: Output from the radioisotope generator keeps declining with age, so a heater load is being turned off to stay within available power.

anchor: Loop B pump tripped, we're carrying the heat load on Loop A.
positive: Pump B on the external cooling loops has shut down, so loop A is now carrying all the heat rejection by itself.

anchor: Survival heaters kicked on, prop lines were getting cold.
positive: Thermostat-controlled heaters that protect hardware at minimum safe temperatures have activated because the propellant lines dropped toward their lower limit.

anchor: Backshell temps running warm but inside limits.
positive: The protective cover on the back of the entry capsule is heating up more than predicted, though it is still within its allowed temperature range.

anchor: Boil-off's running higher than predicted, vent valve's cycling a lot.
positive: Cryogenic propellant is warming and evaporating faster than modelled, so the tank's relief vent is opening more often to release pressure.

anchor: New flight software image is staged, swapping boot banks next pass.
positive: An updated software load has been uploaded to the spare memory bank, and the computer will restart from that bank during the next ground contact.

anchor: SCE to Aux.
positive: Famous Apollo 12 call after the lightning strike: switch the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary power setting, which restored the garbled telemetry on the controllers' screens.

anchor: Bus A's throwing no-response errors, switching to Bus B.
positive: Devices on the primary 1553 bus aren't answering, so traffic is being moved to the redundant second bus.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Uplink's rejecting everything, auth counter's out of sync.
positive: The spacecraft is refusing commands because the anti-replay sequence counter used in command authentication no longer matches the ground's value.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: HGA's off-point, dropping to the LGA.
positive: The high-gain antenna isn't aimed at Earth, so communication is switching to the low-gain antenna, which is wide-beam but supports only low data rates.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Transponder's coherent, we've got two-way Doppler.
positive: The spacecraft's downlink is phase-locked to the ground's uplink, so the ground can measure the spacecraft's velocity very precisely from the frequency shift.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Uplink's getting stomped, looks like terrestrial interference.
positive: Something on the ground is transmitting on or near the uplink frequency and is degrading the signal reaching the satellite.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Carrier lock, still waiting on symbol lock.
positive: The receiver is tracking the radio carrier but hasn't yet synchronised to the data symbol timing, so no telemetry is decoded yet.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Handing over to TDRS West in thirty.
positive: In thirty seconds the spacecraft's communications will switch from the current relay satellite to the western one as its coverage takes over.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Frames are failing CRC, request a playback on the next pass.
positive: Some received telemetry frames are corrupted, so the team wants the spacecraft to resend that recorded data during the next contact.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: Reflected power's spiking, VSWR alarm on the TWTA.
positive: A lot of the amplifier's output is bouncing back from the antenna path, triggering a mismatch alarm on the travelling-wave tube amplifier.

subtopic: Ground station passes and comm link
anchor: One-way light time's twenty-two minutes, so we sit tight.
positive: A signal takes twenty-two minutes to reach the spacecraft, so the team must wait well over forty minutes to see any response to a command.

anchor: Bravo
positive: Spoken word for B. A bare "bee" collapses into dee, pee, tee and vee over a noisy channel, while BRAH-voh has no rhyme anywhere else in the alphabet.

anchor: Delta
positive: Letter D, said DELL-tah. Also the radio callsign of Delta Air Lines, so listeners rely on position in the message to tell the airline from the letter.

anchor: Echo
positive: Stands for E. A lone "ee" is the vowel most easily lost under static, so ECK-oh gives it a hard consonant to hang on.

anchor: fox trot
positive: Two-word rendering of Foxtrot, the letter F. The ICAO list writes it as one word, but speech recognizers and hurried typists often split it.

anchor: Golf
positive: The word for G. Its hard G and closing F keep it apart from "gee", which blurs with jay, dee and zee, and the sport is known almost everywhere.

anchor: Hotel
positive: H in phonetic spelling. ICAO stresses the second syllable, hoh-TELL, and the word is already borrowed into nearly every language on earth.

anchor: India
positive: Letter I, pronounced IN-dee-ah. Replaced "Item" from the wartime alphabet when the international version came in during the 1950s.

anchor: kilo
positive: K on the radio. KEY-loh doubles as the metric prefix everybody already knows, one reason it tested well across languages.

anchor: Lima
positive: Spoken L. Operators say LEE-mah like the Peruvian capital, never LIE-ma like the bean.

anchor: Mike
positive: Letter M, said MIKE. Its long vowel and hard K keep it from blurring into November, which handles N.

anchor: Which letter-words in the alphabet have just one syllable?
positive: Only Golf and Mike. Every other word has two or three syllables, which builds in redundancy: if part of the word is clipped, the rest can still identify it.

anchor: November
positive: N. Three syllables, no-VEM-ber, keep it well clear of Mike. In the US you hear it constantly because every American civil registration starts with N.

anchor: Papa
positive: Letter P. ICAO guidance puts the stress on the second syllable (pah-PAH), though most English speakers stress the first and are still understood.

anchor: Sierra
positive: S, said see-AIR-rah. A plain "ess" dissolves into hiss and static and can be mistaken for F, so the alphabet gives it three full syllables.

anchor: Tango
positive: Letter T, TANG-go. Took over from the WWII word "Tare" and has almost nothing in the list it could be confused with.

anchor: uniform
positive: U. ICAO accepts both YOU-nee-form and OO-nee-form, so speakers of different native languages can use the vowel that comes naturally.

anchor: Victor
positive: V, VIK-tah. One of four words (with Charlie, Mike and X-ray) carried over unchanged from the WWII Able-Baker alphabet into the 1956 version.

anchor: Yankee
positive: Letter Y. Replaced "Yoke" from the wartime alphabet and is written Yankee in every official list.

anchor: Zulu
positive: Z, said ZOO-loo. Two clear syllables with no rhyme in the list; it replaced Zebra from the wartime alphabet.

anchor: Which letter-words are names or places rather than ordinary words?
positive: Charlie, Juliett, Mike, Oscar, Romeo and Victor are personal names; India, Lima and Quebec are places; Hotel, Golf and Tango are everyday words. The mix was tested so each is familiar to English, French and Spanish speakers.

anchor: sierra tango ah alpha romeo
positive: STAR, spelled out letter by letter: S, T, A, R.

anchor: Why does ICAO spell it Alfa instead of Alpha?
positive: Many speakers don't read "ph" as an F sound, so Alpha could come out as "al-pa". Alfa is spelled the way it's pronounced in most European languages.

anchor: Why does Juliett have two t's?
positive: The doubled T tells French speakers not to treat the final T as silent; written "Juliet", it could be read as "Julie-ay".

anchor: Alpha
positive: Everyday, non-ICAO spelling of the A letter-word. Common in US military writing and pop culture; spoken aloud it is identical to the official Alfa.

anchor: Whisky
positive: W. ICAO lists it as Whiskey, while some publications print Whisky. Both are pronounced WISS-key and mean the same letter.

anchor: Is Charlie supposed to be said "char-lee" or "shar-lee"?
positive: ICAO lists both CHAR-lee and SHAR-lee as acceptable, the second for French speakers. Either is understood as C.

anchor: how do you say quebec on the radio
positive: keh-BECK, with a K sound at the start rather than "kwuh-BECK". The ICAO respelling keeps the French place name but makes the first syllable explicit.

anchor: Juliett
positive: J. Spelled with a double T in the ICAO list and pronounced JEW-lee-ETT, with the stress on the last syllable.

anchor: Why does the ICAO respelling of Oscar end in "cah"?
positive: The pronunciation guide was written with non-rhotic English in mind, so OSS-cah signals a soft final R. Pronouncing the R is still perfectly fine.

anchor: niner
positive: ICAO pronunciation of 9 (NIN-er). The extra syllable separates it from five and from the German "nein", meaning no.

anchor: tree
positive: How 3 is said in ICAO radiotelephony. Many speakers can't produce the "th" in three, and "tree" stays unmistakable even when they can.

anchor: fife
positive: The digit 5 as spoken on aviation and military radio. The F ending keeps it apart from nine, which sounds very similar on a weak signal.

anchor: tousand
positive: ICAO pronunciation of thousand (TOU-SAND), again dropping the "th". Heard in altitudes such as "one zero tousand".

anchor: why do pilots say fower
positive: ICAO respells 4 as FOW-er to stretch it into two syllables, making it harder to confuse with "for", a word that shows up constantly in radio messages.

anchor: Do pilots really say "tree" and "fife", or just three and five?
positive: Practice varies. Military and many international crews follow the ICAO forms closely; many US civil pilots say "three" and "five" normally but still use "niner". The ICAO forms remain the standard.

anchor: Why say zero instead of "oh"?
positive: "Oh" can be mistaken for the letter O and is easily swallowed by noise. The standard is ZE-RO, so a heading is "two zero five", not "two oh five".

anchor: tree fife niner
positive: 359, read with ICAO digit pronunciation (three, five, nine).

anchor: When do you say "hundred" or "thousand" instead of each digit?
positive: For round altitudes, heights and visibilities: 2,500 feet becomes "two tousand fife hundred". Headings, codes and frequencies are still read one digit at a time.
Spoken "one zero tousand" in ICAO style, or "ten thousand" in casual US practice: an altitude in feet.

anchor: wun too tree fower
positive: 1234, written phonetically the way the ICAO guide spells out the pronunciation of one, two, three, four.

anchor: Why can't you just say letters normally over the radio?
positive: Spoken letter names are single short syllables, and a burst of static or a clipped mic can erase the one sound that tells them apart. A whole word per letter gives the listener several syllables to recover from.

anchor: What makes a good spelling-alphabet word?
positive: Recognizable to speakers of many languages, impossible to mistake for another letter-word, easy to pronounce without tricky sounds, and still identifiable when clipped or distorted.

anchor: Is the phonetic alphabet only a military thing?
positive: No. Airline pilots, air traffic control, ships, amateur radio and call centres all use it. Some US police agencies still keep their own older APCO alphabet (Adam, Boy, Charles).

anchor: Does it help on ordinary phone calls?
positive: Yes. Phone audio cuts off the high frequencies that separate S from F or B from D, which is why reservation agents read booking codes using the same letter-words.

anchor: Confirm the last letter, Bravo or Delta?
positive: Listener caught a "b" or "d" sound but not which, and resolves it in one step by offering the two letter-words to choose from.

anchor: Unreadable, spell your callsign phonetically
positive: I can't make out what you said; spell your call sign with the letter-words.

anchor: is the phonetic alphabet the same in every country
positive: The ICAO/NATO version is the worldwide standard for aviation, maritime and military radio. Some countries keep national alphabets for domestic phone use, such as Germany's name-based one (Anton, Berta, Cäsar).

anchor: spelling alphabet
positive: General name for any set of code words standing for letters. Radio people call the ICAO version "the phonetic alphabet", though linguists note it spells letters rather than transcribing sounds the way the IPA does.

anchor: When was the NATO phonetic alphabet adopted?
positive: The current version took effect for ICAO civil aviation on 1 March 1956, and NATO adopted it the same year. A 1951 draft had several different words.

anchor: Able Baker alphabet
positive: Joint US/UK spelling alphabet of WWII and the early 1950s: Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog, Easy, Fox, George and so on. Built for English speakers, it was retired when ICAO's international version arrived.

anchor: why does roger mean received
positive: In the older Able-Baker alphabet R was "Roger". Operators acknowledged with R for received, said aloud as Roger, and the habit outlived the alphabet.

anchor: Who did the linguistic testing for the ICAO alphabet?
positive: Linguist Jean-Paul Vinay of the Université de Montréal led much of the work, testing candidate words with speakers of English, French and Spanish for recognizability.

anchor: What words from the 1951 draft were dropped?
positive: The 1951 version used Coca, Metro, Nectar, Union and Extra. After complaints from users, they were replaced by Charlie, Mike, November, Uniform and X-ray in 1956.

anchor: Dog
positive: Letter D in the WWII Able-Baker alphabet, replaced by Delta. It survives in unit histories such as "Dog Company" and "Easy Company" from that era.

anchor: Did the RAF have its own alphabet before WWII?
positive: Yes. British forces used several, including an RAF alphabet beginning Ace, Beer, Charlie, Don. Each service tended to have its own until joint wartime operations pushed standardization.

anchor: Where does "ack-ack" for anti-aircraft fire come from?
positive: British WWI signallers said "Ack" for A, so AA (anti-aircraft) became ack-ack. The slang outlasted the alphabet by decades.

anchor: Ack Emma
positive: Old British signalese for A.M., from the WWI-era words Ack (A) and Emma (M). "Pip Emma" was P.M.

anchor: Which letters get confused most often over a radio?

anchor: Why are fifteen and fifty risky in a speed or altitude instruction?

positive: It joins the callsign to an add-on: /P portable, /M mobile, /MM maritime mobile, or a country prefix when operating abroad. Hams say "stroke" or "slash" aloud.

anchor: you're five nine here in ohio
positive: Ham signal report: readability 5 of 5 (perfectly readable) and strength 9 of 9 (very strong), the classic good report on the RS scale.

anchor: Sorry, could you give me your call sign again, slowly, using the phonetic words?
positive: Please repeat your call, phonetically, slow speed.

anchor: skey bravo two lima uniform
positive: WB2LU, an older-style US amateur callsign from the 2 call area (New York and New Jersey).

anchor: Alfa flag
positive: International code flag A: "I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed."

anchor: Oscar flag
positive: Code flag O, meaning man overboard. Many crews call the recovery drill an "Oscar" drill as well.

anchor: Blue Peter
positive: Nickname for code flag P (Papa) when flown in harbour: everyone should report aboard, because the vessel is about to sail.

anchor: Whiskey Delta Charlie fower fife six seven
positive: WDC4567, the format of a US ship station call sign.

anchor: Bridge, lookout, vessel fine on the starboard bow flying Alfa.
positive: Lookout reports a boat ahead and slightly to the right showing code flag A: divers are down, so pass wide and slow.

anchor: mmsi tree six six niner niner niner eight seven six
positive: MMSI 366999876, a nine-digit maritime identity; 366 is one of the US country codes.

anchor: Is the signal flag alphabet the same as the spoken one?
positive: Yes. The International Code of Signals uses the same letter-words, and many single flags carry their own meaning: flying Kilo says "I wish to communicate with you."

anchor: my vessel name is ocean pearl spelled oscar charlie echo alfa november papa echo alfa romeo lima
positive: Skipper spells the boat's name, OCEAN PEARL, so the coast station logs it correctly.

anchor: Is that S as in Sam or F as in Frank?
positive: Confirm, was that Sierra or Foxtrot?

anchor: your code is uh f as in foxtrot s as in sierra b as in bravo nine two
positive: A call-centre agent reading confirmation code FSB92, pairing each letter with its letter-word because phone audio blurs F and S.

anchor: Break, all stations, use phonetics for all callsigns, interference heavy.
positive: Net control tells every station to spell callsigns with letter-words because heavy interference is garbling plain letters.

anchor: Lost one vehicle, rest of the convoy is Charlie Mike.
positive: One vehicle is out of action, but the convoy is pressing on with its mission rather than stopping.

anchor: my nav set is tango uniform using map and compass
positive: The navigation device has died, so the speaker is falling back on a paper map and compass.

positive: That brief was a complete Charlie Foxtrot.

positive: Lead praising wingman Two for excellent flying, in slang that never appears in a formal debrief.

anchor: We'll be at your location in about ten minutes.
positive: Inbound your position, ten mikes out.

anchor: Tanker on our port beam flying Bravo, give her a wide berth.
positive: Officer of the watch notes a tanker off the left side showing flag B (dangerous cargo) and orders extra clearance.

anchor: Port control, yacht Sea Wren inbound flying Quebec, request free pratique.
positive: A yacht arriving from abroad declares itself healthy and asks permission to enter port without quarantine restrictions.

anchor: request six actual on the net
positive: Asking for the commander personally to come to the radio, rather than an operator speaking on their behalf.

anchor: Contact radar one two seven decimal fife fife.
positive: Call the radar controller next on 127.55 MHz.

anchor: romeo oscar golf echo romeo
positive: ROGER spelled out. Since 1956 the R letter-word is Romeo, and Roger survives only as the word for "received".

anchor: helm come right steer two one zero
positive: Ship's officer orders the helmsman to turn right onto course 210, south-southwest.

anchor: We're going to head down to about eight thousand feet now.
positive: Descending to eight tousand feet.

anchor: eta one seven fower zero zulu
positive: We expect to arrive at 17:40 UTC.

anchor: Pickup grid tree eight fower seven one two, read back.
positive: Speaker passes a six-digit grid, 384712, for the pickup location and wants it repeated to confirm the copy.

anchor: tower cessna fower kilo papa downwind with information golf
positive: Pilot of a Cessna ending in 4KP reports on the downwind leg of the traffic pattern and confirms having ATIS Golf.

anchor: Code is tree fower fife niner.
positive: The code you need is 3459.

anchor: next of kin last name is uh zhang zulu hotel alfa november golf
positive: Speaker passes the surname Zhang and spells it so it isn't recorded as Chang or Jang.

anchor: Could you look up confirmation P4ZK9 for me?
positive: Request check on confirmation Papa fower Zulu Kilo niner.

anchor: Please switch your transponder to standby until we're ready for you.
positive: Squawk standby.

anchor: was that one one or one seven tousand
positive: Pilot isn't sure whether the cleared altitude was 11,000 or 17,000 feet and asks before climbing.

anchor: i spell bravo uniform tango tango echo romeo uh butter
positive: Speaker spells BUTTER, then says the word itself, the usual spell-then-confirm pattern.

anchor: skyhawk niner tree two whiskey kilo ready runway one niner
positive: A Cessna Skyhawk with registration ending 932WK reports ready for departure on runway 19.

anchor: WILCO
positive: Contraction of 'will comply'. In aviation it answers an instruction, but it never replaces a required readback: a hold-short, altitude or heading clearance still has to be read back in full.

anchor: whats the actual difference between roger and wilco
positive: Roger confirms only that a transmission was received; it promises nothing. Wilco adds that you understood and will comply, so answering an instruction with roger alone has not agreed to anything.

anchor: rodger wilco left heading two seven zero cactus twelve oh two
positive: Cactus 1202 acknowledges and will turn left to heading 270. The doubled 'roger wilco' is common but redundant; the heading readback is what actually matters.

anchor: No, that's wrong, you're supposed to stay at eight thousand, not climb.
positive: Jetstar four one, negative, maintain eight thousand.

anchor: Unable
positive: Tells the other station you cannot comply with an instruction, clearance or request, ideally followed by a reason such as 'unable, weather ahead' or 'unable, performance'.

anchor: Denver Center, United seven forty, unable flight level three seven zero due weight, request three three zero.
positive: Too heavy to climb efficiently to FL370, the United crew turns down that level and asks for 33,000 feet instead.

anchor: negative we did not receive the frequency change say again frequency
positive: No, we never got the new frequency; could you repeat just the frequency for us?

anchor: uh affirmative clearance were ready to copy
positive: Yes to the clearance delivery controller: pen and paper are out, so the pilot is prepared to write down the IFR clearance as it is read.

anchor: Is 'ten-four' ever used by pilots talking to ATC?
positive: Not in standard phraseology. Ten-four comes from police and CB ten-codes; ICAO and FAA radio work uses roger, wilco or a full readback instead.

anchor: Why do instructors tell students never to answer a controller with just 'OK'?
positive: OK carries no fixed meaning: heard, agreed or ready could all be intended, so the controller can't tell what was actually accepted. A readback or a defined word such as wilco leaves no doubt.

anchor: united niner zero disregard that was for united niner niner zero
positive: United 90, ignore my last call; it was meant for United 990, a flight with a similar number.

anchor: Correction
positive: Flags an error in the current transmission, with the right version following straight after, as in 'descend four thousand, correction, five thousand'.

anchor: climb flight level two four zero correction two six zero
positive: Controller misspoke and fixed it in the same breath: the assigned level is FL260, and only the value after 'correction' counts.

anchor: Break
positive: ICAO separator between portions of a message. Doubled, 'break break' separates messages to different aircraft on a very busy frequency, unlike the military net, where break break is an urgent interruption.

anchor: Southwest two twelve, turn right heading zero niner zero, break, Delta eight fifty, descend and maintain one zero thousand.
positive: Two aircraft get instructions in one transmission; the break marks that the descent belongs to Delta 850, not Southwest 212.

anchor: you were blocked by another station say again your request
positive: Someone else transmitted on top of you, so I missed it; please repeat what you asked for.

anchor: say agin all after cleared to
positive: Request to repeat only the part of the message that followed the words 'cleared to'; everything before it was received fine.

anchor: Words twice
positive: ICAO request or notice that reception is poor, so each word or group should be transmitted twice. Used with heavy static or very weak signals.

anchor: Wait a moment, I need to check something before I answer, I'll call you back.
positive: Lufthansa four two zero, stand by.

anchor: How is 'monitor' different from 'contact' when a controller hands you to a new frequency?
positive: Contact means switch and check in with your call sign. Monitor means switch and only listen; the next controller will call you when needed.

anchor: Which ATC instructions must always be read back under ICAO rules?
positive: Route clearances; runway instructions to enter, land on, take off from, hold short of, cross or backtrack; runway in use; altimeter settings; SSR codes; level, heading and speed instructions; and transition levels.

anchor: why isnt roger good enough for a hold short instruction
positive: Hold-short instructions require a full readback including the runway designator, so the controller can hear that it was understood. A bare acknowledgement proves only that something was heard.

anchor: Readback correct.
positive: Controller confirms the pilot repeated the clearance exactly as issued; no corrections are needed.

anchor: November five two Foxtrot Tango, negative, maintain six thousand, I say again, six thousand.
positive: A wrong readback has been caught. The pilot repeated a different altitude, and the controller insists on 6,000 feet, repeating the value for emphasis.

anchor: Hearback
positive: Controller's half of the readback loop: actively listening to the pilot's repetition to catch errors. Readback without an attentive hearback is a common link in miscommunication chains.

anchor: cleared to boston as filed climb maintain five thousand expect one zero thousand ten minutes after departure departure frequency one two four point four squawk four two five one
positive: You may fly to Boston on your filed route; climb to 5,000 feet, plan on 10,000 ten minutes after takeoff, call departure on 124.4 and set transponder code 4251.

anchor: CRAFT, the acronym instructors teach for IFR clearances, stands for what?
positive: The order of an IFR clearance: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder code. Writing it down in that order makes the readback come out complete.

anchor: descend flight level one two zero qnh one zero one tree ryanair seven alfa bravo
positive: Ryanair 7AB reads back a descent to FL120 and the QNH of 1013 hPa, ending with its call sign in the ICAO style.

anchor: Where should the call sign go when a pilot reads back an instruction?
positive: ICAO procedures say the readback is terminated with the aircraft's call sign. That tells the controller which aircraft accepted the instruction, especially when similar calls are on frequency.

anchor: Did I hear you right that I'm allowed to cross runway two-two left?
positive: Ground, Skyhawk six one Bravo, confirm cleared to cross runway two two left.

anchor: What should a pilot say on first contact with a new controller?
positive: Who you are calling, who you are, where you are and what you want, often with the ATIS letter: 'Ann Arbor Ground, Cessna three four five Charlie Papa, north ramp, VFR to Jackson with Kilo.'

anchor: chicago center jetblue six two two er with you flight level three five zero
positive: Fresh off a frequency change, JetBlue 622 checks in with Chicago Center and reports level at FL350.

anchor: Abbreviated call sign
positive: Shortened identification such as 'Cessna five Charlie Papa' for N345CP. Pilots may use it only after the controller has abbreviated first, so similar tail numbers aren't mixed up.

anchor: what does readability four mean on a radio check
positive: On the one-to-five readability scale, four is readable; five is perfectly readable, three readable with difficulty, two readable now and then, and one unreadable.

anchor: tower piper four four mike radio check one one eight point tree
positive: Before calling for real, the Piper pilot asks the tower whether its transmission on 118.3 is getting through and how clearly.

anchor: Why would a pilot add 'student pilot' to a radio call?
positive: The FAA encourages it so controllers know to speak more slowly, keep instructions simple and allow extra time. It asks for patience, not emergency handling.

anchor: Similar call sign
positive: Two flights on one frequency whose identities sound alike, such as KLM 1234 and KLM 1243. Controllers warn 'caution, similar call sign', and airlines renumber flights to avoid it.

anchor: ground cessna three four five charlie papa at the fbo with information kilo request taxi vfr departure to the west
positive: I'm a Cessna parked at the FBO, I've heard the current airport broadcast Kilo, and I'd like to taxi out for a visual departure toward the west.

anchor: Medevac three one, priority, inbound to the hospital pad.
positive: The MEDEVAC prefix marks a flight carrying a patient that gets priority handling; in the US it replaced the older 'Lifeguard' designation.

anchor: Is there a difference between starting a US call sign with 'November' versus 'Cessna'?
positive: Both identify the same registration. November is the spoken US nationality prefix N; substituting the maker or model, like 'Cessna three four five Charlie Papa', also tells the controller the aircraft type.

anchor: Delta twenty nine, runway two seven left, taxi via Alpha, Kilo, hold short of runway three three.
positive: Ground routes Delta 29 toward runway 27L on taxiways Alpha then Kilo, but it must stop before runway 33 and get separate permission to cross.

anchor: american tree tree two taxi to holding point runway zero niner via bravo
positive: ICAO-style taxi clearance: American 332 should follow taxiway Bravo to the holding point for runway 09 and stop there.

anchor: Progressive taxi
positive: Turn-by-turn taxi guidance from ground control, given to pilots unfamiliar with an airport or unsure where they are on the surface.

anchor: Hold position
positive: Stop and stay exactly where you are on the ground; ground or tower uses it to halt a taxiing aircraft immediately.

anchor: I'm kind of lost on this airport, can you walk me through it one turn at a time?
positive: Ground, Cirrus four four two Sierra Romeo, unfamiliar with the field, request progressive taxi.

anchor: Give way to the Airbus coming from your left, then taxi to stand one four.
positive: Ground wants the pilot to let the Airbus pass first, then continue to parking stand 14. 'Give way' is ICAO wording for yielding on the surface.

anchor: Why do pilots read back the assigned runway along with the taxi route?
positive: Wrong-runway departures such as Comair 5191 at Lexington in 2006 show the stakes. Repeating the runway gives the controller one more chance to catch a slip before takeoff.

anchor: follow the united seven three seven ahead then join alfa
positive: Get in line behind the United 737 in front of you, then turn onto taxiway A.

anchor: We're all boarded and the doors are shut, can we back out of the gate now?
positive: Ramp, Alaska three one eight, gate Charlie four, request pushback.

anchor: cleveland ground spirit four oh six gate charlie twelve ready to taxi with hotel
positive: Spirit 406 at gate C12 has the current ATIS, Hotel, and wants taxi instructions to the departure runway.

anchor: Hold short
positive: Stop at the marked holding position protecting a runway, painted as two solid and two dashed yellow lines, and do not enter until cleared.

anchor: hold short runway one six right skywest forty forty
positive: SkyWest 4040 confirms it will stop at the hold line for runway 16R and not enter.

anchor: what counts as a runway incursion
positive: Any unauthorized presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a runway. Misheard clearances and skipped readbacks are frequent contributors.

anchor: cross runway two eight then contact ground point nina
positive: Permission to cross runway 28 now, then switch to ground on the frequency ending in .9, controller shorthand for something like 121.9.

anchor: LAHSO
positive: Land And Hold Short Operations: an FAA procedure in which a landing aircraft must stop before an intersecting runway or point. A pilot may refuse by saying 'unable' before starting the approach.

anchor: Stop right where you are, don't go onto the runway, somebody's landing!
positive: Hold position! Traffic landing runway three four.

anchor: what should you do if youre not sure you were cleared to cross a runway
positive: Stop short and ask. FAA and ICAO guidance agree: when in doubt, hold short and query the controller rather than assume.

anchor: uh ground were at hotel four cant see the hold short markings theyre covered in snow
positive: Pilot reports position at taxiway H4 and warns that snow hides the runway hold-short markings, so precise guidance is needed.

anchor: ILS critical area
positive: Protected zone near the localizer and glideslope antennas. In low visibility, aircraft are told to 'hold short of the ILS critical area' so they don't distort the landing guidance signal.

anchor: Hold at holding point Charlie two, runway occupied, expect departure in two minutes.
positive: Stay where you are at taxiway C2; someone is on the runway, and you should be able to go in about two minutes.

anchor: Lufthansa four eight one, wind two six zero degrees one two knots, runway two seven, cleared for take-off.
positive: Tower authorizes Lufthansa 481 to depart runway 27; the wind from 260 at 12 knots comes first so the crew can check the crosswind.

anchor: Why is the word 'takeoff' restricted in ICAO phraseology?
positive: After Tenerife, ICAO limited 'take-off' to the actual clearance and its cancellation. Everywhere else people say 'departure', so no stray use of the word can sound like permission.

anchor: cleared to land two four left delta twenty one twenty
positive: Delta 2120 acknowledges landing clearance for runway 24L.

anchor: Cleared for the option
positive: FAA-only clearance letting the pilot choose a touch-and-go, stop-and-go, low approach, missed approach or full-stop landing. Popular in training; not ICAO phraseology.

anchor: Southwest twelve, cancel takeoff clearance, vehicle on the runway.
positive: Permission to depart is withdrawn because a vehicle has entered the runway; Southwest 12 stays put until told otherwise.

anchor: Air France six five, stop immediately, Air France six five, stop immediately.
positive: Tower orders a jet already rolling to reject its takeoff at once, repeating the call sign so there is no doubt who must stop.

anchor: You can land on runway three-four, the wind is light out of the north.
positive: Shamrock one two three, wind three five zero degrees five knots, runway three four, cleared to land.

anchor: I want to practice landing and taking right back off a few times.
positive: Tower, Warrior four two Papa, request closed traffic, touch and goes runway two four.

anchor: number two following the seven three seven on two mile final continue
positive: You're second to land, behind a 737 that's two miles out; keep coming, but you are not cleared to land yet.

anchor: Tower, Qantas eleven, ready for departure runway one six right.
positive: Qantas 11 tells tower it is at the holding point and able to depart as soon as cleared; the call reports readiness and does not ask to roll.

anchor: Frontier two one six, go around, I say again, go around, aircraft on the runway.
positive: Tower orders the landing aircraft to abandon its approach and climb away because the runway is still occupied.

anchor: going around unstable
positive: Pilot informs tower the landing is being abandoned because the approach did not meet stabilized criteria.

anchor: Missed approach
positive: Published procedure flown when an instrument approach can't be completed, for example no runway in sight at minimums. Crews report 'missed approach' or simply 'going around'.

anchor: Who is allowed to call a go-around?
positive: Either pilot can call one if the approach is unsafe, and tower can order one. Airline training stresses that a go-around call is obeyed first and discussed later.

anchor: We're not landing this time, we're climbing back up to have another go.
positive: Tower, Frontier two one six, going around.

anchor: Delta four two, fly runway heading, climb and maintain three thousand.
positive: Typical instruction right after a go-around: keep flying straight out along the runway's direction and climb to 3,000 feet.

anchor: Tower, Gulfstream one two Echo, request low approach runway one niner, then right closed traffic.
positive: Gulfstream 12E wants to fly down over runway 19 without landing, then circle back around to the right in the pattern.

anchor: is a go around an emergency
positive: No. It is a normal, trained maneuver. A crew going around needs no special phrase beyond 'going around', and controllers treat it as routine sequencing.

anchor: missed approach jazz eight five seven request vectors for another try
positive: Unable to land off the approach, the Jazz crew wants radar headings to set up for a second attempt.

anchor: Ryanair eight lima, go around, wind shear reported on short final.
positive: Abort the landing and climb out, Ryanair 8L: a crew just ahead reported sudden wind changes close to the runway.

anchor: fly heading three one zero climb and maintain one zero thousand contact norcal departure one three five point one
positive: After takeoff turn to heading 310, climb to 10,000 feet, and switch to NorCal Departure on 135.1.

anchor: SID
positive: Standard Instrument Departure: a published route out of an airport with a name like 'BAYYS ONE', letting ATC clear a flight 'via the SID' instead of listing every turn and altitude.

anchor: climb via the sid except maintain one two thousand
positive: Follow all the route and altitude restrictions on the published departure, but stop climbing at 12,000 feet rather than the procedure's top altitude.

anchor: expedite your climb through flight level two zero zero crossing traffic
positive: Climb faster than normal through FL200 to get clear of an aircraft crossing your path.

anchor: FAA controllers say 'climb and maintain' rather than 'climb to'. Why?
positive: 'To' can be heard as 'two', so 'climb to four thousand' might become 'two four thousand'. ICAO keeps 'climb to' but always follows it with 'flight level' or an altitude in feet to reduce the risk.

anchor: After you take off, keep going straight and get up to five thousand feet as fast as you can.
positive: Fly runway heading, climb and maintain five thousand, expedite.

anchor: Easy four five Charlie, contact London Control one two seven decimal four two five, good day.
positive: Handoff: easyJet 45C leaves this frequency and calls London Control on 127.425 MHz.

anchor: Departure release
positive: Coordination in which approach or center lets a tower launch an IFR flight. Until it arrives, the pilot may hear 'hold for release'.

anchor: skyhawk nine kilo hold for release expect one zero minute delay
positive: Hold at the runway: the IFR departure isn't approved yet, and the wait should be about ten minutes.

anchor: clearance void if not off by one five two zero
positive: Be airborne by 15:20 (UTC unless stated otherwise) or this IFR release lapses and you must call ATC back for a new one.

anchor: Vectors
positive: Radar headings assigned by a controller to guide an aircraft, e.g. 'turn left heading two two zero, vectors ILS runway two seven'. The pilot holds the heading until told otherwise.

anchor: Turn left heading two four zero, maintain three thousand until established on the localizer, cleared ILS runway two seven approach.
positive: Approach sets up a 240 intercept to the runway 27 ILS, keeps the aircraft at 3,000 feet until it's on the localizer, and clears the instrument approach.

anchor: expect the r nav zulu two eight right
positive: Plan for the RNAV (GPS) approach labeled Z to runway 28R; the controller is telling you what to brief.

anchor: Established
positive: On the published course of an approach or route, for a localizer typically within half-scale deflection. Clearances hinge on it: 'maintain four thousand until established'.

anchor: reduce speed one eight zero knots maintain until five mile final
positive: Slow down to 180 knots and hold that speed until you're five miles from the runway.

anchor: resume own navigation direct pellston
positive: I'm finished giving you headings; navigate yourself from here, straight to Pellston.

anchor: field insight alaska five five six
positive: The Alaska crew can see the airport, which lets approach clear a visual approach.

anchor: Visual approach
positive: IFR approach flown by visual reference to the runway or to traffic ahead, issued after the pilot reports the field or the preceding aircraft in sight.

anchor: You can head into the airport on your own and land, just talk to the tower on 120.5.
positive: Cleared visual approach runway one niner, contact tower one two zero point five.

anchor: keep your speed up two ten or greater to the marker
positive: Approach wants at least 210 knots until the outer marker so the arrivals behind don't catch up.

anchor: Indianapolis Center, Southwest twenty seven forty, level three six zero, light chop.
positive: Southwest 2740 checks in at FL360 and volunteers a ride report of light chop.

anchor: Ride report
positive: Pilot's description of turbulence at their altitude (smooth, light chop, moderate) shared so controllers and other crews can pick a better altitude.

anchor: proceed direct harty resume the arrival
positive: Center clears a straight line to the fix HARTY, after which the flight rejoins the published arrival route.

anchor: Waypoint
positive: Named point in space, often a five-letter pronounceable name, used to define routes and procedures; pilots get cleared 'direct' to them.

anchor: whats a star in aviation
positive: Standard Terminal Arrival Route: a published path from the en route structure into a terminal area. 'Descend via the STAR' means fly its altitude and speed restrictions.

anchor: Cross the Sparta VOR at and maintain one one thousand.
positive: The aircraft must be level at 11,000 feet by the time it passes over the Sparta VOR, and stay there.

anchor: Is there anywhere smoother? It's really bumpy up here.
positive: Center, Envoy thirty-three twelve, moderate chop at flight level two eight zero, request ride reports, any smoother altitudes?

anchor: pilots discretion descend and maintain flight level two four zero
positive: The pilot may begin the descent to FL240 whenever they choose and may level off temporarily on the way.

anchor: ARTCC
positive: Air Route Traffic Control Center, the US facility handling en route IFR traffic over a large region, addressed by city as in 'Memphis Center'. The ICAO equivalent is an Area Control Centre, e.g. 'London Control'.

anchor: So what are you planning to do now?
positive: November four Golf, say intentions.

anchor: flight level one eight zero
positive: FL180, normally the lowest usable flight level in the US, sitting right at the 18,000-foot transition altitude.

anchor: altimeter two eight niner six
positive: 28.96 inches of mercury, a deep low. A pilot who misses that setting reads higher than the aircraft really is: 'high to low, look out below'.

anchor: transition level flight level six zero
positive: The transition level is FL60. Descending through it, crews stop using standard pressure, set local QNH and start reporting altitude in feet.

anchor: Transition altitude
positive: Altitude at or below which aircraft use local QNH; climbing through it, crews set standard pressure and talk in flight levels. Fixed at 18,000 feet in the US, varies by country elsewhere.

anchor: QFE
positive: Altimeter setting that makes the altimeter read zero on the runway, giving height above the airfield. Seen in some military and European operations, not in US civil flying.

anchor: why do US controllers say one zero thousand and not ten thousand
positive: FAA phraseology states each digit of the thousands for altitudes of 10,000 feet and above, so 'ten' cannot blur into 'two' or 'one' and every altitude readout follows one pattern.

anchor: verify at flight level tree one zero
positive: Controller asks the crew to confirm they are level at FL310, often because the altitude readout on radar disagrees with the assignment.

anchor: descend to altitude four thousand feet QNH niner niner eight
positive: Descend to 4,000 feet above sea level with the altimeter set to 998 hPa, a typical ICAO descent below transition.

anchor: What height are you at right now?
positive: Speedbird three two, report level.

anchor: Why are flight levels written in hundreds of feet?
positive: Dropping the last two zeros keeps cruise altitudes short: FL240 is 24,000 feet of pressure altitude. Fewer digits means quicker, less error-prone transmissions.

anchor: Squawk
positive: Instruction to dial a four-digit code into the transponder so radar can identify the aircraft. The word dates to WWII IFF equipment, nicknamed the 'parrot'.

anchor: Ident
positive: Pressing a dedicated transponder button so the aircraft's radar target briefly highlights on the controller's screen, confirming which return is which.

anchor: What is Mode C, and why does ATC care about it?
positive: Mode C is the transponder's altitude-reporting function. It puts a pressure-altitude readout beside the radar return, which is why controllers ask the pilot to verify a level when the two disagree.

anchor: radar contact tree miles west of the airport
positive: Controller has positively identified the aircraft on radar at that position, so radar services begin.

anchor: Reset transponder, squawk four six two one.
positive: Something's wrong with the code on the radar screen, so the pilot should recycle the transponder and set 4621.

anchor: stop altitude squawk altitude differs by tree hundred feet
positive: Turn off your transponder's altitude reporting; what it shows me is 300 feet off from what you're reporting.

anchor: Push that button on your transponder so I can tell which blip on my radar is you.
positive: Cessna six Echo Romeo, squawk ident.

anchor: radar service terminated squawk vfr frequency change approved
positive: I'm no longer tracking you; set your transponder back to the VFR code and you're free to leave this frequency.

anchor: ATIS
positive: Automatic Terminal Information Service: recorded loop of airport weather, runways in use and notices, updated at least hourly and labeled with a phonetic letter such as 'information Bravo'.

anchor: with information juliet
positive: Pilot confirms having listened to the current ATIS broadcast, the one labeled J (spelled Juliett in ICAO).

anchor: Atlanta information Papa, one five five two Zulu, wind two seven zero at one zero, visibility one zero, ceiling four thousand broken, altimeter three zero zero one.
positive: ATIS Papa issued at 1552 UTC: wind from 270 at 10 knots, 10 miles visibility, broken clouds at 4,000 feet, altimeter 30.01.

anchor: CAVOK
positive: Ceiling And Visibility OK, spoken 'cav-oh-kay': visibility 10 km or more, no cloud below 5,000 feet or the minimum sector altitude, no cumulonimbus and no significant weather. ICAO term, rarely heard in the US.

anchor: pirep meaning
positive: A pilot weather report of turbulence, icing, cloud tops or wind shear. It's passed through ATC to other crews because it describes conditions actually encountered aloft.

anchor: It was really bumpy and we picked up some ice around eight thousand feet in the clouds.
positive: Approach, Horizon two four zero four, pilot report, moderate turbulence and light rime icing between seven and eight thousand, in cloud.

anchor: Wind shear
positive: Sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. Near a runway, controllers relay reports as gains or losses, like 'wind shear, minus two zero knots, two mile final'.

anchor: tower um is the wind still gusting
positive: Before landing, the pilot asks for the current wind, wanting to know whether gusts are still being reported.

anchor: rvr runway two eight right one tousand eight hundred
positive: Runway Visual Range on 28R is 1,800 feet, measured along the runway; values this low decide which approaches are legal.

anchor: In a weather report, how is 'ceiling' different from 'visibility'?
positive: Ceiling is the height of the lowest broken or overcast layer; visibility is the horizontal distance you can see. Landing needs both, since the runway must be seen from the right height and range.

anchor: Traffic, two o'clock, five miles, opposite direction, Boeing seven thirty seven, one thousand feet above you.
positive: Look ahead and to the right: a 737 five miles away is flying toward you 1,000 feet higher.

anchor: negative contact were in the clouds
positive: Pilot hasn't spotted the called traffic and explains why: they're in cloud and can't see out.

anchor: Yep, I see the plane you mentioned, the one off to my right.
positive: Approach, Mooney two Hotel Alfa, traffic in sight.

anchor: how does the clock position thing work for traffic calls
positive: The nose is twelve o'clock, the right wingtip three, the tail six. Controllers base it on ground track, so with a crosswind the traffic may be a little off from where the clock suggests.

anchor: Traffic no longer a factor.
positive: The earlier traffic advisory is cancelled; that aircraft is no longer a conflict.

anchor: There's a small plane ahead of you and a bit to the left, about three miles, at your height, no idea what kind it is.
positive: Traffic, eleven o'clock, three miles, altitude indicates three thousand five hundred, type unknown.

anchor: Maintain visual separation
positive: Instruction that hands separation responsibility to the pilot, who must keep the reported traffic in sight and stay clear of it.

anchor: traffic in sight the high wing at our ten
positive: Pilot sees the reported high-wing airplane at the ten o'clock position.

anchor: Cherokee two Tango, traffic is a Gulfstream on a four mile final, report it in sight.
positive: Cherokee 2T, a Gulfstream jet is four miles out lining up to land; tell me once you can see it.

anchor: Traffic alert, Bonanza six Echo, traffic twelve o'clock, one mile, opposite direction, advise you turn right immediately.
positive: Safety alert: the controller sees a collision risk and urges an immediate right turn. 'Traffic alert' is reserved for this level of urgency.

anchor: Sault Ste Marie at one four three two, flight level three five zero, estimating Thunder Bay one five zero five.
positive: Non-radar position report: the flight passed the Sault Ste. Marie fix at 14:32 UTC at FL350 and expects Thunder Bay at 15:05.

anchor: What goes into a standard ICAO position report?
positive: Call sign, position, time over it, level, next position with its estimated time, and the significant point after that. Extras like fuel or weather are added on request.

anchor: Compulsory reporting point
positive: Fix where a position report is required when not in radar contact; charted as a solid triangle, versus an open triangle for points reported only on request.

anchor: ann arbor traffic cessna four five mike left downwind two four touch and go ann arbor
positive: Self-announcement on the CTAF: the Cessna is on left downwind for runway 24 planning a touch and go. Saying the airport name twice tells listeners which field is meant.

anchor: CTAF
positive: Common Traffic Advisory Frequency: the shared channel at an airport without an operating tower where pilots announce their own positions and intentions.

anchor: I'm turning onto final approach for runway one-three at Bay City.
positive: Bay City traffic, Piper six one Romeo, turning final runway one three, Bay City.

anchor: Downwind
positive: Traffic pattern leg flown parallel to the landing runway in the opposite direction, reported as 'left downwind runway two four'; base and final come next.

anchor: report tree mile final
positive: Tower wants a call when the aircraft is three miles from the runway on its final approach.

anchor: five miles south inbound for the forty five
positive: VFR pilot is five miles south, heading to join the pattern on the standard 45-degree entry to the downwind leg.

anchor: why bother announcing position at an airport with no tower
positive: No controller is sequencing traffic, so radio calls on the CTAF let everyone build a picture of who is where; see-and-avoid backed up by the radio.

anchor: Shanwick
positive: Oceanic control for the eastern North Atlantic, its name blending Shannon in Ireland and Prestwick in Scotland, where its radio station and control centre sit; contact is mostly by HF voice or datalink.

anchor: Gander Oceanic, Delta four four, request oceanic clearance, estimating entry point at one two three zero, Mach decimal eight two, flight level three six zero.
positive: Delta 44 asks for its North Atlantic crossing clearance, giving the time at its entry point, a planned Mach 0.82 and FL360.

anchor: SELCAL
positive: Selective Calling: a ground station sends a four-letter tone code that chimes only in one cockpit, so crews needn't listen to noisy HF all flight. A 'SELCAL check' tests it on first contact.

anchor: Why do oceanic clearances include a Mach number?
positive: Without radar coverage, ATC separates aircraft on the same track by time. Holding an assigned Mach keeps the gap between them from shrinking.

anchor: SLOP
positive: Strategic Lateral Offset Procedure: in oceanic airspace crews may fly one or two nautical miles right of track centerline, spreading out traffic that GPS would otherwise stack precisely on the line.

anchor: uh any aircraft on one two three decimal four five hows the ride at three seven zero
positive: Over the North Atlantic, a pilot uses the 123.45 air-to-air frequency to ask other crews about turbulence at FL370.

anchor: CPDLC
positive: Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications: clearances, requests and reports exchanged as text messages, widely used over oceans where VHF voice doesn't reach.

anchor: Gander, Air Canada eight seventy, request flight level three eight zero.
positive: Air Canada 870 is asking the oceanic controller for permission to climb to 38,000 feet.

anchor: selcal echo hotel dash bravo romeo
positive: SELCAL code EH-BR: four letters from a 16-letter set (A to S, minus I, N and O), sent as two tone pairs that chime only in that aircraft's HF receiver.

anchor: why is hf radio so hard to understand
positive: HF signals bounce off the ionosphere, bringing static, fading and whistles. Crews speak slowly, stick to set phrases and rely on SELCAL and radio operators who relay their messages to controllers.

anchor: MAYDAY
positive: International distress signal, spoken three times, for grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. It comes from French 'm'aider', help me.

anchor: MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, Boston Center, Atlas five one, engine fire, descending through flight level two eight zero, returning to Bangor.
positive: Atlas 51 declares distress for an engine fire, reporting its descent and its plan to divert back to Bangor.

anchor: What information belongs in a MAYDAY call?
positive: Station addressed, call sign, nature of the emergency, intentions, position, level and heading, then persons on board and fuel if time allows. Getting the call out matters more than perfect order.

anchor: mayday mayday cessna two one tango engine failure uh ditching
positive: Small-aircraft distress call: the engine has quit and the pilot expects to put down on water.

anchor: MAYDAY RELAY
positive: Prefix used by a station that heard a distress call and passes it on to someone who didn't; common in oceanic and maritime settings.

anchor: All stations, stop transmitting, MAYDAY.
positive: Controller imposes radio silence on everyone else so the aircraft in distress has the frequency.

anchor: We're in big trouble, both engines quit and we need to get down right now wherever we can.
positive: MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, United two one, dual engine failure, request vectors nearest suitable airport.

anchor: Boston Center, Atlas five one, cancel distress, fire is out, continuing to Bangor.
positive: The emergency is over for Atlas 51 now that the fire is out, though the crew still plans to land at Bangor.

anchor: How many people are on the plane, and how much fuel have you got left?
positive: Atlas five one, say souls on board and fuel remaining.

anchor: MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL, Iberia three one, request direct Madrid.
positive: Fuel emergency under ICAO rules: the crew calculates it will land with less than final reserve fuel and needs the most direct routing.

anchor: PAN-PAN
positive: Urgency signal, spoken three times, for a situation affecting safety that needs prompt attention but isn't grave and imminent danger, like a sick passenger or a minor technical fault. From French 'panne', breakdown.

anchor: PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, Manchester Approach, Channex two four seven, passenger with suspected heart attack, request priority landing.
positive: Urgency call for a medical problem aboard Channex 247; the crew wants priority handling into Manchester.

anchor: When should a pilot choose PAN-PAN instead of MAYDAY?
positive: PAN-PAN fits when safety is at risk but the flight can continue for now; MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger. Upgrading from PAN to MAYDAY later is always allowed.

anchor: pan pan pan pan pan pan cherokee five delta im uh not sure of my position
positive: A student pilot declares urgency because they are lost; radar controllers will help locate the aircraft.

anchor: Minimum fuel
positive: Advisory that fuel has reached a point where no undue delay can be accepted. It is not an emergency: controllers give no priority until the pilot declares one.

anchor: Request priority, bird strike, windshield cracked, no other problems.
positive: We hit a bird and cracked our windshield; nothing else is wrong, but we'd like to land ahead of the others.

anchor: Just so you know, we can't accept long delays, we're getting low on gas.
