positive: Approach, Republic forty-three twelve, minimum fuel.

anchor: how does atc answer a pan pan
positive: Usually with the call sign and 'roger PAN', then questions or instructions. The frequency isn't silenced the way it is for MAYDAY, but the aircraft is handled ahead of routine traffic.

anchor: Declaring an emergency
positive: In US practice, saying 'declaring an emergency' carries the same weight as MAYDAY, giving priority and authority to deviate from rules as needed to deal with it.

anchor: Speedbird nine eight, roger PAN, turn right heading one two zero, expect ILS runway two three right.
positive: Urgency acknowledged; the controller starts giving the most direct path to a landing on runway 23R.

anchor: squawk seven six zero zero
positive: Code 7600: radio failure. It tells radar controllers the aircraft can't talk, and possibly can't hear.

anchor: What route does a US IFR pilot fly after the radios die?
positive: AVEF: the route Assigned, else the one Vectored to, else the one ATC said to Expect, else the one Filed. Altitude is the highest of assigned, minimum en route, or expected.

anchor: NORDO
positive: 'No radio': controllers' shorthand for an aircraft without working communications, often handled with light gun signals at towered airports.

anchor: What does a flashing green light from the tower mean?
positive: On the ground, cleared to taxi; in the air, return for landing. A pilot acknowledges by rocking the wings in flight or moving ailerons or rudder on the ground.

anchor: steady red light from the tower what does that mean
positive: In flight: give way to other aircraft and keep circling. On the ground: stop.

anchor: November six two Kilo, if you hear me, ident.
positive: Suspecting the aircraft can receive but not transmit, ATC offers the transponder as a way to answer: an ident shows up on radar.

anchor: Saratoga four Xray, if you read, rock your wings.
positive: Tower asks the radio-less Saratoga to prove it can hear by rocking its wings within sight of the cab.

anchor: I can't hear anyone, but in case you can hear me, I'm continuing to Detroit at six thousand.
positive: Transmitting blind, Saratoga four Xray, radio failure, continuing to Detroit, six thousand.

anchor: Aircraft with a stuck mic, check your push-to-talk switch.
positive: Someone's transmit button is jammed and blocking the frequency; whoever it is, check your microphone switch.

anchor: Station calling, you're unreadable, try again on one two six point six five.
positive: Whoever just transmitted, I couldn't make out a word; switch to 126.65 and call me there.

anchor: eighty knots thrust normal
positive: Takeoff-roll cross-check: airspeed has reached 80 knots and engine thrust is where it should be. Airbus operators typically make the equivalent call at 100 knots.

anchor: V1
positive: Takeoff decision speed, called aloud by the monitoring pilot. Below it a rejected takeoff can still be started; past it the crew continues even after an engine failure.

anchor: Rotate.
positive: Called at rotation speed: the pilot flying now raises the nose to lift off.

anchor: positive rate gear up
positive: Monitoring pilot confirms the instruments show a climb; only then does the pilot flying order the landing gear retracted.

anchor: airspeed alive both sides
positive: Early in the takeoff roll, both airspeed indicators have started moving, confirming neither is blocked or failed.

anchor: who gets to reject a takeoff and what do they say
positive: At most airlines only the captain makes the reject decision, calling 'stop' or 'reject'. Either pilot may call out a failure, but one decision-maker avoids hesitation at high speed. Policies vary by operator.

anchor: Sterile cockpit
positive: FAA rule (14 CFR 121.542) banning non-essential conversation during critical phases of flight, including taxi, takeoff, landing and all flight below 10,000 feet except cruise.

anchor: Flaps up, after takeoff checklist.
positive: Retract the wing flaps now and let's run through the after-takeoff checklist.

anchor: I have control.
positive: Positive transfer of controls: the other pilot answers 'you have control', so there's never doubt about who is flying.

anchor: Why are takeoff callouts made out loud when both pilots can see the instruments?
positive: Speaking them proves the monitoring pilot is actually watching, exposes instrument disagreements, and triggers each action at a fixed moment instead of relying on one person's silent judgment.

anchor: One thousand, stabilized.
positive: At 1,000 feet above the runway, the monitoring pilot confirms speed, path and configuration meet stabilized-approach criteria; if not, a go-around is expected.

anchor: approaching minimums
positive: About 100 feet above decision altitude: get ready to decide between landing and going around.

anchor: Minimums. Landing.
positive: At decision altitude the monitoring pilot calls minimums; the pilot flying has the runway environment in sight and commits to land.

anchor: minimums no contact go around flaps fifteen
positive: Reaching decision height with no visual references, the crew begins a missed approach and sets flaps to 15.

anchor: Decision altitude
positive: DA (or DH): the point on a precision approach where the pilot must see the runway environment to continue the descent; otherwise go around.

anchor: spoilers up reverse green
positive: Just after touchdown: ground spoilers have deployed and the thrust reversers are confirmed working.

anchor: sixty knots
positive: Rollout cue to bring reverse thrust back toward idle as the aircraft slows.

anchor: What's a 'sink rate' call in the cockpit?
positive: An aural ground proximity warning that descent rate is excessive close to the ground. Crews are trained to correct immediately or go around.

anchor: We're too fast and too high, this isn't going to work, let's try again.
positive: Speed plus fifteen, high on the glidepath, not stable, go around.

anchor: Pilot monitoring
positive: The pilot not flying, responsible for radio calls, checklists and callouts that cross-check the pilot flying. The term replaced 'pilot not flying' to stress active monitoring.

anchor: Affirm
positive: ICAO's word for yes. 'Affirmative' was avoided because a clipped transmission could leave only '-ative', easily confused with 'negative'. The FAA still uses 'affirmative'.

anchor: What replaced 'taxi into position and hold' in the US?
positive: In September 2010 the FAA adopted ICAO's 'line up and wait': enter the runway, align, and stop, ready to depart but without takeoff clearance.

anchor: KLM six eight one, runway two four, line up and wait.
positive: KLM 681 may enter runway 24 and line up for departure, but must not start the takeoff roll until cleared.

anchor: taxi into position and hold runway three one left
positive: Older FAA phrasing, pre-2010, for entering runway 31L to wait for takeoff clearance; today said 'line up and wait'.

anchor: do icao controllers say hold short too
positive: Yes, but ICAO airports also lean on named holding points: 'taxi to holding point Alpha one, runway two seven'. In the US the hold-short instruction itself carries the runway number.

anchor: enter runway two six and backtrack report ready
positive: Taxi onto runway 26, turn and roll back along it toward the far end, and tell me when you're set to depart. The FAA would say 'back-taxi'.

anchor: How do FAA and ICAO altimeter settings sound different on the radio?
positive: The FAA gives inches of mercury, 'altimeter two niner niner two'; most ICAO states give hectopascals, 'QNH one zero one three'. The keyword tells you which unit is meant.

anchor: visibility eight kilometres
positive: Visibility 8 km, reported ICAO style in metres and kilometres; a US report would give statute miles instead, about five here.

anchor: Go ahead
positive: FAA invitation to proceed with your message. ICAO dropped it from standard words, preferring the call sign or 'pass your message', partly because it can be mistaken for permission to proceed.

anchor: vacate left via bravo tree
positive: Leave the runway by turning left onto taxiway B3. 'Vacate' is common ICAO wording; US controllers more often say 'turn left at Bravo three'.

anchor: whats icao level four english
positive: The 'Operational' level on ICAO's six-step scale, the minimum English standard for pilots and controllers on international operations, retested periodically. Level 6 'Expert' needs no retest.

anchor: when is plain language ok on the radio
positive: When standard phraseology doesn't cover the situation, as with unusual emergencies or odd requests. Even then it should be concise, unambiguous and free of idioms.

anchor: There's a dog running loose on the taxiway by the cargo ramp.
positive: Ground, FedEx one two eight, animal on taxiway Golf near the cargo ramp.

anchor: Phraseology
positive: Standardized wording prescribed by ICAO and national authorities for radio exchanges, built so each phrase has exactly one meaning across accents and languages.

anchor: Why can native English speakers cause more confusion than non-native ones?
positive: Native speakers tend to talk fast, slip in idioms like 'hold your horses', and drift from standard phrases, while non-native listeners may only know the standard set. ICAO urges native speakers to stick to phraseology.

anchor: uh we have a passenger um very aggressive not complying request police on arrival
positive: Plain-language report of a disruptive passenger; the crew wants law enforcement to meet the aircraft at the gate.

anchor: speak slower air china niner eight one
positive: Request to cut the rate of speech; the controller was talking too fast for comfortable understanding.

anchor: Why did ICAO bring in language proficiency requirements at all?
positive: Investigations kept finding accidents and incidents where crews or controllers lacked enough English to handle a non-routine situation. ICAO adopted the proficiency rules in 2003 with a 2008 deadline, later relaxed to 2011.

anchor: Confirm you are requesting medical assistance on arrival, how many persons affected?
positive: Can you double-check that you want an ambulance waiting when you land, and tell me how many people need help?

anchor: Is English mandatory for all air traffic control worldwide?
positive: No. ICAO requires English to be available for international flights, but controllers may also use the local language, as in France or Quebec, which can reduce other crews' awareness of nearby traffic.

anchor: We are now at takeoff.
positive: KLM 4805's first officer at Tenerife in 1977 meant they were rolling; the tower took it as 'at the takeoff position'. That ambiguity fed the deadliest accident in aviation history.

anchor: What went wrong with the tower's 'OK' at Tenerife?
positive: The controller said 'OK... stand by for takeoff, I will call you', but a simultaneous Pan Am call blocked everything after 'OK'. The KLM crew heard only approval and kept rolling.

anchor: What caused the Flying Tiger 66 crash in 1989?
positive: Near Kuala Lumpur the controller said 'descend two four zero zero', meaning 2,400 feet. The crew heard 'descend to four zero zero', went down to 400 feet and hit terrain, a textbook case for avoiding 'to'.

anchor: why was avianca 52 not treated as an emergency
positive: In 1990 the crew told New York controllers they were running low on fuel and needed priority but never said 'emergency' or MAYDAY. The 707 ran dry near JFK, and clear emergency declaration became a training staple.

anchor: What role did communication play in the 2002 Überlingen midair?
positive: A controller told a Tu-154 to descend just as its TCAS commanded a climb. The crew obeyed the controller while the other jet followed its own descend RA, and they collided. Rules now make the RA take precedence.

anchor: SkyWest fifty-five sixty-nine, taxi into position and hold runway two four left.
positive: The 1991 Los Angeles clearance that left a commuter waiting on the runway; the controller lost track of it and cleared a USAir 737 to land on top of it.

anchor: Expectation bias
positive: Hearing what you expect rather than what was said, such as reading back an anticipated altitude instead of the one issued; a recurring factor in ATC miscommunication studies.

anchor: Linate, 2001: what does that runway collision teach about radio language?
positive: In fog at Milan, a Cessna Citation crew took the wrong taxiway onto an active runway and was struck by a departing SAS jet. Investigators cited nonstandard phraseology and the mix of Italian and English on frequency.

anchor: which phrase was implicated in the 2024 haneda runway collision
positive: The Coast Guard Dash 8 crew was told they were 'number one' and to taxi to holding point C5. They entered the runway, apparently taking 'number one' as permission, and a landing JAL A350 struck them.

anchor: How did language figure in the 1996 Charkhi Dadri midair near Delhi?
positive: A Kazakh Il-76 descended below its assigned level and collided with a Saudi 747. Investigators pointed to the Kazakh crew's limited English, with only the radio operator handling communications.

anchor: Lansing Approach, Cherokee eight one two Tango Delta, one five miles south at three thousand five hundred, request flight following to Traverse City.
positive: A VFR Cherokee gives position and altitude and asks approach for radar traffic advisories on the way to Traverse City.

anchor: Flight following
positive: Informal name for VFR radar traffic advisories: the controller tracks the aircraft and calls nearby traffic, workload permitting. It is a service, not a clearance.

anchor: What do you need before entering US Class Bravo airspace?
positive: An explicit clearance using the words 'cleared into the Class Bravo'. Being in radar contact or getting a squawk code does not count.

anchor: what counts as two way radio communication for class charlie
positive: The controller must answer using your call sign. 'Aircraft calling, stand by' does not establish it, but 'Cessna one two Kilo, stand by' does.

anchor: maintain vfr at or below four thousand five hundred
positive: Controller caps the VFR pilot at 4,500 feet or lower, usually to keep them beneath arriving traffic.

anchor: Special VFR
positive: Clearance letting a VFR pilot operate within controlled surface airspace when the weather is below basic VFR minimums, still clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile visibility in the US.

anchor: I'd like to fly over downtown for some sightseeing if that's alright.
positive: Approach, Skyhawk two Lima Charlie, request transition over downtown at two thousand five hundred for sightseeing.

anchor: Bonanza six Echo, cleared into the Class Bravo, fly heading zero four zero, maintain three thousand five hundred.
positive: The Bonanza now has explicit permission to enter Class B airspace on a 040 heading at 3,500 feet.

anchor: radar contact remain outside class bravo
positive: Controller has you on radar, but you are NOT cleared into the Class B; stay outside it.

anchor: one two two point eight
positive: 122.8 MHz, a common Unicom/CTAF frequency at small US airports without a control tower.

anchor: Heavy
positive: Suffix on the call sign of large aircraft, such as 'Delta fifteen heavy', warning of strong wake turbulence. FAA: 300,000 lb maximum takeoff weight or more; ICAO: 136,000 kg or more.

anchor: Caution wake turbulence, departing Boeing seven seventy seven heavy.
positive: Tower warns that a large widebody just took off; its wingtip vortices can upset a following aircraft, so adjust timing or flight path.

anchor: speedbird two eight tcas ra
positive: The British Airways crew tells ATC it is following a TCAS resolution advisory and may deviate from its clearance.

anchor: clear of conflict returning to flight level tree four zero
positive: TCAS maneuver complete; the crew is going back to its assigned FL340.

anchor: If TCAS says climb but ATC says descend, which wins?
positive: The resolution advisory. ICAO rules require crews to follow the RA and then report 'TCAS RA'; the controller stops issuing conflicting instructions until the crew reports clear of conflict.

anchor: Traffic advisory
positive: TCAS caution, the aural 'traffic, traffic', that another aircraft is getting close. It calls for looking and preparing, not maneuvering.

anchor: Super
positive: Wake category suffix used for the Airbus A380, as in 'Emirates two zero one super', signalling wake turbulence beyond even heavy jets.

anchor: Why do controllers space departures by time behind heavy jets?
positive: Wake vortices sink and drift but take minutes to decay, so controllers apply timed intervals, commonly two minutes or more, behind heavy aircraft departing the same runway.

anchor: Our collision avoidance system told us to climb, so we can't do what you just said.
positive: Aeromexico six seven, unable, TCAS resolution advisory.

anchor: monitor vertical speed
positive: TCAS voice alert: keep the vertical speed out of the red band on the display, i.e. don't climb or descend into the conflict.

anchor: Hold northeast of the Pullman VOR on the zero four five radial, right turns, ten mile legs, expect further clearance one five three zero Zulu.
positive: Delay instruction: fly a racetrack on the northeast side of the Pullman VOR, right turns, ten-mile straight legs, and plan to be released at 15:30 UTC.

anchor: EFC
positive: Expect Further Clearance time: when the aircraft should expect to leave a hold. It matters most if radios fail, since the pilot would leave the hold at the EFC.

anchor: Why do controllers send aircraft into holding?
positive: To absorb delay when arrivals exceed what the airport can handle, during weather, runway closures or flow restrictions. Holding stacks aircraft vertically over a fix.

anchor: entering holding flight level tree one zero
positive: Pilot reports beginning the holding pattern at FL310.

anchor: Expected approach time
positive: ICAO counterpart to EFC: the time ATC expects an aircraft in a hold to leave it and begin the approach.

anchor: How long are we going to be stuck circling here?
positive: London Control, Turkish one niner seven, request estimated delay in the hold.

anchor: delays at lambourne currently two zero minutes
positive: Controller warns arrivals to expect about 20 minutes circling in the Lambourne hold before starting the approach.

anchor: expect further clearance one four four five zulu
positive: Plan to leave the hold at 14:45 UTC; EFC times are always given as four-digit Zulu times.

anchor: hold west of the barrie vor as published
positive: Fly the racetrack drawn on the chart on the west side of the Barrie VOR; no need for me to describe the turns and legs.

anchor: Leave the hold, descend and maintain four thousand, turn left heading one eight zero.
positive: You can stop circling now: descend to 4,000 feet and turn left to fly heading 180.

anchor: Why do military aviators use brevity words instead of plain English sentences?
positive: Brevity words compress a whole sentence into one or two words, saving airtime on crowded tactical frequencies and cutting misunderstandings, since each word carries a single agreed meaning across the services.

anchor: whats the difference between a brevity code and a call sign
positive: A call sign names who is talking, like Viper one-one or Texaco, while a brevity code carries the message, like bingo or tally. One identifies the speaker; the other describes a condition or action.

anchor: Are military brevity codes secret?
positive: No. Multi-service brevity words are unclassified and openly published so US and allied crews share one vocabulary. Their purpose is speed and clarity; protecting content is the job of encryption, not brevity.

anchor: who publishes the us brevity words anyway
positive: A joint multi-service publication compiles them, issued by the Army as ATP 1-02.1 and under matching Navy, Marine Corps and Air Force numbers. NATO keeps a comparable allied brevity list.

anchor: do brevity words mean exactly the same thing in every air force
positive: Largely within NATO, which maintains an allied list, but some definitions differ between services or nations and words get revised between editions. Mixed formations brief any differences before flight.

anchor: brevity code
positive: A standardized word or short phrase with one fixed meaning, used on tactical radio in place of a longer sentence. Unlike a cipher it hides nothing; it exists only to save time and avoid ambiguity.

anchor: Why should each brevity word have only one meaning?
positive: Under stress, a listener who hears a word with two meanings may act on the wrong one. One word, one meaning lets a pilot react instantly without asking for clarification and tying up the radio.

anchor: What is meant by a directive call versus a descriptive call?
positive: A directive call tells someone to do something, such as buster or break right, while a descriptive call reports what the speaker sees or knows, such as tally or joker. Brevity lists label many words as directive.

anchor: Do civilian air traffic controllers use military brevity?
positive: Generally not. Civil controllers follow ICAO and FAA phraseology. A few words overlap, like squawk and ident, but terms such as bandit, winchester or buster stay on military frequencies.

anchor: why would a fighter pilot switch to plain english on the radio
positive: When no brevity word fits the situation, or the listener may not know the codes, such as a civilian controller or a new coalition partner. Brevity serves clarity; it is never meant to make a message cryptic.

anchor: Why do fighter pilots usually drop "this is" from radio calls?
positive: Airtime is precious on a tactical frequency, so 'Darkstar, this is Viper one-one' shrinks to 'Darkstar, Viper one-one'. The order of the two call signs alone still shows who is calling whom.

anchor: bogey
positive: A radar or visual air contact whose identity is still unknown. It is the starting label before anyone has determined whether the aircraft is friendly, neutral or enemy.

anchor: bandit
positive: An aircraft identified as enemy. The word settles identity only; whether it may be engaged is a separate question answered by the rules of engagement and the hostile declaration.

anchor: hostile
positive: Declaration that a contact is identified as enemy and meets the rules-of-engagement criteria for engagement. It goes one step beyond bandit, which establishes enemy identity alone.

anchor: friendly
positive: Positive identification that a contact is a friendly aircraft, typically given by a controller answering a pilot's request to declare a track.

anchor: neutral
positive: Positive identification of an aircraft whose behavior, origin or nationality shows it is neither supporting nor opposing friendly forces, for example a civil airliner or a third-country military jet.

anchor: declare
positive: Pilot's request for a controller to give the identity of a specific contact. The answer comes back as friendly, neutral, bogey, bandit or hostile.

anchor: spades
positive: An IFF interrogation of the contact got no friendly reply. It is a clue about identity, not by itself a declaration that the aircraft is hostile.

anchor: darkstar viper one one declare single group bullseye two seven zero forty
positive: A fighter is asking the AWACS controller to identify a lone aircraft located 40 miles from the bullseye reference point on a bearing of 270 degrees.

anchor: Viper one-one, Darkstar, group is bogey, no factor.
positive: Darkstar cannot say who that aircraft is but judges it will not affect the flight, so the fighters can ignore it for now.

anchor: uh two bogey low left nine o clock
positive: Spotted below and off the left wing: an unidentified aircraft, flagged before anyone knows if it is friend or foe.

anchor: bogey and bandit, are those the same thing
positive: A bogey is any air contact whose identity is unknown; a bandit has been identified as an enemy aircraft. Once identification happens, a bogey can turn out to be a bandit, a friendly or a neutral.

anchor: Is that aircraft about twenty miles south of the reference point one of ours or not?
positive: Darkstar, Viper two, declare, bullseye one-eight-zero, twenty.

anchor: tally
positive: Eyes-on sighting of a target, bogey, bandit or enemy position, the opposite of no joy. It means the pilot actually sees the threat, not merely a radar return.

anchor: visual
positive: Sighting of a friendly aircraft or friendly ground position, the friendly counterpart to tally. Its opposite is blind.

anchor: no joy
positive: Aircrew lacks visual contact with the target, bogey, bandit or landmark being discussed. Often prompts a description or a talk-on to help the pilot find it.

anchor: blind
positive: No visual contact with a friendly aircraft or friendly ground position. Usually paired with the speaker's altitude so the two aircraft can stay separated until they see each other again.

anchor: padlocked
positive: Aircrew cannot take eyes off an aircraft or ground target without losing sight of it. Other flight members then understand this pilot is not scanning elsewhere or checking instruments.

anchor: twos blind angels two zero
positive: Having lost sight of the leader, number two announces its own altitude, 20,000 feet, so both jets keep vertical separation until someone regains sight.

anchor: viper one padlocked bandit low
positive: Lead has eyes fixed on an enemy aircraft below and cannot look away, so the wingman needs to take over lookout for anything else.

anchor: hornet two one tally one no joy on the second
positive: The pilot sees one of the two reported aircraft but has not yet found the other one.

anchor: two contact single nose twenty
positive: The wingman's radar shows one aircraft straight ahead at 20 miles; this is a sensor return, and the target has not necessarily been seen by eye.

anchor: tally ho bandit right two oclock high
positive: I can see the enemy aircraft, up and to my right at the two o'clock position.

anchor: Lead, I can see you, and I'm sitting behind you.
positive: Viper two, visual, in trail.

anchor: Why say visual for a friend but tally for an enemy?
positive: Separate words prevent a dangerous mixup. Hearing tally means the threat is in sight, while visual confirms only a friendly. A single word for both would leave a flight unsure what a pilot actually sees.

anchor: In air-to-air brevity, how is contact different from tally?
positive: Contact means a sensor, normally radar, has the target; tally means the pilot sees it with their own eyes. A fighter may call contact long before it can call tally.

anchor: bingo
positive: Fuel state at which a jet must head for home, the tanker or a divert field to arrive with the briefed reserve; once reached, the aircraft leaves without delay.

anchor: joker
positive: A fuel state, briefed before the mission and set above the go-home minimum, at which a pilot starts wrapping up the engagement or task.

anchor: two jokr
positive: The wingman reached the briefed joker fuel, an early heads-up that bingo is approaching and the flight should plan its exit.

anchor: lead twos bingo recommend rtb
positive: Only enough fuel remains in the wingman's jet to get home with the required reserve, so the wingman suggests the flight return to base now.

anchor: state
positive: Request or report of fuel and weapons remaining; answers normally give fuel in thousands of pounds, as in 'six point four'.

anchor: Viper two, state. Two's six point four.
positive: Lead asked for a status report and the wingman answered with 6,400 pounds of fuel remaining.

anchor: state four point niner
positive: A fuel report of 4.9, meaning about 4,900 pounds of fuel remaining in the aircraft.

anchor: two's eleven point five
positive: Fuel report from number two: 11.5, or 11,500 pounds remaining on board.

anchor: Why isn't bingo fuel a fixed number?
positive: It depends on distance to the recovery field, cruise altitude, weather and required reserves, so each mission briefs its own bingo in pounds of fuel for each aircraft type.

anchor: Do airline pilots call bingo fuel?
positive: Not as standard phraseology. Airline crews tell ATC "minimum fuel" or declare "MAYDAY fuel" in an emergency. Bingo belongs to military flying, though some civil pilots borrow it informally.

anchor: I'm down to just the fuel I need to get home, so I'm leaving right now.
positive: Viper two, bingo, bingo, RTB.

anchor: ops check
positive: A routine prompt from the flight lead for each pilot to scan aircraft systems and fuel, then reply in order, typically with a fuel figure in thousands of pounds.

anchor: winchester
positive: No ordnance remaining. Heard at the end of an attack, it often prompts the controller to release the aircraft or bring in the next flight.

anchor: vipr two winchester rtb
positive: All weapons are gone, so number two is heading home, since that jet can no longer contribute firepower.

anchor: skosh
positive: Report that an aircraft is out of, or unable to employ, its active radar missiles, even though it may still carry other weapons.

anchor: hog one one winchester playtime one five can provide eyes
positive: The A-10 pilot is out of weapons but still has 15 minutes on station and offers to stay overhead and watch for the ground controller.

anchor: Where does the word winchester come from?
positive: It is commonly linked to the Winchester repeating rifle and the image of firing every round, though the exact origin is folklore. In brevity it simply means no ordnance left.

anchor: fenced in
positive: Report or directive that cockpit switches are set for combat as the aircraft enters the area of operations. Its partner, fenced out, reverses those settings on the way out.

anchor: viper flight fence in
positive: Lead is telling everyone in the formation to set their switches for combat as they cross into the operating area.

anchor: two fenced out
positive: I've put all my switches back to the normal non-combat settings now that we're leaving the area.

anchor: Viper one, Viper two, press.
positive: Keep going with your attack, lead; I'm staying in a supporting position to cover you.

anchor: is winchester about fuel or weapons
positive: Weapons only. Fuel is reported with joker and bingo, so a pilot could be winchester with plenty of gas, or bingo with weapons still aboard.

anchor: angels
positive: Altitude of a friendly aircraft in thousands of feet above sea level, so a following 'two-five' means 25,000 feet.

anchor: cherubs
positive: Altitude of a friendly aircraft in hundreds of feet, used for very low flying, especially by helicopters; a following 'five' means 500 feet.

anchor: angels one six
positive: 16,000 feet, a friendly aircraft's altitude expressed in thousands.

anchor: cherubs eight
positive: 800 feet, a low altitude given in hundreds, typical of helicopter traffic.

anchor: dodge two one say angels
positive: The controller wants the aircraft to report its current altitude in thousands of feet.

anchor: ok angles twenty
positive: The pilot is reporting an altitude of 20,000 feet.

anchor: Why are the altitude words called angels and cherubs?
positive: The imagery works as a memory aid: angels fly high and count in thousands of feet, while cherubs, small angels, stay low and count in hundreds.

anchor: Climb angels three-zero.
positive: Climb up to thirty thousand feet.

anchor: buster
positive: Directive to fly at maximum continuous speed or power, short of afterburner. Controllers use it when they need a fighter somewhere sooner.

anchor: gate
positive: Directive to fly as quickly as possible using maximum power, including afterburner, which burns fuel far faster than buster.

anchor: viper one one vector two seven zero buster
positive: The controller wants the fighter turned to heading 270 and moving at maximum continuous power without afterburner.

anchor: buster or gate which one is the afterburner
positive: Both mean hurry. Buster is maximum continuous power without afterburner, while gate authorizes full afterburner, trading a lot of fuel for speed.

anchor: Viper two-one, gate.
positive: Hurry, go as fast as you possibly can and use afterburner.

anchor: bullseye
positive: A briefed, named reference point from which positions are given as bearing and range. Everyone shares it, so nobody has to broadcast their own location.

anchor: BRAA
positive: Format giving a contact's bearing, range, altitude and aspect measured from the listening aircraft itself rather than from bullseye. Spoken as "bra".

anchor: viper two one darkstar single group braa two two zero thirty five twenty thousand hot
positive: The controller is telling Viper that one aircraft lies 220 degrees from Viper, 35 miles out, at 20,000 feet, and pointed toward Viper.

anchor: feet wet
positive: Now over water, usually after crossing the coastline outbound. Feet dry is the reverse: back over land.

anchor: hornet one one feet dry
positive: The flight has crossed the coastline inbound and is now flying over land.

anchor: pigeons
positive: Magnetic bearing and range to home base or another named point, passed by a controller, for example "pigeons home plate, two-one-zero, eighty."

anchor: home plate
positive: Aviator term for the home airfield or home carrier, the place a flight returns to at the end of its mission.

anchor: ghost one two ah request pigeons home plate
positive: The pilot wants the controller to give the magnetic bearing and distance back to the home field.

anchor: bullseye zero niner zero thirty
positive: A position 30 nautical miles from the bullseye reference point along a bearing of 090 degrees, which is due east of it.

anchor: braa three four five forty five eighteen thousand cold
positive: Contact bears 345 degrees from the listener at 45 miles and 18,000 feet, and is heading away.

anchor: Why give positions from a bullseye instead of from the fighter itself?
positive: A shared bullseye lets every aircraft and controller describe the same contact the same way, wherever they are, without revealing their own position. BRAA is used when a call is meant for one particular aircraft.

anchor: We just crossed the coast and we're out over the ocean now.
positive: Raven one-one, feet wet, outbound.

anchor: picture
positive: Request for, or report of, the overall air situation: the controller describes every group of contacts in the area of interest.

anchor: viper darkstar picture clean
positive: The AWACS controller has no relevant air contacts to report in the area the flight cares about.

anchor: bogey dope
positive: Request for target information on the group nearest the requesting aircraft, or one it names, normally answered in BRAA format.

anchor: darkstar eagle one two bogey dope
positive: The F-15 pilot wants bearing, range, altitude and aspect for the closest group of contacts.

anchor: group
positive: Contacts flying close enough together that a controller describes them as one entity in a picture call, whether that turns out to be one aircraft or several.

anchor: heavy, in an AWACS picture call
positive: A group known to contain three or more aircraft, as opposed to a single. Nothing to do with the civil 'heavy' call-sign suffix, which warns of wake turbulence.

anchor: hot
positive: Aspect word for a contact pointed roughly at the friendly aircraft. Cold is the opposite, heading away; flank and beam describe in-between angles.

anchor: fade
positive: Report that radar contact on a tracked group has been lost, often because it descended, turned or flew out of coverage.

anchor: pop-up
positive: A group that suddenly appears inside the area being described, often because it was flying low or masked by terrain until then.

anchor: Judy
positive: Fighter's call that it has radar or visual contact on the correct target and is running the intercept itself, needing only situational updates from the controller.

anchor: uh viper one one merged
positive: The friendly fighters and the target group have come together so closely that the controller can no longer tell them apart on the scope.

anchor: There's one unknown aircraft twenty-five miles east of the reference point, around fifteen thousand feet, flying toward us.
positive: Single group, bullseye zero-niner-zero, twenty-five, fifteen thousand, hot, bogey.

anchor: group heavy track north
positive: That formation has three or more aircraft in it and is flying northbound.

anchor: What do AWACS and GCI mean?
positive: AWACS is an airborne warning and control system aircraft, such as the E-3 Sentry, that runs radar control from the air; GCI is ground-controlled intercept, the same job from a ground radar site. Both pass picture calls to fighters.

anchor: awacs calls lump planes into groups, why not count each one
positive: Radar often can't separate aircraft flying close together, so nearby contacts get lumped into one group labeled single or heavy, keeping calls short and honest about what the scope actually shows.

anchor: What goes into a typical fighter check-in with a controller?
positive: Call sign, number and type of aircraft, mission number or tasking, position and altitude, weapons available, and playtime, meaning how long the flight can stay on station.

anchor: Darkstar, Viper one-one, two F-16s, checking in as fragged, angels two-four, playtime four-zero.
positive: The lead is telling the AWACS that the two-ship has arrived as planned in the tasking order, at 24,000 feet, and can stay 40 minutes.

anchor: as fragged
positive: Shorthand meaning a flight is operating exactly as listed in its tasking order, the "frag", so the controller does not need aircraft, weapons and timing read out again.

anchor: playtime
positive: Time an aircraft can remain on station before it must leave, usually given in minutes.

anchor: hawg two one two hogs over the ip angels one two playtime three zero
positive: A pair of A-10s is reporting in at the initial point, flying at 12,000 feet, with 30 minutes available on station.

anchor: Ragin' one-one, Darkstar, radar contact, check in with Showtime, button seven.
positive: AWACS confirms it sees the flight on radar and hands it off to another controller, call sign Showtime, on preset radio channel 7.

anchor: words
positive: Request or directive concerning further information or directions for the mission, such as a new tasking or a changed target.

anchor: darkstar viper one one words
positive: Darkstar, Viper one-one here, do you have any new information or instructions for us?

anchor: Hi, we're leaving your area now and switching over to the next controller.
positive: Darkstar, Viper one-one, checking out, switching Showtime.

anchor: Playtime in a check-in: why does the controller need it?
positive: Controllers juggle many flights and need to know how long each can stay before refueling or heading home, so they can assign tasks and line up tankers or replacements.

anchor: fox one
positive: Call announcing the launch of a semi-active radar-guided air-to-air missile. Each fox number names a guidance category, not a particular missile model.

anchor: fox two
positive: Spoken at the launch of an infrared, or heat-seeking, air-to-air missile.

anchor: fox three
positive: Call announcing the launch of an active radar-guided air-to-air missile, one that carries its own radar seeker.

anchor: splash
positive: Air-to-air report that the target aircraft has been destroyed, so controllers can update the picture and nobody wastes another shot on it.

anchor: viper two fox three
positive: An active radar missile has just left the wingman's jet; the call warns friendlies and tells the controller a shot is in the air.

anchor: Darkstar, Eagle one-one, splash one bandit.
positive: The fighter is confirming that one enemy aircraft has been shot down.

anchor: Why announce a missile shot over the radio at all?
positive: Shot calls tell wingmen and controllers a weapon is in the air so they can avoid duplicate shots and track results; in training they also let debriefers assess simulated kills.

anchor: eagle one one fox to
positive: Eagle one-one is announcing the launch of an infrared, heat-seeking missile.

anchor: Viper two, guns, guns, guns.
positive: I'm firing my cannon right now.

anchor: Is fox four a real brevity call?
positive: No. Pilots joke that fox four means a midair collision or ramming, but it is slang and appears in no official brevity list.

anchor: magnum
positive: Launch call for a friendly anti-radiation missile, one that homes on enemy radar emissions.

anchor: rifle
positive: Call announcing the launch of a friendly air-to-surface missile, such as a Maverick.

anchor: pickle
positive: Informal aviator slang for releasing ordnance, from the pickle button on the control stick; heard in conversation and training more than in formal radio calls.

anchor: shack
positive: Aviator slang for a direct hit on the target, especially on a practice range, carried over from old bombing-range scoring.

anchor: weasel one one magnum
positive: An anti-radiation missile has just left the Wild Weasel jet; the call warns friendlies it is heading for an enemy radar.

anchor: hog two one rifle
positive: The A-10 pilot has just fired an air-to-surface missile.

anchor: Why do magnum and rifle sound nothing like the weapons they describe?
positive: They are arbitrary but distinctive code words. Short, unusual words cut through radio noise better than technical weapon names, and each maps to exactly one weapon category.

anchor: is pickle an official radio call
positive: Not usually. It is common pilot slang for pressing the weapons release button, but formal calls to controllers use defined brevity such as rifle, magnum or the in and off calls.

anchor: cleared hot
positive: Terminal attack controller's clearance for an aircraft to release ordnance on that pass. Without it the pilot may not drop or fire.

anchor: continue dry
positive: Permission to keep flying the current attack run without releasing any weapons, used for rehearsal passes or when release isn't authorized.

anchor: ABORT, ABORT, ABORT.
positive: Stop the attack now and release nothing; saying the word three times ensures it is heard even through noise or a partly blocked transmission.

anchor: JTAC
positive: Joint terminal attack controller, the qualified service member on the ground who directs close air support aircraft and issues clearances such as cleared hot.

anchor: hawg two one in from the east
positive: The A-10 is announcing it is starting its attack run from the east, so the JTAC can confirm its position before giving clearance.

anchor: hog two one cleared hot
positive: The ground controller is authorizing the A-10 to release weapons on this pass.

anchor: Hawg two-two, off west.
positive: I've finished my attack run and I'm pulling away to the west.

anchor: talk-on
positive: Verbal description, working from large landmarks down to small details, that a controller uses to guide a pilot's eyes onto a target or friendly position.

anchor: no joy request talk on
positive: The pilot can't see what the JTAC described and wants to be guided onto it landmark by landmark.

anchor: spot
positive: Laser seeker acquisition: the aircraft's seeker has picked up the laser energy marking a target.

anchor: sparkle
positive: Marking of a target with an infrared pointer, visible to aircrew wearing night vision goggles.

anchor: What is a CAS check-in?
positive: On arrival, close air support aircraft brief the JTAC on call sign, number and type, position, altitude, weapons and playtime, so the controller knows what is overhead and for how long.

anchor: What is meant by Type 1, 2 or 3 control in close air support?
positive: Labels for how closely the JTAC controls attacks, from Type 1, where the JTAC sees both aircraft and target and clears each pass, to Type 3, where multiple attacks are cleared within set limits.

anchor: spike
positive: Radar warning receiver indication of an airborne threat radar in track or launch mode, usually reported with a clock position so others know where it is coming from.

anchor: cobra two spike nine oclock
positive: The radar warning receiver in Cobra two shows an enemy fighter's radar tracking the jet from its left side.

anchor: Hammer two, nails, north.
positive: Somebody's airborne radar is sweeping from the north in search mode; it is looking but has not locked on.

anchor: Hawg one-one, mud, six o'clock.
positive: Warning gear in the A-10 is showing a ground-based threat radar behind the aircraft.

anchor: Darkstar, Rocco one-one, buddy spike, bullseye two-two-zero, fifteen.
positive: A radar appears to be locking Rocco, apparently from a friendly fighter at that location, and Rocco wants the controller to sort out who it is.

anchor: Why do so many brevity words depend on the radar warning receiver?
positive: It is a cockpit system that detects other radars illuminating the aircraft. Words such as spike, nails, mud and naked are one-word summaries of what it is showing.

anchor: Why is buddy spike a separate call from spike?
positive: A spike implies a threat, but a buddy spike says the lock seems to come from a friendly aircraft. The distinct word keeps a pilot from reacting defensively to, or firing at, their own side.

anchor: Jedi two, break right.
positive: Two, turn as hard as you can to the right, right now!

anchor: two defending defending spiked south
positive: Under a radar lock from the south, the wingman is now maneuvering defensively against the threat.

anchor: lobo two mud spike three oclock
positive: My warning receiver shows a ground-based radar tracking me from my right side.

anchor: Snake one, naked.
positive: My radar warning display is empty; nothing is looking at me right now.

anchor: We're leaving this fight for good and heading south, not coming back to it.
positive: Bolt flight, bugout south, bugout south.

anchor: What does weapons free mean?
positive: Crews may fire at any target not positively identified as friendly. It is the least restrictive of the three weapons control statuses.

anchor: weapons tight vs weapons hold which one is stricter
positive: Weapons tight allows firing only at targets positively identified as hostile. Weapons hold allows firing only in self-defense or when specifically ordered, making it the most restrictive.

anchor: All Dagger, Darkstar, weapons tight.
positive: Every Dagger flight is being told it may fire only at targets positively identified as hostile.

anchor: darkstar all players weapons hold weapons hold
positive: Firing is now limited to self-defense or a direct order; the controller repeats it so every listener catches the change.

anchor: commit
positive: Intent to engage or intercept a particular group, announced by the fighter or directed by the controller, who then keeps feeding information during the intercept.

anchor: Attention all fighters: from now on you may shoot at anything not confirmed as one of ours.
positive: All players, Darkstar, weapons free.

anchor: Mako one-one, committing south group.
positive: I'm going after the formation to the south to intercept it.

anchor: Why are weapons control statuses announced by a controller instead of chosen by each pilot?
positive: They flow from rules of engagement set by commanders, so one controlling agency broadcasts them to everyone at once, keeping the whole package under the same restrictions.

anchor: Darkstar, all players, hold fire, hold fire, friendlies in the area.
positive: An emergency order to stop shooting immediately, given here because friendly aircraft may be mixed in near the target.

anchor: knock it off
positive: Training-rules call that stops all tactical maneuvering by every participant in the exercise. Any participant may make it for a safety problem, and each flight acknowledges in turn.

anchor: terminate
positive: Training-rules call that stops one local engagement without ending the whole exercise, so other parts of the training can continue.

anchor: knock it off knock it off tusk one knock it off
positive: Tusk lead is halting all maneuvering in the exercise, repeating the words so everyone hears and acknowledges before anyone moves.

anchor: tusk two knock it off
positive: Acknowledgment from the wingman: maneuvering has stopped and the jet is flying wings level and predictable.

anchor: If knock it off stops everything, when would a pilot say terminate instead?
positive: Knock it off stops every participant in the training exercise, while terminate stops only a specific engagement or aircraft and lets the rest continue. Real problems like an emergency call for knock it off.

anchor: Puma one, fight's on.
positive: Okay, the practice dogfight starts now, so we're both free to maneuver.

anchor: puma two kill f sixteen left hand turn eighteen thousand
positive: Puma two is claiming a simulated kill and describes the target jet, its turn and its altitude so the right opponent knows it has been shot.

anchor: bandit two one copy kill
positive: Playing the adversary, Bandit two-one acknowledges being killed in the simulation and will leave the fight as briefed.

anchor: Who is allowed to call knock it off during training?
positive: Anyone who sees a safety issue, such as an aircraft below the altitude floor, a lost sight situation, a malfunction or a bingo fuel state, regardless of rank or role in the flight.

anchor: terminate terminate sabre two below the floor
positive: Stop this engagement: my wingman has dropped below the minimum altitude we set for the training.

anchor: Why do training rules need special stop words at all?
positive: Realistic training puts fast jets close together at high energy. A short, unmistakable stop word that everyone obeys instantly keeps simulated combat from turning into a real accident.

anchor: We've arrived in our assigned area and are ready to start work.
positive: Darkstar, Ghost one-one, on station.

anchor: ghost one one off station rtb ops normal
positive: Ghost flight is leaving its area and heading home, with no problems to report.

anchor: Two, ops normal.
positive: Everything in my aircraft is working fine and I have nothing to report.

anchor: popeye angels one five
positive: In cloud or poor visibility at 15,000 feet, the pilot is warning others that visibility outside is very limited.

anchor: What does ops normal mean, and when is it said?
positive: Operations normal: aircraft and crew are fine. It answers a lead's ops check or a controller's status request so that silence is never mistaken for a problem.

anchor: why say rtb instead of just going home
positive: RTB, return to base, is short, unmistakable and familiar across services and allies. It covers every reason for leaving, fuel, weapons, weather or mission complete, without explanation.

anchor: Sabre one-one, RTB.
positive: We're done with our job and heading back to our home airfield.

anchor: twos rtb winchester nine point oh
positive: Out of weapons, the wingman is heading home, though 9,000 pounds of fuel are still aboard.

anchor: Darkstar, Lobo one-one, mission complete, checking out.
positive: Lobo's tasking is finished, and the flight is leaving the AWACS frequency.

anchor: precontact
positive: Stabilized position just behind and below the tanker's boom or refueling basket where a receiver waits before being cleared in to connect.

anchor: shell six one raven one one pre contact
positive: Raven has settled into the waiting spot behind the tanker and is ready to be cleared in.

anchor: Okay Raven, you can move in and hook up with the boom now.
positive: Raven one-one, Shell six-one, cleared contact.

anchor: shell six one contact
positive: The boom operator reports the boom is latched into the receiver's receptacle and fuel can begin flowing.

anchor: disconnect disconnect
positive: The boom or probe has separated from the receiver, ending fuel transfer for now.

anchor: BREAKAWAY, BREAKAWAY, BREAKAWAY.
positive: Emergency during refueling: the receiver must disconnect at once and drop back clear of the tanker. Repeating the word three times matters because a collision may be close.

anchor: raven one one return to precontact
positive: Back off to the waiting position, the boom operator says, perhaps to reset alignment after an unstable approach or a disconnect.

anchor: How does boom refueling differ from probe-and-drogue?
positive: With a boom, an operator in the tanker flies a rigid pipe into a receptacle on the receiver. With probe and drogue, the receiver pilot flies a probe into a basket on a hose. USAF jets mostly use the boom; Navy and many allied aircraft use probe and drogue.

anchor: why does contact mean something different on the tanker
positive: On a tanker frequency, contact means the boom or probe is physically connected. On a tactical net it means a radar return. The context of who is talking keeps the two meanings apart.

anchor: plugged and taking gas
positive: I've got my probe in the basket and fuel is flowing into my jet.

anchor: Why are tankers so often called Texaco or Shell on the radio?
positive: Tankers are frequently given call signs borrowed from oil companies, such as Texaco, Shell or Exxon, so the name instantly says gas station. The practice is informal and varies by exercise.

anchor: Exxon two-two, Raven one-one, flight of two, joining, angels two-two, request ten thousand each.
positive: Two fighters are joining up on the tanker at 22,000 feet and each one wants 10,000 pounds of fuel.

anchor: offload one two point five
positive: 12.5, meaning the tanker is to transfer 12,500 pounds of fuel to the receiver.

anchor: raven flight exxon two two cleared observation left wing
positive: The tanker lets the fighters fly up alongside its left wing and wait their turn to refuel.

anchor: refueling track vs anchor, how do they differ
positive: A track is a published route the tanker flies while refueling, and an anchor is a racetrack orbit over a fixed area. Receivers are told which one to meet the tanker on.

anchor: What is meant by EMCON refueling?
positive: Emission control: tanker and receivers refuel using little or no radio, relying on briefed procedures, lights and signals so as not to reveal their position. Stricter EMCON levels restrict transmissions further.

anchor: Raven two, offload complete, seven point two.
positive: We've finished passing you fuel; you took on 7,200 pounds.

anchor: uh exxon two two raven two fuel complete thanks for the gas
positive: Raven two has its fuel and is leaving the tanker, adding the informal thank-you common on tanker frequencies.

anchor: We're two fighters and each of us needs about eight thousand pounds of fuel.
positive: Texaco four-one, Hammer one-one, two-ship, request eight point oh each.

anchor: request one zero point zero each
positive: 10.0 each, meaning every receiver in the flight is asking for 10,000 pounds of fuel.

anchor: ball
positive: The meatball, the lighted glide-slope indicator beside the carrier's landing area. Reporting it tells the landing signal officer the pilot sees the light and is flying it down.

anchor: three zero five hornet ball five point two
positive: Side number 305, a Hornet, sees the glide-slope lights and has 5,200 pounds of fuel; this is a standard ball call on final approach.

anchor: Three-oh-five, roger ball.
positive: Acknowledging the ball call, the LSO confirms the jet is being watched and will talk the pilot down if needed.

anchor: Clara
positive: Report that the pilot cannot see the meatball. The LSO then helps with calls or waves the aircraft off; "Clara ship" means the pilot cannot see the ship itself.

anchor: Four-one-two, Super Hornet, Clara, six point oh.
positive: Aircraft 412 is on final but can't see the glide-slope lights, so the LSO must step in; it has 6,000 pounds of fuel.

anchor: Why is the landing signal officer called paddles?
positive: Before optical landing aids, LSOs stood at the deck edge waving colored paddles to signal pilots. The tools are gone, but the nickname stuck for the officer and the radio call sign.

anchor: Four-oh-two, power, power.
positive: The LSO wants more thrust immediately, usually because the jet is settling low or slow on the glide slope.

anchor: right for lineup
positive: You're drifting left of the landing area centerline; come right to line back up.

anchor: You're high.
positive: Your approach is above the glide slope; bring the aircraft down onto it.

anchor: wave off wave off
positive: A mandatory order from the LSO: abandon this landing attempt, add power and go around.

anchor: bolter bolter bolter
positive: The tailhook missed every wire, so the pilot must keep full power, fly off the angled deck and come around again.

anchor: bolter vs wave off whats the difference
positive: A wave off is the LSO ordering the pilot to abandon an approach before touchdown. A bolter happens when the jet touches down but the hook misses the wires, sending it back into the air.

anchor: Why does a carrier ball call include fuel state?
positive: The LSO and air boss need each jet's fuel to decide what happens next; a low state after a bolter may mean sending the pilot to the tanker or a divert field instead of another pass.

anchor: four one two little power
positive: Aircraft 412, add just a small amount of power.

anchor: marshal
positive: The holding stack behind the carrier where returning aircraft wait their turn to approach, and also the controller who runs it.

anchor: We're forty-five miles southwest of the carrier at twelve thousand feet with seven thousand pounds of fuel.
positive: Marshal, Ernie one-one, mother's two-four-zero for forty-five, angels one-two, state seven point oh.

anchor: What are Case I, Case II and Case III carrier recoveries?
positive: Recovery types chosen by weather and light. Case I is daytime good weather with visual patterns, Case II lets aircraft descend through weather and finish visually, and Case III, at night or in poor weather, runs fully instrument approaches from marshal.

anchor: Ernie one-one, signal Charlie.
positive: The carrier is telling the flight overhead to come down and land now.

anchor: charlie time one four three five
positive: 1435 is the assigned Charlie time, the moment the aircraft is expected to land aboard the carrier.

anchor: four zero two commencing angels six state eight point one
positive: Leaving the marshal stack, aircraft 402 starts its instrument approach at 6,000 feet with 8,100 pounds of fuel.

anchor: four zero two platform
positive: During a Case III approach, the pilot reports passing 5,000 feet, the point where the descent rate is reduced.

anchor: trap
positive: An arrested landing, when the tailhook catches one of the cross-deck wires and stops the jet. Pilots often say which wire they caught; the target wire depends on how many the carrier rigs.

anchor: four one two bingo bingo
positive: Aircraft 412, stop trying to land; fly to the shore divert field now with the fuel you have left.

anchor: Foul deck, foul deck.
positive: The landing area isn't clear, so an approaching jet cannot land yet and should expect a wave off if it stays blocked.

anchor: Clear left. Clear right.
positive: Crew members at each side of the helicopter confirm there are no obstacles near the rotors or fuselage as it moves.

anchor: forward two one stop
positive: A crew member counts down the last few feet as the pilot inches the helicopter forward, then calls for it to hold position.

anchor: tails clear come left
positive: Nothing is near the tail rotor, the crew chief reports, so the pilot can swing the nose to the left.

anchor: hooks set loads off the deck cleared to climb
positive: The sling load is attached and lifted clear of the ground, so the pilot may start climbing.

anchor: brownout
positive: Loss of outside visibility when rotor downwash kicks up dust or sand near the ground. Crews counter it with precise callouts of drift and height; the snow version is whiteout.

anchor: youre drifting aft steady steady
positive: You're sliding backward; stop and hold right there.

anchor: chalk one chalk two what does chalk even mean
positive: A group of passengers or troops assigned to one aircraft for a lift, numbered in order as chalk one, chalk two and so on. The name comes from numbers chalked on aircraft and gear for loading.

anchor: Why do helicopter crews make so many calls during a landing?
positive: Pilots often can't see below or behind the aircraft, so crew chiefs at the doors become their eyes, calling distance, drift and obstacle clearance in short standard words.

anchor: I need you to slide right a little and then hold it right there.
positive: Slide right... steady, steady... hold.

anchor: Chalk two, one minute.
positive: The second helicopter load is about a minute from landing, so passengers should get ready to get off.

anchor: What is Dustoff?
positive: The traditional call sign of US Army air ambulance helicopters, dating from early-1960s medical evacuation units in Vietnam, and still widely used for Army medevac flights.

anchor: who is pedro on the radio
positive: Pedro is a call sign long associated with US Air Force rescue helicopters, carried by HH-60 Pave Hawk crews flying rescue and medevac missions in Iraq and Afghanistan.

anchor: What does Jolly mean in rescue radio talk?
positive: Taken from the Vietnam-era Jolly Green Giant helicopters, Jolly is a traditional call sign for US Air Force combat rescue helicopters.

anchor: Who is Sandy during a rescue?
positive: Sandy is the call sign of the aircraft that escort rescue helicopters and coordinate the on-scene effort in combat search and rescue, flown in Vietnam by A-1 Skyraiders and later by A-10s.

anchor: dust off two four inbound lz two minutes pop smoke
positive: The medevac helicopter is two minutes from the landing zone and asks the ground unit to mark it with a smoke grenade.

anchor: jolly one one sandy one one survivor authenticated cleared in
positive: The escort coordinating the rescue has confirmed the downed pilot's identity and is clearing the rescue helicopter in for the pickup.

anchor: The air ambulance is lifting off now with two patients aboard.
positive: Dustoff two-four, wheels up, two patients.

anchor: Sandy one-one, on scene, assuming on-scene commander.
positive: Sandy has arrived over the rescue area and is taking charge of coordinating it.

anchor: Why have rescue call signs stayed the same for decades?
positive: Traditional call signs carry unit history and pride, and they announce the speaker's role at once: hearing Dustoff or Jolly tells everyone a rescue helicopter is talking.

anchor: viper check two three four
positive: Lead calls a check-in and each wingman answers only with a position number, confirming the whole flight is on frequency.

anchor: two rejoin left echelon
positive: Lead wants the wingman to come back into close formation, stacked diagonally off the left side.

anchor: Bolt two, you have the lead. Bolt two has the lead.
positive: Lead is handing control of the formation to the wingman, who says it back so there is never doubt about who is leading.

anchor: Two, move back and fly behind me in a line.
positive: Bolt two, Bolt one, go trail.

anchor: Why do wingmen answer a check-in with just their number?
positive: It confirms in a fraction of a second that each aircraft is on frequency and listening, keeps the channel free, and the order of replies confirms the formation sequence.

anchor: Why must a lead change be acknowledged out loud?
positive: If two pilots each believe the other is leading, nobody is navigating the formation. Saying and confirming the change leaves no doubt about who is responsible.

anchor: Hey lead, I'm going to move over to your left side and fly close formation with you.
positive: Lead, Viper two, rejoining left side.

anchor: Two, lost wingman.
positive: I've lost sight of you in the clouds and I'm flying the briefed procedure to keep us separated.

anchor: fingertip
positive: Four-ship formation arranged like the fingertips of a hand held flat, with lead at the front and the others stepped back on either side.

anchor: How do two-digit fighter call signs like Viper two-one work?
positive: The first digit names the flight and the second the aircraft's position in it, so Viper two-one leads the Viper two flight and Viper two-four is its fourth jet.

anchor: cowboy one three
positive: Call sign Cowboy 13, the third aircraft in the Cowboy one flight.

anchor: Two, tell me where you are.
positive: Cowboy two, Cowboy one, say posit.

anchor: viper push button five
positive: Lead tells the whole flight to switch radios to preset channel 5.

anchor: lobo one one parrot sour
positive: No proper reply is coming back from Lobo's IFF transponder, so the controller flags it as not working.

anchor: sweet and sour
positive: Pair meaning the named equipment is working as expected (sweet) or not (sour), often said about IFF, datalink or a radio check.

anchor: lobo one one strangle parrot
positive: Directive for Lobo to switch off its IFF transponder, typically requested by the controller.

anchor: Two's radar is bent, I'll take the visual lookout.
positive: My radar has failed, so I'll concentrate on watching the sky with my eyes instead.

anchor: What is IFF, and why is it called parrot?
positive: IFF, identification friend or foe, is a transponder that answers coded interrogations from friendly radars. Brevity calls it parrot because it repeats a reply back whenever it is asked.

anchor: Okay everyone, switch over to the backup frequency on channel seven.
positive: Mako flight, push button seven.

anchor: lobo one one flash mode three
positive: The controller wants Lobo to briefly trigger the identification feature on IFF Mode 3 so its return blinks on the scope, the brevity counterpart of a civil 'squawk ident'.

anchor: Is splash in air combat the same as splash from artillery?
positive: No. In air-to-air brevity splash reports a target destroyed, while an artillery fire direction center says splash to warn that rounds will impact in about five seconds. Same word, different nets.

anchor: bingo or joker which one comes first
positive: Joker comes first: it is the earlier, higher fuel warning. Bingo is the lower limit at which the pilot must leave. Mixing them up means leaving too early or far too late.

anchor: uh two bingo i mean joker correction joker
positive: The wingman misspoke and fixed it: the jet has reached joker, the warning fuel state, not bingo, so it doesn't have to leave yet.

anchor: What does break mean when it's also a radio proword?
positive: As a proword, break separates parts of a message or messages to different stations. As brevity, break right or break left directs an immediate maximum-performance turn. The attached direction tells them apart.

anchor: tally tally no wait visual its a friendly
positive: First reporting a threat in sight, the pilot self-corrects: the aircraft in sight is friendly, so visual, not tally.

anchor: Why can angels confuse new listeners?
positive: In brevity angels means friendly altitude in thousands of feet, but early radar operators also used angels for unexplained radar echoes such as birds. On a fighter net it almost always means altitude.

anchor: bandit bandit uh bogey correction bogey
positive: Retracting the enemy identification, the caller now says only that there is an unknown aircraft, not that it is hostile.

anchor: why is it bad to say bandit when you mean bogey
positive: Calling an unknown aircraft a bandit falsely labels it enemy and may push others toward engaging a friendly or neutral. Saying bogey keeps identity honest until it's confirmed.

anchor: no toy on the bogey
positive: "No toy" is a speech-to-text mishearing of no joy: the pilot has not spotted the unknown aircraft.

anchor: helo one cheribs five
positive: Cheribs is a misspelling of cherubs; the helicopter is reporting its height as 500 feet.

anchor: How is abort different from knock it off?
positive: Abort cancels a specific action, such as an attack run or a mission, in training or combat. Knock it off is a training-rules call that halts all maneuvering in an exercise.

anchor: Darkstar, Hammer one-one, tumbleweed.
positive: I've lost track of what's going on out here and can't see anyone; please give me the picture.

anchor: chicks north ten miles
positive: The friendly aircraft are ten miles north of you.

anchor: There's a big dogfight with our jets and enemy jets all mixed together, and I can't sort them out.
positive: Hammer, Darkstar, furball, bullseye one-eight-zero, twenty.

anchor: Come down to three hundred feet.
positive: Jolly one-two, descend cherubs three.

anchor: Keep flying your attack run but don't drop anything.
positive: Hawg two-one, Bulldog, continue dry.

anchor: Over
positive: Proword that ends a transmission when the sender expects a reply. Saying it hands the channel to the other station, which should now answer.

anchor: Out (proword)
positive: Closes the exchange entirely: no answer is required or expected, and the net is free for other traffic. Normally said by the station that opened the call or the senior station.

anchor: why is over and out wrong on a military net
positive: Over asks the other station to respond, while out declares the conversation finished with no response expected. Combining them is contradictory, so trained operators end with one or the other; the phrase survives mostly in movies.

anchor: Bravo Six, this is Bravo Two, request resupply at checkpoint four, over.
positive: Bravo Two is asking its commander (Bravo Six) for a resupply at checkpoint four, then handing the frequency back and waiting for an answer.

anchor: copy all bravo two this is six out
positive: Everything Bravo Two sent was received by the commander, who closes the exchange; no further reply is needed.

anchor: Okay, I'm done talking, your turn to answer.
positive: On the net that whole thought collapses into one word at the end of a transmission: over.

anchor: Romeo One Two, this is Romeo One, message received, nothing further, out.
positive: Romeo One got the message from Romeo One Two and has nothing else to say, so the conversation is finished and nobody needs to answer.

anchor: Who is supposed to say 'out' at the end of a radio exchange?
positive: By convention the station that initiated the call, or the net control station. The other party ends its last transmission with over or a simple acknowledgment, and the originator closes with out.

anchor: red one this is red three roger your last uh out
positive: Red Three acknowledges receiving Red One's previous message and closes the exchange without expecting a reply.

anchor: the proword roger
positive: Stands for 'I have received your last transmission satisfactorily.' Often tied to the item received, as in 'roger your last' or 'roger, grid follows', to show exactly what was heard.

anchor: Sierra Four, move your vehicles to the north lot by fourteen hundred, over. Wilco, out.
positive: An instruction to relocate vehicles to the north lot by 2:00 p.m.; Sierra Four replies that it understands and will do it, and closes the exchange.

anchor: wilko on the move to phase line blue
positive: The unit will comply with the order and is already heading toward the boundary line named Blue.

anchor: is it right to say roger wilco
positive: No. Wilco already contains the meaning of roger, so saying both is redundant. Proper usage is wilco alone when you will comply, or roger alone when you are only acknowledging information.

anchor: roger but unable vehicle is deadlined
positive: Message received, but we can't do it because the vehicle is broken down and officially out of service for maintenance.

anchor: Got your message about the weather delay, thanks.
positive: Roger weather delay, out.

anchor: Ops, Tango Three. Roger your last, passing to the platoon sergeant now.
positive: Tango Three confirms it received the operations center's message and is relaying it to the platoon sergeant.

anchor: If a commander tells everyone to 'roger up', what are they asking for?
positive: Each station or person should acknowledge in turn that they received the message. Informal shorthand for a roll-call acknowledgment, heard on Army nets and in briefings.

anchor: convoy departs at zero niner hundred i say again zero niner hundred over
positive: Departure time sent twice with 'I say again', the proword for deliberately repeating a key portion: 0900.

anchor: Why do military operators say 'say again' instead of 'repeat'?
positive: With artillery, 'repeat' is reserved to request firing the same mission again. Using it for 'please resend' could cause a dangerous misunderstanding, so 'say again' is the standard request.

anchor: Say again all after 'checkpoint', over.
positive: The receiver caught the message up to the word checkpoint but missed the rest, and asks for everything after that word to be resent.

anchor: say agin word before kilometers
positive: Request to resend just the single word that came before 'kilometers', probably a number that was garbled.

anchor: I say again, rally at the bridge, not the church, over.
positive: Emphasis on the key point: the meeting place is the bridge, and the church is wrong.

anchor: Sorry, you cut out in the middle, can you resend the part between the time and the location?
positive: Say again all between time and location, over. A targeted repeat request that names the two words bracketing the lost part.

anchor: comms are bad words twice words twice over
positive: Poor reception reported; the operator asks that every phrase be sent two times so nothing is lost.

anchor: What does 'say again all before' mean?
positive: Resend everything that came before a named word, because the beginning of the message was lost. Partner forms are all after, word after, word before, and all between.

anchor: wait one gotta find the frequency card
positive: Hang on a few seconds while the frequency list gets looked up; the speaker will be right back on this channel.

anchor: Wait out (proword)
positive: The sender must pause for longer than a few seconds and will call back later; until then the other station is free to use the net.

anchor: What's the difference between 'wait' and 'wait out' on the radio?
positive: Wait signals a short pause of a few seconds, so the other station stays ready. Wait out means the delay will be longer and the conversation is suspended until the sender calls back.

anchor: kilo two that was a long wait one you still there
positive: The caller has been left hanging well past a few seconds and checks that Kilo Two is still on the net; a delay that long should have been a wait out.

anchor: uh this is base wait out uh correction wait one
positive: Base first said it would call back later, then corrected itself to a short pause: stay on, the answer is coming in seconds.

anchor: Give me ten minutes to find out and I'll call you back.
positive: Wait, out; will call you back with the answer.

anchor: Echo One, this is Echo Five, reference your request for vehicles, wait out.
positive: Echo One's vehicle request is acknowledged but can't be answered yet; Echo Five will call back, so Echo One shouldn't hold the channel waiting.

anchor: copy wait one passing you to the duty officer
positive: Got it, hang on a moment while I hand you over to the duty officer.

anchor: Break break
positive: Spoken to cut into ongoing net traffic with urgent or priority information. Everyone else should stop transmitting and listen.

anchor: Break break, all stations, this is Watchtower, convoy approaching gate two, out.
positive: An urgent interruption: the net control (Watchtower) tells every station that a convoy is nearing gate two; no reply needed.

anchor: break break break this is bulldog six all stations hold your positions
positive: Bulldog Six, the commander, forcefully interrupts the net and orders every unit to stay where it is.

anchor: When is it acceptable to say 'break break' on a net?
positive: Only when you have traffic more urgent than what is already on the air, such as a safety issue, a casualty or a critical change. Using it for routine matters wears out its urgency.

anchor: Hotel Two, this is Hotel Six, move to the ridge, break, report when set, over.
positive: Two instructions in one transmission: move to the ridge, and then report when in position, with 'break' separating them.

anchor: Sorry to cut in, everyone, I've got something urgent.
positive: Break break, followed by call signs and the urgent message; other stations go quiet to let it through.

anchor: Why might an operator say 'break' in the middle of a long message?
positive: To divide it into chunks, giving the receiver a moment to write things down. A short pause after break also lets another station interject with emergency traffic.

anchor: this is whiskey one break uh request medevac
positive: Whiskey One identifies itself, uses break to separate the call-up from the content, and begins a request for medical evacuation.

anchor: Any station this net, this is Foxtrot Two Two, radio check, over.
positive: Foxtrot Two Two asks whoever is listening to report how well its signal is being received.

anchor: Foxtrot Two Two, this is Base, read you loud and clear, over.
positive: Base reports that Foxtrot Two Two's signal is strong and perfectly understandable.

anchor: where does five by five come from
positive: Older signal-report scales rated strength and readability each from one to five. Five by five meant maximum strength and perfect readability, the same as loud and clear; the phrase stuck in speech.

anchor: got you weak but readable say again slower
positive: The signal is faint yet understandable, and the listener wants the message repeated at a slower pace.

anchor: What answers are standard for a radio check besides 'loud and clear'?
positive: Strength is described with words like good, weak, very weak or fading, and readability with clear, readable, distorted, intermittent or unreadable. Pairing them, like 'weak but readable', tells the caller what to fix.

anchor: you were lima charlie a minute ago now youre fading
positive: The signal had been loud and clear but is getting weaker, a hint that the sender should move or check the antenna.

anchor: how copy over
positive: Short for 'how do you copy?': the sender asks the other station to confirm it received and understood; replies range from solid copy to broken.

anchor: Comm check on the new handsets, how do you read me, over?
positive: Someone testing new handheld radios asks for a report on signal strength and clarity before relying on them.

anchor: You're broken and unreadable, recommend you change position.
positive: I can't make out what you're saying because your signal keeps cutting out; try moving somewhere with better reception.

anchor: All stations, this is Sabre Base, net opened, check in by call sign, over.
positive: The net controller announces the radio net is active and asks each unit to report in, one at a time.

anchor: sabre one one checking in sabre one two checking in
positive: Two subordinate stations report, in order, that they're on the net and listening after the controller's roll call.

anchor: Why does military radio say 'X, this is Y' rather than just starting to talk?
positive: The called station comes first so the right listener's attention is caught, and the sender identifies itself second. On a busy net, this order prevents confusion about who the message is for.

anchor: Seven (in a call sign)
