positive: Common US Army suffix for a unit's senior NCO: Bravo Seven is usually the company first sergeant and Two-Seven a platoon sergeant, while Five often marks the executive officer. Conventions vary by unit.

anchor: What is an abbreviated call on a radio net?
positive: Once contact is established and there's no risk of confusion, stations may drop the full exchange of call signs, answering with just 'Two, roger, out.' It saves airtime on a crowded net.

anchor: Unknown station, this is Granite Base, identify, over.
positive: Granite Base heard a transmission without a recognizable call sign and demands that the caller identify itself.

anchor: Is anyone on this channel? I need to talk to the convoy leader.
positive: Any station this net, this is Two Four, request contact with convoy commander, over. Procedure names the target and the sender explicitly.

anchor: base base this is two zero
positive: Station Two Zero is calling the base, repeating the call sign to get attention, and will deliver its message once Base answers.

anchor: two one this is zero send over
positive: Zero answers Two One's call with 'send': go ahead with your message, I'm ready to receive. Typical British and Commonwealth phrasing.

anchor: Correct
positive: Proword meaning 'you are correct' or 'what you have transmitted is correct', typically said after the other station reads a message back. Not to be confused with correction, which fixes your own mistake.

anchor: the proword wrong
positive: Proword used after hearing a readback: your last transmission was incorrect, and the correct version follows. Correction is for your own slip; wrong is for the other station's.

anchor: Request a pickup at grid, correction, at checkpoint seven, over.
positive: The sender misspoke 'grid' and fixes it mid-transmission: the pickup is actually at checkpoint seven.

anchor: water count is three correction four cases
positive: A slip caught mid-sentence: the count is four cases, not three. 'Correction' tells the receiver to replace the wrong word.

anchor: Bravo One, this is Bravo Two, disregard this transmission, out.
positive: Bravo Two cancels the message it just sent; Bravo One should act as if it never arrived.

anchor: village name is uh i spell bravo echo romeo golf echo november
positive: Spelling a place name, BERGEN, so whoever plots it on the map isn't guessing the letters from the sound.

anchor: Black Two, read back, over.
positive: Black Two, repeat my whole message back to me exactly as you heard it so I can check you got it right.

anchor: figures two five zero meters
positive: 250 meters; the figures proword signals that the digits two-five-zero follow.

anchor: What should a receiver do when they hear 'correction' mid-message?
positive: Strike the mistaken part and resume from the last word sent correctly. If it's unclear where the correction applies, ask the sender to say again that portion.

anchor: i spell bravo romeo alpha victor oh
positive: BRAVO, spelled phonetically; the last letter came through lazily as 'oh' instead of Oscar, a shortcut that can be confused with zero.

anchor: Flash (precedence)
positive: Top message precedence in US and NATO military messaging, reserved for initial enemy contact or operational emergencies. Flash traffic is handled ahead of everything else.

anchor: What are the standard message precedences from lowest to highest?
positive: Routine, Priority, Immediate and Flash, with some US systems adding Flash Override above Flash. Precedence tells operators which messages to handle first.

anchor: minimize is in effect on this net until further notice
positive: Only essential traffic is allowed on this radio net for now; routine chatter must wait until the order is lifted.

anchor: All stations, this is Control, radio silence until zero six hundred, out.
positive: Control orders every unit to stop transmitting until 6:00 a.m.

anchor: Why is unnecessary chatter discouraged on a tactical net?
positive: A net is shared by many stations; every extra word delays someone else's message and makes transmissions easier to detect. Brief, standardized phrasing keeps the channel open for what matters.

anchor: Please keep your messages short, we need this frequency clear.
positive: All stations, minimize transmissions, essential traffic only, out.

anchor: priority traffic for six standby to copy
positive: A priority message is waiting for the commander, who should get ready to write it down.

anchor: Why do operators pause briefly after pressing the push-to-talk button?
positive: Many radios, especially encrypted ones, need a moment to synchronize before audio goes out. Talking immediately clips the first word, which is often the call sign.

anchor: two thirty pm in military time is what
positive: Fourteen thirty, written 1430. Soldiers often add 'hours' (fourteen thirty hours), while sailors and Marines commonly drop it.

anchor: zero six hundred
positive: Six o'clock in the morning, written 0600; the leading zero is always voiced in military time.

anchor: oh seven forty five
positive: 0745, quarter to eight in the morning. 'Oh' for zero is common in casual speech, though formal procedure prefers 'zero'.

anchor: is midnight zero zero zero zero or twenty four hundred
positive: Both appear: 0000 marks the start of a day and 2400 its end. Many units sidestep the ambiguity by setting deadlines at 2359 or 0001.

anchor: Be back here by quarter past nine tonight.
positive: Return to this location NLT twenty-one fifteen, which is 2115 on the 24-hour clock.

anchor: formation at zero five thirty uniform is pts
positive: Everyone must be in formation at 5:30 a.m. wearing physical training clothes.

anchor: nineteen hundred hours
positive: Seven in the evening, written 1900; adding 'hours' is typical of Army and Air Force speech.

anchor: eta two three hundred maybe two three thirty
positive: Expected arrival is around 11:00 p.m., possibly as late as 11:30 p.m.

anchor: What's the point of the military's 24-hour clock?
positive: It removes a.m. and p.m. confusion, which matters when orders and logs span day and night. Every minute of the day becomes a unique four-digit number.

anchor: twelve hundred
positive: Noon, written 1200. Orders prefer it to 'noon' or '12 o'clock' so nobody confuses it with midnight.

anchor: We have to get up ridiculously early tomorrow.
positive: We're up at zero dark thirty tomorrow.

anchor: brief is at fourteen hundred juliett
positive: The briefing is at 2 p.m. by the local clock, so nobody has to convert from UTC.

anchor: Which military time-zone letters sit on either side of the date line?
positive: Mike is UTC plus 12 and Yankee is UTC minus 12, so a time in Mike and the same time in Yankee are a full day apart.

anchor: meet at the pz at one six hundred local not zulu
positive: Pickup is at 4 p.m. local time; the speaker stresses it is not UTC to avoid a time-zone mix-up.

anchor: Why might a soldier convert times to Zulu in an operations log?
positive: Logs, aircraft and higher headquarters often sit in different time zones. Recording in Zulu keeps every entry on one reference, so events line up when reports are merged.

anchor: Effective two zero zero zero zulu, all traffic on alternate frequency.
positive: Starting at 8 p.m. UTC, everyone moves their radio traffic to the backup channel.

anchor: zero three one eight four five zulu
positive: The 3rd of the month at 18:45 UTC, written as the date-time group 031845Z.

anchor: SITREP
positive: Situation report: a periodic or on-demand summary of a unit's position, activities, status and needs, sent up the chain so commanders can track the picture.

anchor: Six, Two, SITREP follows: at checkpoint three, all personnel accounted for, no change, over.
positive: Platoon Two tells the commander it is at checkpoint three, everyone is present, and nothing new has happened.

anchor: send sitrep when you hit the rp
positive: Higher wants a status update as soon as the unit reaches the RP, which means rally point or release point depending on the plan.

anchor: What usually goes into a SITREP?
positive: Formats vary by unit SOP, but most cover location, current activity, personnel and equipment status, significant events since the last report, and requests or upcoming plans.

anchor: Nothing has changed since my last update.
positive: SITREP, no change from last report, over.

anchor: sitrep negative contact all quiet at the bridge
positive: Status report: no encounter with the enemy or anything of note, and the bridge area is quiet.

anchor: Request SITREP at top of every hour until relieved.
positive: Higher headquarters wants a status report on the hour, every hour, until another unit takes over.

anchor: SITREP: all elements set, no change, standing by.
positive: All our teams are in position, nothing new to report, and we're ready for the next instruction.

anchor: How is a SITREP different from a SPOT report?
positive: A SITREP summarizes your own unit's overall status, often on a schedule. A SPOT report goes out immediately to pass time-sensitive information about something observed.

anchor: SALUTE report
positive: Mnemonic format for describing observed activity: Size, Activity, Location, Unit or uniform, Time, Equipment. Taught to every soldier so observations arrive complete and in order.

anchor: Why does the U in SALUTE cover both unit and uniform?
positive: Observers often can't name an enemy unit, but they can describe what people wear: patches, insignia, camouflage or civilian clothes. That description helps analysts work out who it was.

anchor: SPOT report
positive: An immediate report of time-sensitive information, typically structured with SALUTE fields. Sent as soon as something is observed rather than waiting for a scheduled update.

anchor: spot report follows size two vehicles activity parked
positive: Start of an immediate observation report: two vehicles seen, currently stationary.

anchor: I saw about ten people in civilian clothes near the market around noon, carrying bags.
positive: As a SALUTE: size ten, activity walking, location market, uniform civilian clothes, time twelve hundred, equipment bags.

anchor: Why does the military teach a fixed order for observation reports?
positive: Under stress people forget details or tell them out of order. A fixed mnemonic makes the sender check every field and lets the receiver write it straight into a form.

anchor: Time, one three one five. Equipment, two trucks and a trailer, over.
positive: Closing lines of a SALUTE-style report: the sighting happened at 1:15 p.m. and involved two trucks and a trailer.

anchor: Unit, unknown. No markings observed.
positive: We couldn't tell who they were; no insignia or uniform markings were visible.

anchor: no time for full salute send it as a salt
positive: Speed over detail: send a SALT report with only Size, Activity, Location and Time instead of the full SALUTE format.

anchor: 9-line MEDEVAC request
positive: Standard nine-part radio format for requesting medical evacuation by helicopter or ground vehicle. Each numbered line carries a fixed item, from pickup location to patient counts, so the request is fast and complete.

anchor: What does line 1 of a 9-line MEDEVAC contain?
positive: The location of the pickup site, usually as a grid. It comes first because the evacuation crew needs to know where to go before anything else.

anchor: What are the patient precedence categories on line 3 of a MEDEVAC request?
positive: Urgent, urgent surgical, priority, routine and convenience, each reported with a count. They tell the medical system how quickly each patient must be moved.

anchor: line five two litter one ambulatory
positive: Line five of a MEDEVAC request: two patients must be carried on stretchers and one can walk.

anchor: Litter patient
positive: A casualty who must be carried on a stretcher, called a litter in US military usage. An ambulatory patient, by contrast, can walk with or without help.

anchor: Line seven, marked by green smoke.
positive: For the incoming aircraft, the pickup site will be identified by green smoke.

anchor: MEDEVAC versus CASEVAC?
positive: MEDEVAC uses dedicated medical vehicles or aircraft with medical care en route. CASEVAC moves casualties on whatever non-medical transport is available when no dedicated asset can come.

anchor: line four none
positive: No special equipment, such as a hoist, is needed for this pickup.

anchor: medevac medevac medevac nine line to follow ready to copy
positive: Urgent medical evacuation request flagged; the caller checks that the receiver is ready to write down all nine lines.

anchor: MEDEVAC line eight, what goes there?
positive: Patient nationality and status, for example US or allied military, civilian or detainee. It affects where patients are taken and who must be notified.

anchor: LACE report
positive: Quick post-incident status report: Liquids (water), Ammunition, Casualties, Equipment. Squad and team leaders send it up so the platoon knows what each element needs.

anchor: ACE report
positive: Same idea as LACE without the liquids line: Ammunition, Casualties, Equipment. Which version a unit uses depends on its SOP.

anchor: lace is green green green amber
positive: Water, ammunition and casualties are all fine (green), while equipment is partly degraded (amber). Color codes are a common unit shorthand in these reports.

anchor: When would a squad leader send a LACE report?
positive: Typically after a significant event or at consolidation, once the leader has checked the team and can report water, ammo, casualty and equipment status upward for resupply planning.

anchor: Everyone's okay, we're low on water, plenty of everything else.
positive: LACE: liquids amber, ammunition green, casualties none, equipment green.

anchor: Two Alpha, send ACE, over.
positive: Team Two Alpha is asked for an Ammunition, Casualties, Equipment status report.

anchor: status amber on water red on fuel
positive: Traffic-light status: water is running low (amber) and fuel is critical (red). Exact thresholds come from unit SOP.

anchor: ACE: ammo amber, no casualties, equipment green, over.
positive: Our ammunition is getting low, nobody is hurt, and all our gear is working.

anchor: opord brief at eighteen hundred bring notebooks
positive: The full five-paragraph operation order for the mission will be briefed at 6 p.m.; attendees should come ready to take notes.

anchor: WARNO
positive: Warning order: an early heads-up that a mission is coming, giving whatever is known so units can start preparing before the full OPORD arrives.

anchor: FRAGO
positive: Fragmentary order: a short update modifying an existing OPORD, sending only what changed rather than reissuing the whole order. Also heard as 'frag order'.

anchor: Here's the big-picture plan for how the whole thing will play out.
positive: This is the CONOPS, the concept of operations for the whole mission.

anchor: What is commander's intent?
positive: A brief statement of an operation's purpose and desired end state. It lets subordinates make sensible decisions when the plan breaks down or new orders can't reach them.

anchor: frago two just dropped departure moved up an hour
positive: Fragmentary order number two has arrived and changes the plan: departure is now one hour earlier.

anchor: What does SMEAC stand for?
positive: Situation, Mission, Execution, Administration and logistics, Command and signal: the Marine Corps layout for a five-paragraph order. The Army version uses Sustainment for the fourth paragraph.

anchor: Heads up, we'll probably get tasked with something tomorrow, start packing.
positive: Expect a WARNO; begin preparation now, full order to follow.

anchor: Sergeant, back-brief me on the route before you step off.
positive: Before departing, the sergeant must explain back the plan and the route as understood, so any misunderstanding gets caught early.

anchor: Order's at sixteen hundred in the TOC, squad leaders and up.
positive: Mission briefing at 4 p.m. in the tactical operations center; all squad leaders and more senior leaders must attend.

anchor: FOB
positive: Forward operating base: a secured base close to the area of operations, supporting tactical missions with billeting, logistics and command facilities.

anchor: toc wants a headcount by twenty hundred
positive: The tactical operations center, the unit's command post, wants every person accounted for by 8 p.m.

anchor: lz falcon secure two birds inbound
positive: The helicopter landing zone named Falcon is secured, and two helicopters ('birds') are on their way in.

anchor: Everybody meet at the field where the helicopters will pick us up.
positive: All elements, move to the PZ for pickup, over.

anchor: What is the difference between a FOB and a COP?
positive: A COP (combat outpost) is smaller and more austere, often holding a company or platoon close to the local population. A FOB is larger, with more support, and frequently supplies several COPs.

anchor: were rtb to the fob eta one five mikes
positive: Returning to base: the unit is heading back to the forward operating base and expects to arrive in about fifteen minutes.

anchor: Entering our AO now, all callsigns heads up.
positive: The convoy is crossing into the area of operations assigned to this unit, so every station should be alert.

anchor: Go to the dining hall, eat, and then meet back at the operations center.
positive: Hit the DFAC for chow, then link up at the TOC.

anchor: DFAC
positive: Dining facility, the Army's term for the mess hall. Marines and sailors are more likely to say chow hall, galley or mess deck.

anchor: quebec romeo foxtrot standing by
positive: QRF, the quick reaction force, reporting that it is on standby and ready to launch if needed.

anchor: NCO
positive: Noncommissioned officer: an enlisted leader such as a corporal or sergeant (a petty officer in the Navy). NCOs run day-to-day training, discipline and small teams.

anchor: xo is in charge till the commander gets back
positive: The executive officer, the unit's second in command, runs things until the commander returns.

anchor: get me my rto i need the battalion net
positive: The leader wants the soldier carrying the radio, the radiotelephone operator, right away to talk on the battalion frequency.

anchor: What do S-1 through S-6 mean on an Army battalion staff?
positive: Staff sections by function: S-1 personnel, S-2 intelligence, S-3 operations, S-4 logistics, S-6 communications, with S-5 usually plans or civil affairs. Division and higher use G- instead of S-.

anchor: OIC and NCOIC
positive: Officer in charge and noncommissioned officer in charge: the people responsible for a particular task, detail or section, regardless of their normal job.

anchor: whos the ncoic for the range detail
positive: Someone wants to know which sergeant is in charge of the group running the firing range.

anchor: Who should I call about getting a ride?
positive: Who's the POC for transportation?

anchor: why do soldiers call the medic doc
positive: A traditional nickname of respect for Army combat medics and for Navy corpsmen serving with Marines, used regardless of their rank.

anchor: QRF is spun up and rolling in two zero mikes.
positive: Alerted and prepared, the quick reaction force will depart in about twenty minutes.

anchor: Packets due to the S-1 NLT close of business Friday.
positive: Paperwork must reach the personnel office by the end of the workday Friday at the latest.

anchor: ETA
positive: Estimated time of arrival, given on the net either as a clock time or a duration, such as 'ETA one zero mikes'.

anchor: h minus two all elements in final positions
positive: Two hours before the operation's start time (H-hour), every element should be in its final position.

anchor: D-day
positive: The unnamed day an operation starts. Like H-hour, it anchors planning: D+1 is the day after, D-3 three days before.

anchor: one zero mikes
positive: Ten minutes. 'Mikes' is slang for minutes, taken from M in the phonetic alphabet.

anchor: sp time is zero four hundred dont be late
positive: Start point time, when the unit departs, is 4:00 a.m.; the speaker warns everyone to be on time.

anchor: eta vs etd whats the difference
positive: ETA is when you expect to arrive; ETD is when you expect to depart. Both are estimates and get updated on the net as plans change.

anchor: We need to leave no later than six tomorrow morning.
positive: SP NLT zero six hundred tomorrow.

anchor: How do you address a sergeant first class in the Army?
positive: As 'Sergeant', like most Army NCO grades. First sergeants and sergeants major are the exceptions and are addressed by their full titles.

anchor: why do sergeants get annoyed when you call them sir
positive: Sir and ma'am are reserved for commissioned officers. Enlisted leaders are addressed by rank, so calling a sergeant sir is a mistake, often answered with the old joke 'I work for a living'.

anchor: First Sergeant
positive: Senior enlisted leader of an Army company, addressed as 'First Sergeant' and often nicknamed 'Top'. Same pay grade (E-8) as a master sergeant but a leadership position.

anchor: Colonel Reyes, ma'am, the company is formed.
positive: Report to an officer that the unit is assembled. Lieutenant colonels are also called just 'Colonel' in speech, so she could be an O-5 or O-6.

anchor: Specialist
positive: Army enlisted rank E-4, the same pay grade as corporal but without NCO authority. Addressed as 'Specialist' and abbreviated SPC.

anchor: sierra foxtrot charlie
positive: SFC, the abbreviation for sergeant first class, an Army E-7, spelled out phonetically.

anchor: How are Army warrant officers addressed?
positive: Commonly as 'Mister' or 'Ms.' plus last name, or as 'Chief' for chief warrant officers. Warrant officers are technical specialists, helicopter pilots among them, ranked between enlisted and commissioned officers.

anchor: top wants all squad leaders in the cp now
positive: The first sergeant, nicknamed Top, wants every squad leader at the command post immediately.

anchor: Are both privates and privates first class called 'Private' in speech?
positive: Yes. E-1 through E-3 in the Army are all spoken as 'Private' plus last name, and the rank insignia sorts out the exact grade.

anchor: Sergeant Major Thompson wants the barracks inspected at noon.
positive: The senior enlisted adviser is named by full title; Army E-9s are never shortened to just 'Sergeant', even in passing.

anchor: Why is a Navy captain much more senior than an Army captain?
positive: Navy captain is O-6, equal to an Army colonel, while an Army captain is O-3, equal to a Navy lieutenant. Same word, very different pay grades.

anchor: skippers on the bridge
positive: The ship's commanding officer, informally called the skipper, has arrived on the bridge.

anchor: Who is called 'Captain' on a Navy ship?
positive: The commanding officer, by custom, whatever their actual rank. A commander (O-5) in command of a destroyer is still 'Captain' aboard.

anchor: Chief
positive: Navy and Coast Guard address for a chief petty officer (E-7), and informally for senior and master chiefs too. Chiefs form the ship's senior enlisted leadership, the chiefs' mess.

anchor: Petty officer: which grades does the title cover?
positive: A Navy or Coast Guard noncommissioned officer in grades E-4 through E-6 (third, second and first class), addressed as 'Petty Officer' plus last name.

anchor: Rating (Navy)
positive: A sailor's occupational specialty, such as boatswain's mate or hospital corpsman. Combined with pay grade it forms the rate, like BM2 for a second class boatswain's mate.

anchor: Aye aye, ma'am. Petty Officer Ruiz reporting as ordered.
positive: Acknowledging an order from a female officer, the sailor announces arrival as instructed.

anchor: lima tango juliett golf
positive: Spelled-out abbreviation for lieutenant junior grade (LTJG), the Navy and Coast Guard O-2 rank.

anchor: Ensign
positive: Lowest commissioned rank in the Navy and Coast Guard (O-1), equivalent to an Army second lieutenant. Also the name for the national flag a ship flies.

anchor: senior chief said muster at zero seven on the mess decks
positive: A senior chief petty officer ordered everyone to assemble for roll call at 7:00 a.m. in the crew's eating area.

anchor: Do Marines shorten sergeant ranks the way the Army does?
positive: No. Marines use the full title, such as 'Staff Sergeant' or 'Gunnery Sergeant', while Army soldiers say just 'Sergeant' for most NCO grades.

anchor: gunny wants the platoon formed up in five
positive: Gunnery sergeant's order: the platoon must be assembled in formation within five minutes.

anchor: Lance Corporal
positive: Marine Corps enlisted rank E-3, the backbone of many infantry fire teams. The US Army has no lance corporal, though the British Army does.

anchor: What rank titles does the Air Force use for enlisted members?
positive: Airman Basic, Airman, Airman First Class, Senior Airman, then Staff, Technical, Master, Senior Master and Chief Master Sergeant. Technical sergeant is usually shortened to 'Tech Sergeant'.

anchor: Chief, in the Air Force
positive: Address for a chief master sergeant, the highest enlisted grade (E-9). Unlike the Navy's broader use, the Air Force reserves 'Chief' for that top grade.

anchor: Staff Sergeant, Lance Corporal Ortiz, the working party is mustered.
positive: A Marine reports to a staff NCO: title first, then the Marine's own rank and name, then the report. A working party is a group detailed for manual labor.

anchor: How is an Air Force second lieutenant addressed in speech?
positive: As 'Lieutenant', exactly like a first lieutenant; every US service drops the 'second' or 'first' in conversation.

anchor: Corporal, have your fire team police call the area by sixteen hundred.
positive: Litter sweep ordered: the Marine NCO's four-person team must pick up all trash in the area by 4 p.m.

anchor: What does 'O-3' or 'E-5' mean?
positive: Pay grades: O for commissioned officers, E for enlisted, W for warrant officers, with the number showing seniority. They let people compare ranks across services, since titles differ.

anchor: Two One, this is Zero, fetch Sunray, over.
positive: Headquarters asks station Two One to bring its commander, known by the appointment title Sunray, to the radio to speak personally.

anchor: What does 'roger so far' mean on a British net?
positive: A check partway through a long message, asking the receiver to confirm they have everything up to that point before the sender continues.

anchor: All stations, this is Zero, exercise ends at sixteen hundred, acknowledge, over.
positive: Headquarters announces the exercise finishes at 4 p.m. and requires every station to confirm it received and understood.

anchor: How do British forces pronounce 'lieutenant'?
positive: As 'leftenant', the traditional British and Commonwealth pronunciation. Americans say 'loo-tenant'; both name the same junior officer rank.

anchor: NATO rank codes (OR and OF)
positive: STANAG 2116 compares ranks across nations: OR-1 to OR-9 for other ranks (enlisted) and OF-1 to OF-10 for officers. A US Army captain and a British Army captain are both OF-2.

anchor: Hello all stations, this is Zero, radio check, over.
positive: British-style net call: the headquarters, call sign Zero, asks every station to report signal quality.

anchor: hello two one this is zero message over
positive: Zero, the headquarters, tells station Two One it has a message to pass and waits for Two One to say it's ready.

anchor: Brew's on, scoff in ten.
positive: British soldier slang: the tea is ready and food will be served in about ten minutes.

anchor: Do NATO allies all use the same prowords?
positive: Allied Communications Publication ACP 125 gives a common English set, so over, out, wilco and say again work across NATO. National habits still differ, like British 'Sunray' or US call sign suffixes.

anchor: Squaddie
positive: British slang for a private soldier, roughly the equivalent of the American 'grunt' or 'GI'. Affectionate rather than insulting.

anchor: Hooah
positive: Army all-purpose word for yes, understood, good, or general enthusiasm. Marines say 'oorah' and Navy special warfare 'hooyah' for the same spirit; using the wrong one marks you as an outsider.

anchor: Ruck
positive: Short for rucksack, the soldier's backpack, and also a verb: 'we ruck at zero five' means a loaded foot march. 'Ruck up' means put your pack on and get ready to go.

anchor: Never go anywhere on base alone, always take your partner.
positive: Where's your battle buddy? Nobody goes anywhere alone.

anchor: rally point is two klicks east of the river
positive: The meeting point sits about two kilometers east of the river; a klick is slang for a kilometer.

anchor: hooah sergeant were good to go
positive: Enthusiastic answer to the sergeant: the team understands and is fully ready.

anchor: What does 'hurry up and wait' describe?
positive: The common military experience of rushing to be somewhere on time only to stand around for hours before anything happens. Said with resigned humor across all services.

anchor: Fobbit
positive: Mildly teasing slang for someone who rarely leaves the FOB during a deployment, blending FOB and hobbit.

anchor: Grab your gear, we're about to leave on foot.
positive: Ruck up, we step off in five mikes.

anchor: you tracking yeah tracking
positive: One person checks that the other understands; the answer 'tracking' means yes, I'm following.

anchor: Head
positive: Navy and Marine word for a toilet or restroom, from the bow of old sailing ships where crews relieved themselves. The Army says latrine; airmen usually say restroom or latrine.

anchor: whose gear adrift by the hatch
positive: Somebody left equipment unsecured next to the doorway, and the owner had better claim it before it gets confiscated.

anchor: Oorah
positive: Marine Corps spirited cry signaling acknowledgment, approval or motivation. Saying 'hooah' to a Marine, the Army version, is a classic faux pas.

anchor: Scuttlebutt
positive: Navy and Marine word for rumor or gossip, from the scuttled cask (butt) of drinking water where sailors once gathered. Drinking fountains are still called scuttlebutts.

anchor: Why do Marines call the floor a 'deck' even on land?
positive: As a naval service, the Marine Corps uses shipboard vocabulary everywhere: deck for floor, bulkhead for wall, overhead for ceiling, hatch for door, ladderwell for stairs.

anchor: I'm going to bed.
positive: Alright, I'm hitting the rack.

anchor: field day tonight nineteen hundred all hands
positive: Everyone must take part in a thorough barracks cleaning tonight at 7:00 p.m.; for Marines, field day means cleaning, not a sports event.

anchor: Aye aye
positive: Navy and Marine reply to an order meaning 'I understand and will carry it out', the naval counterpart to wilco. A single 'aye' simply means yes.

anchor: There's a rumor going around that we're getting extra days off.
positive: Scuttlebutt is we're getting a ninety-six, meaning a four-day pass.

anchor: Wingman
positive: Originally the pilot flying beside and behind the lead aircraft for mutual support; in Air Force culture it also means a peer who looks out for you, like the Army's battle buddy.

anchor: meet me on the flightline by tail two zero
positive: Rendezvous in the aircraft parking and servicing area, next to the jet whose tail number ends in two zero.

anchor: He's in crew rest, don't call him until oh-five.
positive: The pilot is in a protected rest period before flying and should not be disturbed until 5 a.m.

anchor: Step
positive: Aircrew term for walking out from the squadron to the aircraft. 'Step time' is when crews leave for their jets after the brief.

anchor: what does chair force mean
positive: A teasing nickname for the Air Force from other services, joking that airmen work at desks. Airmen usually fire back with jokes about the Army's living conditions.

anchor: brief at oh six step at seven fifteen
positive: Flight briefing at 0600, with the aircrew walking out to the aircraft at 0715.

anchor: Fini flight
positive: A pilot's final flight with a unit or before retirement, traditionally ending with the pilot being hosed down with water on the flightline.

anchor: does the air force have its own hooah
positive: There is no Air Force-wide equivalent of the Army's hooah or the Marines' oorah. Airmen sometimes borrow hooah informally, though it stays associated with the Army.

anchor: SNAFU
positive: World War II slang, politely 'Situation Normal, All Fouled Up': things have gone wrong, as usual. It has since entered general English.

anchor: FUBAR
positive: Polite gloss: 'Fouled Up Beyond All Repair (or Recognition)'. Describes something hopelessly broken or ruined, a step worse than SNAFU.

anchor: my pcs orders finally dropped were going to germany in march
positive: Orders for a permanent change of station, a move to a new duty assignment, have been officially issued; the family relocates to Germany in March.

anchor: Disregard the slides, that tasking is OBE.
positive: Forget preparing the slides; circumstances changed and the task has been overtaken by events.

anchor: BLUF
positive: Bottom line up front: state the conclusion or request first, then the details. Standard advice for military emails and briefings.

anchor: Do it the way our unit always does it, by the book.
positive: Execute per SOP, the unit's standard operating procedure.

anchor: Are SNAFU and FUBAR acceptable in formal reports?
positive: No. They are informal soldier slang, fine in conversation but replaced by plain descriptions in official writing.

anchor: range day was total snafu buses never showed
positive: Complaint that range training went wrong in the usual way: the transport never arrived.

anchor: bluf need two more trucks nlt zero eight hundred
positive: Main point first: we need two additional trucks by 8:00 a.m. at the latest.

anchor: As you were
positive: Command to go back to what you were doing, or to cancel a preceding command. Also said by a senior entering a room after people stood up, so they can return to work.

anchor: On me
positive: Instruction to gather on or follow the speaker. A leader saying 'on me' wants the team to form up around them or move with them.

anchor: second squad set
positive: Second squad reports it is in position and ready for the next step.

anchor: Alpha team, moving to the treeline.
positive: Alpha team announces it is relocating to the line of trees so others won't expect it at its old position.

anchor: Morning, Marines, carry on.
positive: A passing officer releases the Marines to continue what they were doing instead of stopping to render courtesies.

anchor: At ease and as you were sound alike to civilians; how do they differ?
positive: At ease is a drill position allowing some relaxation while staying in place and quiet. As you were returns people to whatever they were doing before, or cancels a command.

anchor: on me on me rally here
positive: Urgent call from a leader for the team to gather around them at this spot.

anchor: Okay everyone, line up in formation right now.
positive: Fall in, platoon, right here by the flagpole.

anchor: belay my last wrong grid
positive: Cancel my previous transmission; it had the wrong grid. 'Belay' is naval-origin slang for stop or cancel.

anchor: Battalion net is up, all stations checked in.
positive: The radio network is working and every station has reported in; up here means operational.

anchor: 1MC
positive: General announcing system on a US Navy ship, heard in every space. Orders like general quarters and the daily routine are passed over it.

anchor: Now hear this, now hear this.
positive: Traditional opener on a ship's announcing system, alerting everyone that an important announcement follows.

anchor: General quarters, general quarters. All hands man your battle stations.
positive: Highest readiness ordered: every sailor must go to their assigned emergency station immediately.

anchor: sweepers sweepers man your brooms
positive: Daily call for sailors to clean the ship's decks and passageways, a long-standing Navy routine announcement.

anchor: Taps, taps, lights out. Maintain silence about the decks.
positive: Night announcement: lights go off in berthing areas and the crew should keep noise down.

anchor: Officer of the deck
positive: Officer on watch responsible for the ship's safe navigation and routine on behalf of the captain. The Royal Navy and many allied navies call the role officer of the watch.

anchor: I relieve you. I stand relieved.
positive: Formal exchange when one watchstander takes over from another, making clear exactly when responsibility transfers.

anchor: very well make it so
positive: Shipboard approval: 'very well' acknowledges the report and 'make it so' authorizes carrying out the proposed action.

anchor: man overboard man overboard port side
positive: Someone has fallen off the ship on the left side; every sailor responds immediately to recover them.

anchor: Bridge, combat, contact bearing two seven zero, opening.
positive: Combat information center reporting to the bridge: a radar or visual contact due west (bearing 270) is moving away.

anchor: is saying come in bravo two proper radio procedure
positive: It's a movie habit. Proper procedure simply calls the station and identifies yourself, 'Bravo Two, this is Bravo Six, over'; the over already invites the reply.

anchor: What does 'watch your OPSEC on the net' mean?
positive: Operations security: don't say names, locations, times or plans in the clear that a listener could piece together, because the radio may not be secure.

anchor: is copy the same thing as roger
positive: Both acknowledge receipt in practice. Roger is the formal proword; copy is informal but common. Neither means yes or I will comply.

anchor: rodger wilko over and out
positive: Three mistakes stacked: misspelled roger and wilco, which are redundant together, plus the contradictory over and out. A proper reply would be just 'wilco, out'.

anchor: repeat repeat the grid
positive: Someone wanted the grid resent but used 'repeat', which in artillery means fire again. 'Say again grid' is the correct request.

anchor: Yes, I understood, and I'll do it.
positive: Wilco: one word covers acknowledgment, understanding and intent to comply.

anchor: Why shouldn't you say 'roger' to mean 'yes'?
positive: Roger only confirms you received the message. If someone asks a yes-or-no question, answering roger leaves it unanswered; use affirmative or negative instead.

anchor: Uh, Base, it's me, Jenkins, are you there?
positive: Untrained caller using a name instead of a call sign and asking an open question. Correct form: 'Base, this is Two Three, over.'

anchor: What happens if two stations transmit at once?
positive: On most military and aviation radios the signals collide, leaving a squeal or garble so neither message gets through. That is why stations wait for over and keep transmissions short.

anchor: negative negative i say again do not cross
positive: No, and I'm repeating it for emphasis: you must not cross.

anchor: Two-one, moving.
positive: Element two-one has started moving. The call lets the element staying put know to keep watch over that lane and not lose track of them.

anchor: bravo team set over
positive: Bravo team has reached its spot, stopped and is ready, so the other team may now move. 'Over' hands the turn back to the leader.

anchor: alpha set bravo move
positive: Alpha team reports it's in place and ready, and the leader tells Bravo to start moving now that it's covered.

anchor: bounding
positive: Alternating movement where one element moves while another stays in place watching, then they swap. On the radio it sounds like a steady rhythm of 'moving' and 'set' calls.

anchor: why do teams say moving before they get up instead of just going
positive: Announcing movement keeps everyone's picture current. A teammate who doesn't know you've shifted can lose track of you, so the call prevents confusion and lets others acknowledge first.

anchor: Hey, we're stopping here for a bit to wait for the others to catch up.
positive: All stations, Two, halting at current location, waiting for link-up, over.

anchor: one is up on the left two is moving to the right of the trail
positive: Team one has reached its place on the left side; team two is now shifting over to the right side of the trail.

anchor: Hold what you've got.
positive: Stop where you are and keep the ground you currently occupy; no advancing or falling back until the leader gives further word.

anchor: Moving versus move: why does one syllable matter on a team net?
positive: 'Moving' is a report: I, or my element, am now in motion. 'Move' is a leader's instruction to start. Confusing them can make a leader think an order was already carried out.

anchor: lead element halting short of the road crossing uh wait one
positive: Point element has stopped just before a road and asks everyone to pause briefly while it checks the crossing.

anchor: Contact
positive: Called the instant someone sees or runs into something significant, usually a hostile presence. It is shouted first and loud so every head turns to the caller before any details.

anchor: What information should follow a contact call?
positive: A common teaching sequence is direction, distance and description: where it is relative to you or a landmark, how far, and what it is. Others can then orient without a long conversation.

anchor: Contact front, two hundred, by the lone tree.
positive: Something has been spotted ahead of the group about two hundred meters out, near the single tree everyone can see.

anchor: contact left uh tree hundred near the white building
positive: Sighting off to the left roughly 300 meters away, close to the white building.

anchor: Clock direction
positive: Describing direction as a clock face with twelve o'clock straight ahead along the direction of travel. Fast for ground teams and pilots, but only works if everyone shares the same twelve.

anchor: why would someone say by the red barn instead of giving a compass bearing
positive: Under stress a shared landmark is faster to say and to find than 'zero-six-five degrees.' Bearings are precise but take time to plot; landmarks give everyone the same picture instantly.

anchor: I just saw two people walking along the ridge off to our right, maybe five hundred meters out.
positive: Two personnel, right, five hundred, moving along the ridgeline, how copy?

anchor: Spotter to all, vehicle moving south on the main road, one minute from your location.
positive: An observer warns the team that a vehicle heading south on the main road will reach them in about sixty seconds.

anchor: negative contact east side all quiet
positive: Nobody and nothing has been seen on the east side; things are calm there.

anchor: Cease fire
positive: Order to stop shooting immediately and completely. Unlike check fire it is not a pause: nobody resumes until a new order to fire is given.

anchor: check fire
positive: Temporary halt, used especially with artillery, mortars and range control when something may be wrong. Firing stops until the issue is sorted out and can then resume; on many ranges anyone, of any rank, may call it.

anchor: Why is 'cease fire' echoed by everyone who hears it?
positive: Noise and wind swallow voices. Repeating the call down the line makes sure people far from the original caller stop too; on the radio it's often said three times for the same reason.

anchor: Danger close
positive: Warning in a request for supporting fire that friendly troops are very near the intended impact area. It flags higher risk, and the person on the ground has to accept that risk explicitly.

anchor: who actually signs off on danger close
positive: Under US joint doctrine the ground commander accepts the risk, typically by passing their initials over the radio. The step exists so nobody can say they didn't know friendlies were that close.

anchor: check fire check fire check fire range is fouled
positive: Stop firing at once: a person, vehicle or animal has entered the impact area or another hazard has appeared, so the range is not safe.

anchor: range control check fire lifted resume firing
positive: The temporary halt is over: the problem has been fixed and firing may start again.

anchor: Everyone stop shooting right now, there are people walking downrange.
positive: Cease fire, cease fire, cease fire. Personnel downrange.

anchor: Range control, Tower, all lanes are cold.
positive: The range tower reports no firing on any lane, so it is safe for people to walk forward and check targets.

anchor: In position
positive: Report that an element has reached its assigned spot and is ready. Usually paired with the team name, like 'Charlie in position,' so a leader can track who is where.

anchor: all clear
positive: An area has been checked and nothing dangerous found. Fire crews, rescue teams and patrols all use it, for a room, a building, a sector or a whole site.

anchor: room two clear moving to three
positive: Searchers have checked the second room, found it empty and are heading into the third.

anchor: Sector north, no change.
positive: The person watching the northern sector has seen nothing new since the last report.

anchor: alpha up bravo up charlie up all up
positive: Each team answers the roll call in turn, and the leader concludes that every element is present and ready.

anchor: Why does a leader ask for a status roll call instead of assuming everyone heard?
positive: Silence on a radio might mean agreement, a dead battery or someone out of range. A roll call makes each station speak, proving they're there and that the message reached them.

anchor: Two-two, status?
positive: Team two-two, tell me where you are and how things are going.

anchor: we got to the spot by the bridge and we're ready whenever you are
positive: Bridge position, in position and ready, awaiting your call, over.

anchor: Charlie element, all personnel accounted for.
positive: Charlie element reports every member is present and known to be safe.

anchor: yeah were up an set at the hold point waitin on you
positive: The team has reached the agreed holding spot, is ready, and is waiting for the other group or the leader's go-ahead.

anchor: Phase line
positive: A named line on the map, often along a road, river or ridge, used to coordinate and report progress. 'Crossing phase line Gold' tells everyone where you are without reading coordinates.

anchor: rally point
positive: Pre-agreed place where people regroup if they get separated or a plan falls apart. Everyone learns it before setting out so no radio talk is needed to reunite.

anchor: We just got to the second stop on the route, a few minutes ahead of schedule.
positive: Checkpoint two, five minutes ahead of time, continuing.

anchor: ORP
positive: Objective rally point: a spot short of the final destination where a team stops, organizes and makes final checks before continuing.

anchor: Six, this is Three, crossing PL Red, time one-four-two-zero.
positive: Unit Three tells its commander, call sign Six, that it is passing the map line named Red at 14:20.

anchor: at checkpoint four on time no issues
positive: The team reached the fourth checkpoint on schedule and has nothing to report.

anchor: Why are phase lines named with colors or words instead of numbers?
positive: Names like Red or Gold are hard to confuse with coordinates, distances or times, which are all numbers. A distinct word on a busy net is far less likely to be misheard as a figure.

anchor: If we get split up, everyone meet back at the old stone bridge.
positive: Rally point is the stone bridge. Acknowledge, over.

anchor: tree tree whiskey at checkpoint niner
positive: Call sign 33W reporting that it has reached checkpoint 9.

anchor: what does release point mean when a group is moving
positive: It's where a group leaves a larger formation or controlled route and continues on its own, or splits into smaller elements. Reporting it marks a handover of control.

anchor: LZ cold
positive: The landing zone is safe: no threat and no fire at or near it. Aircrew take it to mean they can come in normally.

anchor: lz hot
positive: Landing zone is under threat or taking fire. Pilots may change their approach, delay or abort based on that single word.

anchor: Why does the ground team say 'popping smoke' but let the pilot name the color?
positive: If the ground announced the color first, an adversary could pop the same color elsewhere to lure the aircraft. Having aircrew report what they see and the ground confirm it prevents spoofing.

anchor: Dustoff two-four, popping smoke now, identify.
positive: The ground team tells the medevac helicopter, Dustoff 24, that a smoke marker is going off and asks the pilot to say what color they see.

anchor: i see yellow smoke on the east side of the clearing
positive: Pilot reports spotting yellow smoke at the clearing's east edge; the ground now confirms or denies that it's theirs.

anchor: Confirm yellow. Wind from the north, light. LZ cold.
positive: Ground agrees the yellow smoke is the correct marker, gives a light northerly wind for the landing and says the zone is safe.

anchor: marking with orange panel on the north edge of the field
positive: The ground team says the landing spot is shown by an orange panel at the field's north edge.

anchor: The field's safe, nobody around, wind is blowing from the west, come on down by the orange panel.
positive: LZ cold, wind west, land at the orange panel, over.

anchor: lz is hot lz is hot wave off
positive: The landing area has turned dangerous; abort the approach and do not land.

anchor: What does 'one minute out' mean from an inbound helicopter?
positive: The aircraft expects to arrive in about sixty seconds. It's the ground team's cue to finish marking and get everyone clear of the landing area.

anchor: Infil
positive: Short for infiltration: moving a team into an area, often discreetly. Names the phase of an operation where people are inserted on foot, by vehicle, boat or aircraft.

anchor: exfil
positive: Exfiltration: getting a team out of an area when the mission ends. Plans usually carry a primary method plus alternates in case the first one fails.

anchor: is extract the same thing as exfil
positive: Close but not identical. Extraction usually means someone else picks you up, like a helicopter or boat; exfil covers any way of leaving, including walking out on your own.

anchor: Nomad, Rover, infil complete, beginning movement to the hide site.
positive: Rover tells its controlling station, Nomad, that it got in successfully and is starting toward its concealed observation spot.

anchor: were at the exfil point ready for pickup in five
positive: The team has reached the place it will be collected from and expects to be ready to board in five minutes.

anchor: insertion delayed thirty mikes due to weather
positive: Dropping the team off has been pushed back half an hour because of the weather.

anchor: We're out of the area and on our way back now, everybody's with us.
positive: Exfil underway, all personnel accounted for, returning to base.

anchor: Request emergency extract at alternate PZ, time now.
positive: We need to be picked up immediately, from the backup pickup location rather than the planned one.

anchor: What is a lost comms plan?
positive: An agreement made before setting out about what to do if radios fail: where to go, how long to wait, and when the base should assume trouble. It means silence triggers action instead of guesswork.

anchor: Authenticate
positive: Proword asking the other station to answer a challenge drawn from the current code table; the reply is checked against your own copy before anything else is trusted.

anchor: Why would a station ask for authentication on a radio net?
positive: Anyone with a transmitter can try to impersonate a unit. Asking the caller to authenticate checks they hold the same codes, so a spoofed order to move or cease fire gets caught.

anchor: Challenge and password
positive: Pair of words where a sentry says the challenge and the approaching person must give the password. They change often and mean nothing unless both sides know the current pair.

anchor: i authenticate uh hotel
positive: A station answering an authentication challenge with the letter its code table gives; the challenger checks it against their own copy.

anchor: radio silence
positive: Order not to transmit at all, or only in emergencies. It keeps a group from revealing its presence, or keeps a channel quiet for priority traffic.

anchor: why keep transmissions short if nobody can decode them
positive: Encryption hides the words, not the signal. Long or frequent transmissions from one spot let direction-finding equipment locate the transmitter, so short calls also protect position.

anchor: Hang on, I'm not sure that's really you on the radio. Prove it.
positive: Authenticate using today's table, over.

anchor: why do they use call signs instead of peoples names on the radio
positive: Call signs hide identities and unit details from eavesdroppers and stay stable when individuals rotate. They're also short and chosen to be easy to hear.

anchor: Nomad to all stations, silence lifted, resume normal traffic, out.
positive: The earlier order to stay off the air is cancelled; stations may transmit normally again.

anchor: Net control station
positive: NCS: the station that runs a radio net, deciding who talks when, authorizing traffic and keeping order. Ham operators, emergency services and military units all use the role.

anchor: PACE plan
positive: Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency: four layers of communication agreed in advance, so if the main radio fails a team already knows what to switch to next.

anchor: Why do teams agree on code words for key events before a mission?
positive: Short pre-briefed words for moments like 'reached the river' or 'need pickup' let a team pass a whole update in one word, saving airtime and telling eavesdroppers little.

anchor: We'll turn the radio on and call you every two hours on the hour, starting at noon.
positive: Comm windows every two hours on the hour, first at one-two-zero-zero.

anchor: push
positive: Slang for a radio frequency or channel, as in 'go to push three' or 'switch to the fire push.' Heard across military aviation, ground units and wildland fire.

anchor: All stations, switch to alternate, I say again, switch to alternate.
positive: Everyone should change to the backup frequency; the instruction is repeated so no station misses it.

anchor: your coming in loud but distorted back off the mic a little
positive: Your signal is strong but garbled, probably because you're too close to the microphone or shouting; hold it a little farther away and speak normally.

anchor: I've got a bunch of stuff to tell you, have you got something to write with?
positive: I have traffic for you, ready to copy?

anchor: Azimuth
positive: Horizontal angle measured clockwise from a north reference, 0 to 360 degrees or 0 to 6400 mils. Land navigators talk about 'shooting an azimuth' when they take one with a compass.

anchor: back azimuth
positive: The reverse direction: add 180 degrees if the azimuth is under 180, subtract 180 if it's over. Used to retrace steps or confirm you're on the line you think.

anchor: whats the difference between a bearing and an azimuth
positive: Day to day they're often used interchangeably. Strictly, azimuth runs clockwise from north through 360 degrees, while traditional bearings can be quadrant style like N45E; mariners and pilots also split bearings into true, magnetic and relative.

anchor: Declination
positive: Angle between true north and magnetic north at a given place. Map margins state it so compass readings can be converted to map directions; it varies by location and drifts over the years.

anchor: G-M angle
positive: Grid-magnetic angle: the difference between grid north on a military map and magnetic north. Navigators apply it to convert a map azimuth into a compass azimuth and back.

anchor: azimuth two seven fife degrees magnetic
positive: 275 degrees magnetic, a little north of due west.

anchor: back azimuth to the trail junction is two niner zero
positive: Heading back to the trail junction means walking on 290 degrees, the reverse of the outbound line.

anchor: Why do some navigators use mils instead of degrees?
positive: A circle holds 6400 NATO mils, a much finer unit, and one mil spans roughly one meter at one kilometer. That makes quick estimates of distance and small corrections easier.

anchor: Keep walking roughly northeast, about forty-five degrees on your compass.
positive: Maintain azimuth zero-four-five magnetic.

anchor: Relative bearing
positive: Direction measured from the bow or nose of a vessel or vehicle rather than from north, often given in degrees off the bow or as clock positions. Mariners use it for traffic, pilots for 'two o'clock' calls.

anchor: MGRS
positive: Military Grid Reference System: NATO's standard way of stating a location as a grid zone, a 100-kilometer square ID and an even string of digits. Anyone with a matching map can find the same spot.

anchor: how precise is an eight digit grid
positive: Eight digits, four for easting and four for northing, pin a location to a 10-meter square. Six digits give 100 meters and ten digits give 1 meter.

anchor: What is a polar plot when sending a location?
positive: Giving a location as direction and distance from a known point, often the sender's own position, as in 'azimuth one-two-zero, eight hundred meters', instead of reading out a full grid.

anchor: grid zone one eight sierra
positive: Grid zone designator 18S: longitude zone 18 plus latitude band S, the opening part of an MGRS reference.

anchor: grid tango quebec fower seven niner one six zero two six tree eight
positive: MGRS square TQ followed by a ten-digit reference, easting 47916 and northing 02638, which pins the spot to about 1 meter.

anchor: grid uh november victor six eight seven four two two
positive: Grid NV 687 422, a six-digit reference accurate to roughly 100 meters.

anchor: Correction on that grid: easting is four-six-one, not four-one-six.
positive: The sender fixes an earlier mistake: two easting digits were transposed, and the right value is 461.

anchor: Why do operators pause between the easting and northing when reading a grid?
positive: Long digit strings are easy to lose. Chunking them, with a clear break between the two halves, helps the receiver write them correctly and notice a missing digit.

anchor: rally point grid is eight one five two zero four
positive: The regroup location is at grid 815 204, a six-digit reference good to about 100 meters.

anchor: Why might teams avoid sending grids in the clear?
positive: A grid in plain language tells anyone listening exactly where you are or will be. Units use encrypted radios or agreed reference points with offsets so locations aren't given away.

anchor: Pace count
positive: Number of steps, usually counting one foot, a person takes to cover 100 meters. Navigators learn theirs on a measured course and adjust for slope, load and vegetation.

anchor: uh im at six beads so we done about six hundred
positive: The pacer is tallying on pace-count beads: six beads slid down means roughly 600 meters walked.

anchor: pace count says were about six hundred meters from the creek
positive: Going by counted steps, the navigator estimates the group is roughly 600 meters from the creek.

anchor: Saddle
positive: Low point between two hilltops along a ridge. Teams name one as a meeting place because it's easy to recognize on both the map and the ground.

anchor: team moving up the draw west side of hill two one four
positive: The team is climbing the shallow gully on the western side of the hill marked 214 on the map.

anchor: handrail
positive: A linear feature like a stream, fence or road that a navigator follows alongside to stay on course without constant compass checks.

anchor: Catching feature
positive: Something beyond your target, such as a river or road, that tells you you've overshot if you reach it. Navigators brief it so the team knows when to stop and backtrack.

anchor: What are the five major terrain features?
positive: US Army land navigation teaches hill, ridge, valley, saddle and depression as the majors, with draw, spur and cliff as minor features and cut and fill as supplementary.

anchor: We're walking along the stream with it on our left, and we'll stop where it meets the road.
positive: Moving along the creek, creek on our left, will halt at the road intersection.

anchor: Navigator to team leader, we're on the spur, not the ridge; we drifted about two hundred meters west.
positive: The navigator admits a position error: the team is on a smaller finger of high ground than planned and has strayed roughly 200 meters west.

anchor: SAR
positive: Search and rescue: finding and helping people in distress on land, at sea or in the air. Run by agencies such as the Coast Guard, mountain rescue teams and air force rescue units.

anchor: CSAR
positive: Combat search and rescue: recovering isolated personnel, such as a downed aircrew, from hostile territory. Its radio procedures stress authenticating the survivor so a decoy can't lure rescuers.

anchor: On-scene coordinator
positive: OSC: the unit or person assigned to coordinate all search assets at the scene, tracking who is searching where. Older maritime texts call it the on-scene commander.

anchor: Sector, Coast Guard helo six-five-zero-one, on scene at datum, commencing expanding square.
positive: Helicopter 6501 tells the sector it has reached the most probable survivor position and is starting its outward spiral search.

anchor: EPIRB
positive: Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon: a marine distress beacon transmitting on 406 MHz to satellites, alerting rescue centers with the vessel's identity and usually a GPS position.

anchor: What is an expanding square search?
positive: A pattern that starts at datum and spirals outward in legs that lengthen after every two turns, tracing a square. It suits cases where the location is fairly well known.

anchor: Sector, Rescue one-two, survivor in sight, one person in the water, orange life jacket.
positive: Rescue unit 12 tells the Coast Guard sector it has eyes on one person in the water wearing an orange life vest.

anchor: strobe in sight strobe in sight bearing about tree one zero from us
positive: The search crew can see a flashing strobe, likely the survivor's signal light, in the direction of 310 degrees from their position.

anchor: We've gone over our whole area and didn't find anyone. What do you want us to do next?
positive: Search area Bravo covered, negative results, request further tasking.

anchor: when you relay someone elses mayday whose name goes after this is
positive: Your own. The relaying vessel says 'Mayday relay', then 'this is' plus its own name, then passes the distressed vessel's name and details, so rescuers know who is in danger and whom to call back.

anchor: Seelonce Mayday
positive: Imposed by the station controlling a distress situation to silence everyone else on the channel. Only distress traffic may be sent until it's lifted.

anchor: seelonce feenee
positive: From French 'silence fini': the announcement that distress traffic has ended and the channel can return to normal use.

anchor: Securite
positive: Pronounced 'say-cure-ee-TAY,' it prefixes a safety message such as a navigation hazard or gale warning. Ranks below Mayday and Pan-Pan in priority.

anchor: Channel 16
positive: VHF marine channel on 156.8 MHz, the international distress, safety and calling frequency. Vessels monitor it and, once in contact, move to a working channel.

anchor: Why do mariners leave channel 16 after making contact?
positive: Channel 16 has to stay open for distress and safety calls. Routine conversations shift to a working channel so they never block someone calling for help.

anchor: Mayday, Blue Heron, two miles south of Point Judith, taking on water, four persons aboard, require immediate assistance.
positive: The body of a maritime distress call after the triple-Mayday opening: vessel name, position, nature of distress, people aboard and the help needed.

anchor: pan pan pan pan pan pan this is fishing vessel marie we have lost our engine
positive: Urgency call from fishing vessel Marie: the engine has failed and they need assistance, though no one's life is in immediate danger.

anchor: There's a big floating log in the channel near the north buoy, everyone watch out.
positive: Securite, Securite, Securite, all stations, hazard to navigation, large log adrift near the north channel buoy.

anchor: Prudonce
positive: Spoken form of the French 'prudence,' announced late in a distress situation to allow restricted, essential working on the channel while full silence is relaxed.

anchor: in what order do mayday pan pan and securite rank
positive: Mayday is top: grave and imminent danger. Pan-Pan is next: urgent, but no immediate threat to life. Securite carries safety information like weather or hazards and ranks third.

anchor: Right ten degrees rudder.
positive: The conning officer orders ten degrees of starboard rudder; the helmsman repeats it, applies it and reports when the rudder is at ten.

anchor: steady as she goes
positive: Keep the ship on whatever heading it's on at this moment; the helmsman notes that heading and holds it.

anchor: midships aye rudder is amidships
positive: The helmsman repeats the order to center the rudder and reports it's now at zero angle.

anchor: Conn
positive: Control of the ship's movements. 'I have the conn' tells the bridge team who is giving helm and engine orders, and every handoff is announced aloud.

anchor: Captain, I'm ready to hand over the watch; we're on course two-seven-zero and nothing's nearby.
positive: Captain, OOW, ready to be relieved, steady on two-seven-zero, no contacts.

anchor: Northern Star, this is tug Resolute, propose one-whistle passing, port to port.
positive: The tug asks the other vessel to agree that they pass with port sides facing each other, the arrangement signaled by one short blast.

anchor: Helmsmen repeat every helm order out loud, why?
positive: Repetition lets the conning officer catch a mishearing, like port for starboard, before the rudder moves. It's the maritime counterpart of a pilot's readback.

anchor: mark your head
positive: Tell me the exact heading the ship is on right now.

anchor: CPA
positive: Closest point of approach: the predicted minimum distance between two vessels on their present courses. Bridge teams call it out to judge whether a crossing is risky.

anchor: Plain language
positive: The US National Incident Management System calls for plain English rather than ten-codes at multi-agency incidents, because codes differ between departments and caused confusion when agencies worked together.

anchor: size-up
positive: First assessment given by the first-arriving unit: building type, what's visible, hazards and initial actions. It shapes what every unit still en route does.

anchor: Engine Seven on scene, two-story wood frame, smoke showing from the second floor, Engine Seven establishing Maple Street Command.
positive: The first engine gives its size-up, a two-story wooden house with smoke upstairs, and its officer takes command, naming the incident after the street.

anchor: Incident Commander
positive: IC: the single person in overall charge of an incident under ICS. Addressed on the radio simply as 'Command' or by the incident name.

anchor: CAN report
positive: Conditions, Actions, Needs: quick format for updating command on what a crew sees, what it's doing and what help it wants.

anchor: command division two we got heavy heat on the bravo side need another line
positive: The division two supervisor tells the incident commander there's intense heat on side B of the building and asks for an additional hoseline.

anchor: engine nine staging at the corner of fifth and oak
positive: Engine 9 tells command it has arrived and is waiting, uncommitted, at Fifth and Oak until it gets an assignment.

anchor: why do firefighters call the sides of a building alpha bravo charlie delta
positive: It gives everyone the same reference: Alpha is usually the address side, then clockwise Bravo, Charlie, Delta. 'Fire on the Charlie side' means the same wall to every crew.

anchor: I'm handing control of this fire over to the battalion chief who just pulled up.
positive: Engine Seven to Battalion Two, transfer of command, Battalion Two now has Maple Street Command.

anchor: LCES
positive: Wildland fire safety system: Lookouts, Communications, Escape routes and Safety zones. Crews confirm all four are in place before engaging a fire.

anchor: Emergency traffic
positive: Phrase that clears the radio for an urgent message such as an evacuation order or collapse warning. Everyone else stops transmitting at once.

anchor: Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, Ladder Four, firefighter Diaz, lost on floor three, Charlie side.
positive: A firefighter declares a life-threatening emergency: Diaz from Ladder 4 is disoriented on the third floor at the rear of the building. All other traffic stops.

anchor: LUNAR
positive: Mnemonic for a firefighter Mayday: Location, Unit, Name, Assignment, Resources needed. Gets the key facts to rescuers fast.

anchor: PAR
positive: Personnel Accountability Report: each company officer confirms all their members are accounted for. Command calls for one after a Mayday, a collapse or a change in strategy.

anchor: command engine twelve par four
positive: Engine 12's officer tells command that all four crew members are accounted for.

anchor: RIT
positive: Rapid Intervention Team, also called RIC: a crew standing by on scene whose only job is rescuing firefighters in trouble.

anchor: Everybody get out of the building right now, the roof might come down.
positive: Emergency traffic, emergency traffic, all units evacuate the structure, I say again, evacuate, report PAR once out.

anchor: What does switching from offensive to defensive mean on a fireground radio?
positive: Offensive means crews are inside putting the fire out; defensive means everyone works from outside and protects nearby exposures. Announcing the switch ensures nobody is left inside when the strategy changes.

anchor: Ladder Four, Command, we have your Mayday, RIT is on the way to floor three, Charlie side.
positive: The incident commander acknowledges the Mayday and tells the trapped firefighter the rescue team is heading to their location.

anchor: Overwatch
positive: A position from which one element watches over another's movement, ready to warn or support. Calls such as 'overwatch has you' reassure the moving group.

anchor: overwatch eyes on second team there at the gate
positive: The watching element confirms it can see the second team and reports they've reached the gate.

anchor: eyes on
positive: Having direct visual contact with someone or something, as in 'eyes on the vehicle'; it tells the team someone is actually watching, not just aware of it.

anchor: Let's stop for a second, everybody kneel down and watch outward while I check the map.
positive: Security halt, all-around, two minutes.

anchor: LP/OP
positive: Listening post and observation post: small positions placed forward of a larger group for early warning. An OP watches, an LP listens, usually at night.

anchor: OP two, relief in place complete, next check-in at oh-two-hundred.
positive: The observation post's fresh team has taken over from the old one and will report again at 02:00.

anchor: what does nstr stand for
positive: Nothing Significant To Report. Used in routine check-ins to show a station is alive and watching but has nothing new.

anchor: Can you keep an eye on us from the hill while we cross the field?
positive: Request overwatch from the hilltop during our crossing, over.

anchor: Lost visual on Two, last seen moving into the tree line.
positive: We can no longer see team two; when we last did, they were heading into the woods.

anchor: Flight, EECOM.
positive: A controller hailing the Flight Director on the main loop, listener first and caller second. Flight answers 'Go, EECOM' and the controller states the issue in a sentence or two.

anchor: Go, GNC.
positive: The Flight Director's reply to a hail from the guidance and navigation controller, giving them the floor to speak on the flight loop.

anchor: Flight, Surgeon, recommend we push tomorrow's wake-up an hour after tonight's late EVA.
positive: The flight surgeon advises the Flight Director to shift the crew's schedule so they get enough rest after a long spacewalk day.

anchor: Flight, INCO, heads up, we'll lose Ku for about two minutes during the antenna handover.
positive: The communications officer warns the Flight Director that the high-rate data and video link will drop for roughly two minutes while it switches over.

anchor: All flight controllers, Flight, let's keep the loop quiet through the next twenty minutes.
positive: The Flight Director asks every console to hold non-essential calls on the main loop during a critical stretch.

anchor: flight eecom stand by one ill have an answer for you shortly
positive: The environmental and electrical controller asks the Flight Director to wait briefly while they work out the answer.

anchor: Flight, PAO, we'd like to carry the crew's next call live on the broadcast.
positive: Public affairs asks the Flight Director's approval to air the upcoming air-to-ground conversation to the public.

anchor: how many voice loops does a flight controller listen to at once
positive: Often several, set to different volumes: their own position's loop and the Flight loop loudest, support loops and air-to-ground lower. Picking your call sign out of that mix is a core skill.

anchor: What is the 'back room' in mission control?
positive: Support rooms behind the main control room, staffed by specialists who advise each front-room controller on separate loops. That keeps detailed engineering talk off the Flight Director's loop.

anchor: Why do mission control console names like FIDO and EECOM sound so odd?
positive: They are compact position call signs, many dating from Mercury and Apollo: FIDO for the flight dynamics officer, EECOM for the electrical and environmental systems officer. Being unique words, they cut through a crowded loop.

anchor: Hey boss, I need to tell you something about the cooling system when you've got a second.
positive: Flight, ETHOS, when you're ready.

anchor: Flight, FDO, nothing new, data looks nominal, no action required.
positive: The trajectory officer tells the Flight Director that everything in their area is as expected and nothing needs doing.

anchor: CAPCOM
positive: Capsule Communicator: the mission control position that talks directly with the crew, traditionally staffed by an astronaut. The name dates from Project Mercury, when the spacecraft was a one-person capsule.

anchor: Why is CAPCOM usually an astronaut?
positive: Astronauts know the vehicle and the crew's workload and can phrase requests the way a crewmate would. That builds trust and cuts misunderstandings.

anchor: can anyone besides capcom ever talk straight to the crew
positive: Sometimes, with the Flight Director's okay: flight surgeons hold private medical conferences, and specialists may join a call to troubleshoot hardware. Routine direction still flows through CAPCOM.

anchor: Station, Houston on Space to Ground One, we'd like to talk about the afternoon timeline when you've got a minute.
positive: CAPCOM calls the ISS crew on the first voice loop to discuss schedule changes, without asking for an immediate reply.

anchor: houston station we're ready for your words go ahead
positive: Crew to CAPCOM: they're free to listen now and invite the ground to pass the information.

anchor: What does CAPCOM mean by 'we have some words for you'?
positive: ISS shorthand for a short spoken briefing, such as background on a procedure change or an answer to a crew question. The crew picks a convenient moment to take it.

anchor: The engineers want you to hold off on that last step until they double-check something.
positive: Station, Houston, request you hold at step six while the team reviews; we'll call you back shortly.

anchor: Houston, Station, we're picking up a lot of background noise on your end, someone may have a hot mic.
positive: Extra noise is coming through on the ground's transmissions, and the crew suspects someone in Mission Control has left a microphone open.

anchor: CAPCOM, Flight, go ahead and pass up the new time for the press event.
positive: The Flight Director authorizes CAPCOM to tell the crew the updated schedule for a media event.

anchor: houston we didnt catch your last can you repeat after the tdrs handover
positive: The crew missed the previous transmission and suggests repeating it once the relay satellite switch is done and the link improves.

anchor: Station, Houston, nothing for you, just checking in, enjoy your lunch.
positive: Courtesy call from CAPCOM with no tasks attached, letting the crew know the ground has nothing pending.

anchor: Eurocom
positive: ESA's counterpart to CAPCOM, talking to crews from the Columbus Control Centre in Germany, mostly about European modules and experiments.

anchor: GO/NO-GO poll
positive: Roll call where the Flight Director or launch director asks each console in turn whether its systems and team are ready. Each answers go or no-go; a single no-go stops things until it's resolved.

anchor: Retro? Go! FIDO? Go! Guidance? Go!
positive: Fragment of the Apollo 11 landing poll: each controller in turn confirms their area supports continuing, giving Gene Kranz a fast, unambiguous answer.

anchor: Why do controllers answer a poll with a single word?
positive: A poll has to finish in seconds. One word is easy to hear and hard to misread; any nuance gets discussed before or after, not during.

anchor: what happens if one console says no go
positive: The process stops. The Flight Director asks what's wrong, and the team either fixes it, accepts it with a documented rationale, or holds and recycles the procedure.

anchor: flight surgeon is go
positive: The flight surgeon's answer in a poll: from a medical standpoint, the activity can proceed.

anchor: Okay everyone, are we all ready to let them head outside?
positive: All flight controllers, Flight, go/no-go for EVA egress.

anchor: Station, Houston, you are go for depress.
positive: Ground tells the crew all teams agree they may begin lowering the airlock pressure ahead of a spacewalk.

anchor: Who runs the launch-day poll for an Artemis launch?
positive: NASA's Launch Director at Kennedy polls the launch team and gives the final go; once the rocket clears the tower, control passes to the Flight Director in Houston.

anchor: flight eva were no go we need another look at the tether config
positive: The spacewalk officer can't approve proceeding yet; the team wants to review how the safety lines are arranged.

anchor: OPS PLAN, go. ROBO, go. EVA, go. Surgeon, go.
positive: A quick sweep of station consoles, each giving a one-word go; the Flight Director then relays the decision to the crew through CAPCOM.

anchor: We're in a hold while EVA looks at the data; expect to recycle back to step three.
positive: Things are paused while the spacewalk team reviews information, and the procedure will likely restart from step three.
