anchor: is go in a poll the same as saying roger
positive: No. Roger only says a message was received; go says your area is ready and you support proceeding. A controller who heard the plan but has a concern answers no-go, not roger.

anchor: EV1
positive: Lead spacewalker, extravehicular crewmember one. On ISS EV1 traditionally wears the suit with red stripes so the ground can tell the two apart on video.

anchor: IV
positive: Intravehicular crewmember: the astronaut inside who choreographs the spacewalk, reads procedure steps, tracks the timeline and helps the spacewalkers through the airlock.

anchor: EV1, IV, when you're at the worksite let me know and we'll pick up at step twelve.
positive: The inside crewmember asks the lead spacewalker to say when in place so they can resume the procedure at step twelve.

anchor: ev2 here im at the handrail just aft of the hatch
positive: Second spacewalker reports holding a handrail just behind the hatch, so the IV and ground can keep track of them.

anchor: why do spacewalkers have stripes on their suits
positive: Two suited astronauts look almost identical on camera. Stripes on one suit, a practice going back to Apollo commanders, let the ground and IV tell who is who instantly.

anchor: What does the IV say compared with what CAPCOM says during a spacewalk?
positive: The IV walks the spacewalkers through the step-by-step script, while CAPCOM brings in ground decisions and changes. They coordinate so the crew never hears two conflicting instructions.

anchor: The person inside is going to read you the next few instructions now.
positive: EV1, EV2, IV, I'll read you the next block of steps, call when ready.

anchor: EV1 has the lead, EV2 will follow on the starboard side.
positive: The first spacewalker goes first and the second comes behind along the right-hand side of the station.

anchor: Houston, IV, both crewmembers are out of the airlock and on their safety tethers.
positive: The inside crewmember tells the ground that both spacewalkers have exited and are attached by their tethers.

anchor: iv ev1 im gonna need a second set of eyes on this connector
positive: Lead spacewalker asks the inside crewmember to look closely at the helmet camera view and help check a connector.

anchor: On Apollo moonwalks, who talked to whom?
positive: Commander and lunar module pilot both spoke directly with CAPCOM in Houston, who relayed requests from the science back room. There was no IV; the command module pilot stayed in lunar orbit.

anchor: EV2, EV1, I've got the bag, you're clear to let go.
positive: Lead spacewalker confirms they now hold the equipment bag, so the second spacewalker can release it safely: a handoff made explicit by voice.

anchor: Why do spacewalkers keep their calls so short?
positive: Everyone shares one loop: two spacewalkers, the IV and CAPCOM. Long transmissions block others, including a call that might matter for safety, so terse reports are the norm.

anchor: ev2 you stepped on houston say your last again
positive: One crewmember points out that the second spacewalker transmitted over the ground, garbling both, and asks for the call to be repeated.

anchor: ev1 ev2 hold your call houston is talking
positive: One spacewalker tells the other to wait, because the ground is transmitting and speaking now would block it.

anchor: Houston, EV2, I'll be quiet for a minute while I work this bolt.
positive: Second spacewalker warns the ground they'll go silent while concentrating on a tough task, so the silence won't be read as trouble.

anchor: During an EVA, what's a 'verify' call?
positive: Before an irreversible step, crew and ground confirm out loud, say that a tether hook is closed. 'Verify' asks the other side to check and state the result, not merely acknowledge.

anchor: EV1, IV, verify local tether hook closed and locked before you release the other.
positive: The inside crewmember asks the lead spacewalker to check and confirm one safety tether is secure before letting go of the second, so they're never untethered.

anchor: Wait, two people are talking at once and I can't make out either of you.
positive: Two stations transmitting, one at a time, EV1 first.

anchor: why do spacewalkers narrate what theyre doing even when nobody asked
positive: The ground and IV can't always see clearly. Brief narration such as 'moving to the next handrail' keeps everyone's mental picture current and lets them catch a mistake early.

anchor: ev1 youre weak but readable can you get clear of the truss
positive: The listener hears the lead spacewalker faintly but intelligibly and suggests moving away from station structure that may be blocking the radio signal.

anchor: Cuff checklist
positive: Small flip book worn on a spacewalker's sleeve with key procedures and reminders, a fallback when voice contact with the IV or ground is lost.

anchor: What do spacewalkers do if they lose voice contact with the ground?
positive: They first rely on the IV aboard the station. If that link goes too, they follow pre-briefed lost-comm rules, typically pausing work in a safe configuration until contact returns.

anchor: How come the ground goes quiet while spacewalkers handle tricky tasks?
positive: Every word competes for attention and for the shared loop. Ground saves non-urgent items for a natural pause, and the crew can ask for a quiet loop when they need to focus.

anchor: LOS
positive: Loss of Signal: the moment contact with a spacecraft drops, because it moves out of range, behind a planet or into a coverage gap. Crews and ground plan their conversations around predicted LOS times.

anchor: What does AOS mean in a mission transcript?
positive: Acquisition of Signal: the point where a ground station or relay satellite regains contact with the spacecraft. CAPCOM often makes a call right after AOS to re-establish the conversation.

anchor: why did apollo crews lose radio behind the moon
positive: With the Moon between spacecraft and Earth, the radio path was physically blocked. Every lunar orbit had a predictable blackout, so some critical burns happened out of contact, with tension until AOS.

anchor: Station, Houston, LOS in about five, we'll pick you up on the next TDRS.
positive: CAPCOM warns the crew that the link drops in roughly five minutes and will return through the next relay satellite.

anchor: houston station with you at aos how do you hear
positive: The ISS crew calls as soon as the signal returns and asks how well the ground is receiving them.

anchor: How does the ISS stay in touch with Houston almost all the time now?
positive: NASA's Tracking and Data Relay Satellites in geostationary orbit relay voice and data, giving near-continuous coverage instead of brief passes over individual ground stations.

anchor: Houston, Station, Ku's back, we have your uplink video again.
positive: High-rate link is back: the ground's video feed is showing on board once more.

anchor: We're about to lose you for a few minutes, talk to you on the other side.
positive: Station, Houston, LOS in one minute, see you at AOS.

anchor: Houston has you for another eight minutes this pass.
positive: The ground can stay in contact for about eight more minutes before this coverage window closes.

anchor: whats a comm gap on the station timeline
positive: A planned period without relay coverage, marked on the schedule so the crew doesn't start anything needing ground support right before it. Gaps are much shorter now than in the early station years.

anchor: Houston, Station, we'll hold that until after the gap, nothing urgent.
positive: The crew decides to wait until coverage returns to discuss an item and reassures the ground it isn't pressing.

anchor: We've lost the video feed, but we can still hear you fine.
positive: Houston, Station, lost Ku video, still have you on S-band voice.

anchor: what is a challenge and response checklist
positive: One person reads an item, the challenge, and another states its actual condition, the response, such as 'Hatch, closed.' Two people agreeing out loud catches slips that one would miss.

anchor: Panel one-oh-one, circuit breaker three, verify closed. Closed.
positive: One crewmember names a specific breaker and asks for it to be checked; the other confirms it's in the closed position.

anchor: both of you release on my mark tree two one mark
positive: The leader counts down so both people act at the same instant, on the word 'mark'.

anchor: Why say the switch name back instead of just 'done'?
positive: Echoing the item proves you acted on the right one. 'Done' shows you did something; 'fuel cell two, on' shows you did the correct thing.

anchor: Why do crews read checklists aloud even when working alone?
positive: Speaking each item forces attention onto it and leaves an audible record for others to catch errors. It's a defense against skipping a line out of habit.

anchor: Okay, I've finished that page, what's next?
positive: Page four done, ready for page five.

anchor: reading step six configure for ingress ev2 call when your stowed
positive: The reader announces step six, preparations for coming back inside, and asks the second spacewalker to report once their gear is put away.

anchor: IV, EV1, bag latched; reading back, two latches closed, strap secured.
positive: Lead spacewalker confirms the equipment bag is fastened and repeats the specifics so the inside crewmember can match them against the procedure.

anchor: Ever heard of a pen-and-ink change to a procedure? What is it?
positive: A handwritten correction to a printed procedure, radioed up from the ground. The crew reads it back word for word so both sides' copies match before it's used.

anchor: read-do versus do-verify checklists, how do they differ
positive: In read-do, each item is read and then performed in order; in do-verify, the crew performs the steps from memory or flow and then runs the checklist to confirm nothing was missed.

anchor: Houston, Station, we skipped step four by mistake, going back to it now.
positive: The crew reports it missed a procedure step and is returning to do it before moving on.

anchor: Before you do anything, tell me which switch you're touching.
positive: Call the switch before you throw it.

anchor: Roger, Twan... Tranquility, we copy you on the ground. You got a bunch of guys about to turn blue.
positive: CAPCOM Charlie Duke acknowledging the Apollo 11 landing, tripping over the brand-new call sign and joking that controllers had been holding their breath.

anchor: Why did Armstrong call 'Tranquility Base' instead of 'Eagle' after landing?
positive: Once down, the crew switched to a call sign for the surface site. The change itself told everyone they had landed, and Charlie Duke's stumble over the new name shows how fresh it was on the loop.

anchor: Why does 'Roger' appear constantly in Apollo transcripts?
positive: It confirmed a message had been received. Crews and CAPCOMs used it all the time, often followed by a readback of numbers that proved they'd heard them correctly.

anchor: houston apollo ready to copy the pad
positive: Forms out and pencils ready, the crew tells the ground it can start reading up the block of numbers.

anchor: PAD
positive: Pre-Advisory Data, sometimes expanded as Preliminary Advisory Data: blocks of numbers such as burn times and attitudes that CAPCOM read up for the crew to copy onto preprinted forms, then read back to confirm.

anchor: why are there long pauses in apollo moon audio
positive: Light-time delay: radio takes about 1.3 seconds each way between Earth and the Moon, so a reply came at least 2.6 seconds later, longer if the crew was busy.

anchor: Columbia, Houston, you are go for TEI.
positive: Mission control clears the Apollo command module crew to fire the burn that leaves lunar orbit and starts the trip home.

anchor: VOX
positive: Voice-operated transmission: the mic keys itself when someone speaks. Apollo crews switched between VOX and push-to-talk, since VOX could pick up breathing and clip first syllables.

anchor: The Eagle has wings.
positive: The lunar module has separated from the command module and is now flying on its own.

anchor: houston apollo eleven lots of static on your end want us on omni
positive: The crew reports a noisy signal and asks whether the ground wants them to switch to the wide-coverage omnidirectional antenna.

anchor: Houston, Station on Space to Ground Two for a comm check.
positive: The ISS crew calls Mission Control on the second voice loop to test the link; the expected answer is something like 'loud and clear.'

anchor: Station
positive: Call sign the ISS crew uses toward Houston, whichever astronaut is speaking. 'Station, Houston' means Houston is calling the crew.

anchor: who is moscow on iss radio
positive: Russian Mission Control near Moscow, also called TsUP from its Russian acronym. ISS crews talk with both Houston and Moscow depending on the segment and the task.

anchor: What language is spoken on ISS voice loops?
positive: English is the working language with Houston and among partners, while Russian is used with Moscow; most long-duration crewmembers speak both.

anchor: How does Houston keep in touch with an Orion crew out near the Moon?
positive: Through NASA's Deep Space Network, big antennas in California, Spain and Australia spaced so that one of them can always see the spacecraft as Earth turns.

anchor: station houston were losing your first words try pausing a beat after you key
positive: The ground keeps missing the start of each crew transmission and asks the speaker to wait a moment after pressing push-to-talk before talking.

anchor: Station, Houston, we've got your request, we'll work it on the ground and get back to you this afternoon.
positive: Ground acknowledges a crew request, says engineers will study it and promises an answer later in the day.

anchor: Everyone up here is awake, fed and ready to start today's work.
positive: Houston, Station, good morning, crew is up and ready for the DPC.

anchor: What is the DPC on the ISS?
positive: Daily Planning Conference: a scheduled call at the start and end of the workday where crew and control centers review the plan and open questions.

anchor: Station, Houston, we see you on the downlink, you're clear to proceed.
positive: Mission Control can watch you on the video feed and you can go ahead with the next action.

anchor: Why does NASA say 'loud and clear' rather than 'five by five'?
positive: Plain words carry better across a mixed audience of engineers, international partners and public listeners, so NASA crews and controllers favor 'loud and clear' over military or ham shorthand.
